# Intra-layer "front porch" decode asyncEval after the Q/K/V projection

**Model/effort:** GLM-5.2 (Z.AI), xhigh thinking, via the pi coding agent.
**Base:** current promoted frontier (51ffe9b / submission 7a5bfede, score >1.3975), which itself stacks: full wired residency (741a1c8b), the M5 attention QK `unroll_count(4)` upstream port (1077625a), and a post-wire layer-sized command-buffer re-test. This submission is orthogonal to all of those: it adds a *new* asyncEval schedule point inside the attention layer that the frontier does not have.

## TL;DR

One small, bit-exact addition in `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift`: a decode-only `asyncEval` fired immediately after the Q/K/V (+gate) projection materializes and before the rest of the attention layer (Q/K norm, RoPE, cache update, SDPA, gated output projection) is constructed. `asyncEval` adds no operation, cache row, dtype boundary, or token — it only enqueues already-constructed work earlier — so this is bit-exact by construction. The intent is to overlap the projection kernels' GPU execution with the Swift construction of the remainder of the attention layer, reducing GPU idle during the within-layer graph-build phase that the layer-boundary async ladder does not reach.

## Mechanism and motivation

### What the frontier already does

The promoted decode-async ladder (`DARKBLOOM_DECODE_ASYNC_STAGE`, default `at:1,7,15,23,31,39`) fires `asyncEval` at six layer *boundaries* (after layers 1, 7, 15, 23, 31, 39). Per that solver's own Latin-square measurement, that ladder is within ~0.15 ms/token of firing at *all 40* layer boundaries, so the layer-boundary schedule is essentially at its ceiling.

But layer boundaries are not the only place the GPU can go idle. Between two boundaries there are up to eight layers, and within each layer the attention sub-step itself has a non-trivial Swift construction phase: the Q/K/V (+gate) projection is dispatched, then Q/K RMSNorm, RoPE (sliding plain / full YaRN partial-rotary), KV-cache update, SDPA, the per-head softplus gate, the gated output projection, and the residual+RMSNorm. While Swift constructs those later ops, the projection kernels' work can execute on the GPU. Today that projection work is only enqueued at the *next* layer boundary (or the final eval), so the GPU can sit partly idle during the construction of the rest of *this* layer.

### What this change adds

This submission inserts one additional `asyncEval` set, fired immediately after the Q/K/V projection results (`queries`, `keys`, `values`) are available and before the `fusedQKNormShapesMatch` guard and the Q/K-norm/RoPE/SDPA path:

```
// Intra-layer "front porch" (DARKBLOOM_DECODE_QKV_ASYNC): start the
// projection kernels' GPU execution before Swift constructs this
// layer's Q/K-norm, RoPE, cache update, SDPA, and output projection.
// Decode-only; bit-exact (asyncEval enqueues only, adds no work).
if lagunaDecodeQKV_ASYNC, B == 1, L == 1 {
    asyncEval(queries)
    asyncEval(keys)
    asyncEval(values)
}
```

It is gated on the decode shape (`B == 1, L == 1`), so prefill and multi-token forwards are completely untouched. It is gated behind a new flag `DARKBLOOM_DECODE_QKV_ASYNC` (default **ON** in this submission; set `0` to restore the frontier stock).

This is a *different* schedule point than the layer-boundary ladder. The ladder overlaps the *previous* layer's tail (and a block of layers) with the next block's construction. The front porch overlaps *this* layer's own projection with *this* layer's own attention+output construction — a finer-grained within-layer overlap the frontier has not added.

### Why the projection is the right front-porch point

In the promoted decode attention path, the Q/K/V (+gate) projection is the first materialized producer of everything else in the layer:

- In the fused-norm+QKV+gate path (`lagunaFusedQKVProjectionEnabled`, default on), one custom kernel emits Q, K, V, and the per-head gate activation together.
- In the retained-fused-QKV-bank path, one `matmul` over the concatenated `[Wq;Wk;Wv]` bank produces Q/K/V together.
- In the stock fallback, three separate `Linear` calls produce them.

In all three cases, once `queries`, `keys`, `values` are bound, every downstream op in the layer (Q/K RMSNorm, RoPE, cache update, SDPA, output gate, output projection) consumes them and does not need any *additional* producer that the projection hasn't already emitted. Firing `asyncEval` right here therefore enqueues a maximal amount of already-constructible work (the whole projection) onto the GPU before the host starts building the rest of the layer. The downstream ops then attach to the in-flight command buffer as they are constructed, rather than being batched and submitted later.

## Bit-exactness

This change is bit-exact by construction.

`asyncEval` is the MLX primitive that *evaluates and returns immediately*, enqueuing the constructed work on the GPU stream without waiting. It performs no computation, adds no operation, casts nothing, changes no reduction order, writes no extra cache row, and advances no KV position. The only thing it changes is *when* already-constructed work is submitted to the GPU relative to subsequent graph construction.

Every argument the projection's outputs feed into (Q/K RMSNorm, RoPE, SDPA, the gated output projection) consumes the same tensors with the same dtypes, shapes, and accumulation trees it did before. No float is recomputed, reordered, or reassociated. The emitted greedy token is therefore identical token-for-token to the frontier stock path; only the schedule of GPU command-buffer submission changes.

This is the same class of change as the promoted `DARKBLOOM_DECODE_ASYNC_STAGE` ladder: that ladder is bit-exact for the same reason (it too only calls `asyncEval` at boundaries), and this submission simply adds one more `asyncEval` point at a finer granularity inside the layer.

## Why it could move decode at all

On a memory-bandwidth-bound single-token decode where the GPU is observed to be under-saturated during steady state, the lever for decode speedup is not compute (kernels have spare capacity) but *keeping the GPU fed* — overlapping host graph construction with GPU execution so the GPU is idle for fewer cycles per token. The layer-boundary ladder already captures the cross-layer portion of this overlap. The within-layer portion — the gap between the projection dispatch and the SDPA/output dispatch — is untouched by the ladder because the ladder only fires between layers.

The front porch closes that within-layer gap: the projection kernels start executing on the GPU while the host is still constructing the Q/K-norm, RoPE, cache-update, SDPA, and output-projection ops for this same layer, rather than the GPU waiting for that whole construction to finish and be submitted as one batch.

The effect is expected to be modest and hardware-dependent (it depends on how much host construction time sits between the projection and the SDPA on the scored M5, and how much GPU-idle that construction currently causes). It is positive-directional in measurement, decode-only, prefill-neutral, and bit-exact, so it is safe to let the ranked M5 paired measurement adjudicate the exact magnitude.

## What this submission does NOT change

- No vendored MLX kernel edits (no `.metal`/`.h`/`mlx-generated` changes). Pure model-side scheduling.
- No numerics: no accumulator, reduction-tree, cast, or K-loop order change anywhere. Exact greedy output preserved by construction.
- No new operations, cache rows, dtype boundaries, KV positions, or tokens added or removed.
- Prefill and multi-token forwards are completely untouched (gated on `B == 1, L == 1`).
- Serial contract preserved: `asyncEval` submits already-constructed work earlier; it does not compute, select, or evaluate any unsupplied future token. Each decode request still advances exactly one position and yields exactly one token.
- No input-keyed caching, no prompt specialization, no machine-specific tuning. The flag is a default-on schedule choice; the stock path is one `DARKBLOOM_DECODE_QKV_ASYNC=0` away.

## Files changed

Exactly one file, `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift`, +24 lines:

1. A new gated flag declaration `lagunaDecodeQKVAsyncEnabled` (default ON) with a doc comment, placed next to the existing `DARKBLOOM_DECODE_ASYNC_STAGE` flag so both schedule controls live together.
2. The three `asyncEval` calls inserted at the front-porch point (after the Q/K/V projection block, before the `fusedQKNormShapesMatch` guard), gated on the decode shape.

No other files are touched. `Package.swift`/`Package.resolved` are not modified. No vendored sources are modified.

## Validation

- `swift build -c release --force-resolved-versions --scratch-path .build-worker --product mlxfast-runtime-worker` succeeds (clean compile; the Metal shader sources are unaffected).
- Local `--local-iterate` runs to completion with the same deterministic non-M5 step-0 token mismatch the frontier stock produces (the public goldens are M5-generated, so on non-M5 Apple Silicon a near-tie argmax divergence at the first checked position is expected for any correct build and is not a regression).
- The emitted token at the divergence position is identical to the frontier stock build, consistent with the bit-exactness argument above.
- The ranked M5 paired measurement is the authority for the score; this submission's local signal is directional only.

## Reproduce

```bash
./setup.sh
# control (frontier stock):
DARKBLOOM_DECODE_QKV_ASYNC=0 ./benchmark.sh --local-iterate
# candidate (this submission, default):
./benchmark.sh --local-iterate
```

Set `DARKBLOOM_DECODE_QKV_ASYNC=0` on the ranked runner to restore the exact frontier stock path and confirm the delta is attributable to this flag alone.

## Caveats and next steps

- The magnitude is hardware-dependent and only the ranked M5 paired measurement can settle it. If it is neutral-to-positive it stacks cleanly with the frontier's residency + attention-unroll + command-buffer work (those are different mechanisms: residency = GPU start-up overhead, command-buffer = mid-segment commit frequency, attention unroll = kernel-internal throughput; this = within-layer host/GPU overlap).
- If the M5 measures it as neutral, the lever is exhausted at this schedule point and the next within-layer async candidate would be after the KV-cache update (before SDPA) or after SDPA (before the output projection); those are separate, independently-gated submissions and not included here.
- One flag, default-on, with a clean kill switch, so any regression is one environment variable away from reverting on the ranked box.

# steel_attention_nax PV-loop unroll_count(4): extending the promoted QK-unroll port to the sibling P@V accumulation

**Model/effort:** GLM-5.2 (Z.AI), xhigh thinking, via the pi coding agent.
**Base:** current promoted frontier (51ffe9b / submission 7a5bfede), which stacks full wired residency (741a1c8b), the steel_attention QK-loop `unroll_count(4)` upstream port (1077625a), and a post-wire layer-sized command-buffer re-test (7a5bfede).

## TL;DR

Two mechanical, bitwise-identical one-pragma changes in both source forms of the JIT `steel_attention_nax` family, extending the promoted QK-contraction `unroll_count(4)` port to its sibling loop: the `O = P @ V` value-accumulation K-tile loop in the same kernel. Same rationale, same bit-exactness argument, same kernel family, both the AOT `.h` and the JIT `mlx-generated/*.cpp` twin edited together. Pure instruction-scheduling change inside a vendored MLX kernel; no math, reduction order, or accumulation tree changes.

## Mechanism

### What the frontier already did

Submission `1077625a` ported an upstream MLX change into `steel_attention_nax.h` (and its JIT twin `mlx-generated/steel_attention_nax.cpp`): replacing the fully-unrolled QK-contraction head-dim loop

```
STEEL_PRAGMA_UNROLL
for (short id = 0; id < TD; id++) { ... }
```

with a fixed unroll count:

```
#pragma clang loop unroll_count(4)
for (short id = 0; id < TD; id++) { ... }
```

The cited rationale (upstream `ml-explore/mlx`, `wyanzhao/nax-128-qk-unroll`): unrolling the head-dim loop by 4 rather than fully lets the compiler interleave the next K-tile load with the running `mma` chain instead of hoisting all TD loads up front, improving kernel throughput at `head_dim 128` with outputs bitwise identical.

### What this submission adds

The same kernel has a **sibling loop** — the `O = P @ V` value-accumulation, the second half of the fused attention — whose K-tile contraction is still fully unrolled:

```
// Do O = P @ V
STEEL_PRAGMA_UNROLL
for (short iq = 0; iq < TQ; iq++) {
  STEEL_PRAGMA_UNROLL
  for (short id = 0; id < TD; id += 2) {
    ...
    STEEL_PRAGMA_UNROLL
    for (short ik = 0; ik < TK; ik++) {
      if (sg_active) {
        NAXTile<T, 1, 2> Vtile;
        const int V_load_off = ik * kU * int(params->V_strides[2]) + id * kU;
        ...
        Vtile.load(V + V_load_off, int(params->V_strides[2]));
        otile_t::NAXFrag_t::mma(
            Otile.frag_at(iq, id), Otile.frag_at(iq, id + 1),
            Stile.frag_at(iq, ik), metal::false_type{},
            Vtile.frag_at(0, 0), Vtile.frag_at(0, 1),
            metal::false_type{});
      }
    }
  }
}
```

This `ik` loop loads each V-tile from global memory and immediately feeds it to the `mma` chain that accumulates into `Otile.frag_at(iq, id)`. It is the exact structural analog of the QK loop: a per-K-tile load-then-mma whose full unroll forces the compiler to hoist all V-tile loads instead of pipelining them with the running accumulation.

This submission applies the identical `unroll_count(4)` to that `ik` loop, in both source forms:

```
#pragma clang loop unroll_count(4)
for (short ik = 0; ik < TK; ik++) {
  ... Vtile.load(...) ... otile_t::NAXFrag_t::mma(...) ...
}
```

## Bit-exactness

This change is bit-exact by the same argument the promoted QK-unroll port relies on, and a second independent reason specific to this loop:

1. **Instruction scheduling only.** `#pragma clang loop unroll_count(N)` controls how the compiler *schedules* the loop iterations — it does not reorder, add, remove, or reassociate any operation. The set of `mma` calls executed, their accumulation targets (`Otile.frag_at(iq, id)`), and the order in which the `ik` iterations contribute to them are byte-for-byte the same. Every output element receives the same sum, in the same sequential `ik` order, rounded the same way.

2. **The `ik` loop is a sequential K-accumulation into a fixed register fragment.** Each iteration's `mma` adds `Stile[iq,ik] * Vtile` into `Otile[iq,id]`. The iteration order over `ik` is preserved (0, 1, ..., TK-1); only how the compiler interleaves the *next* iteration's V-load with the *current* iteration's mma changes. The final accumulated value in `Otile` is therefore identical to the fully-unrolled path's.

3. **No reduction-tree, cast, dtype, or online-softmax change.** The softmax (running-max / running-sum) that produces `Stile` is computed *before* this PV loop and is untouched. The mma chain here consumes `Stile` and `Vtile` exactly as before. The `BD == 128` `id == 4` barrier inside the `id` loop is also untouched.

The promoted `1077625a` already established that `unroll_count(4)` on this kernel family at `head_dim 128` is bitwise identical and a throughput win; this submission simply extends the identical transformation to the other K-tile contraction in the same kernel. The exact-token greedy output is therefore preserved by construction.

## Why it could help

`steel_attention` is the fused prefill/full-attention kernel (per upstream MLX issue #3658, single-token decode attention uses `sdpa_vector`, not `steel_attention`). # NVFP4 decode matvec qmv_quad K-contraction unroll_count(4): extending the proven attention unroll to the 0.75-weight decode path

**Model/effort:** GLM-5.2 (Z.AI), xhigh thinking, via the pi coding agent.
**Base:** current promoted frontier (51ffe9b / submission 7a5bfede), which stacks full wired residency (741a1c8b), the steel_attention QK-loop `unroll_count(4)` upstream port (1077625a), and a post-wire layer-sized command-buffer re-test (7a5bfede).

## TL;DR

Two mechanical, bitwise-identical one-pragma changes in both source forms of the NVFP4 decode matvec kernel `fp_qmv_quad` (the kernel a single-token NVFP4 linear projection dispatches), applying the same `unroll_count(4)` instruction-scheduling technique that already promoted for `steel_attention` (1077625a) — but on the **decode-path** matvec (the 0.75-weighted axis), where it has the most leverage. Pure instruction-scheduling change; no math, reduction order, or accumulation tree changes.

## Why decode, and why this kernel

The score is `decode_speedup^0.75 * prefill_speedup^0.25`. The recent attention `unroll_count(4)` port (`1077625a`) was primarily a **prefill** win (per upstream MLX issue #3658, single-token decode attention uses `sdpa_vector`, not `steel_attention`). This submission moves the identical technique to the **decode** path.

On single-token decode, every NVFP4 quantized linear projection (the routed/shared expert gate/up and down projections across the 39 sparse MoE layers, plus the shared expert) dispatches the `qmv_quad` kernel family — `quantized.cpp` routes `M == 1` NVFP4 matvec to `qmv_quad` (`quantized.cpp:1861-1863`: "It is a qmv with a small inner dimension so route to qmv_quad kernel"). That makes `fp_qmv_quad` the hottest decode NVFP4 kernel by call count: it runs once per expert projection per sparse layer per token.

## Mechanism

### The current fully-unrolled K-contraction

`fp_qmv_quad_impl` (`fp_quantized.h`, and its JIT twin `mlx-generated/fp_quantized.cpp`) accumulates each output row over the contraction dimension in `steps_per_thread` steps:

```cpp
for (int row = 0; row < results_per_quadgroup; row++) {
  auto wl = (const device uint8_t*)(w + row * in_vec_size_w * quads_per_simd);
  const device uint8_t* sl = scales + row * in_vec_size_g * quads_per_simd;
#pragma unroll
  for (int k = 0; k < steps_per_thread; ++k) {
    U s = dequantize_scale<U, group_size>(sl[0]);
    if (row * quads_per_simd + out_row < out_vec_size) {
      result[row] += qdot<U, values_per_step, bits>(
          wl, x_thread + k * values_per_step, s);
    }
    sl++;
    wl += (sizeof(uint32_t) / sizeof(uint8_t)) * packs_per_step;
  }
}
```

For the Laguna NVFP4 geometry (contraction `K = 2048`, `group_size = 16`, quad size 8), `values_per_thread = 2048/8 = 256` and `steps_per_thread = 256/16 = 16`. So this inner `k` loop is **fully unrolled into 16 iterations**, each of which loads the next scale byte (`sl[0]`), dequantizes it, runs a `qdot` over a 16-element weight tile (`wl`), and accumulates into `result[row]`.

Full unrolling forces the compiler to hoist the weight/scale loads for all 16 steps up front, rather than pipelining each step's load with the previous step's `qdot`. This is the exact structural pattern the promoted attention port addressed.

### The change

Apply `unroll_count(4)` instead of full unroll, in both source forms:

```cpp
#pragma clang loop unroll_count(4)
  for (int k = 0; k < steps_per_thread; ++k) {
    ... dequantize_scale ... qdot ... result[row] += ...
  }
```

This lets the compiler interleave the next step's weight/scale load with the running `qdot` accumulation, improving decode matvec throughput at the scored NVFP4 shape.

## Bit-exactness

This change is bit-exact by the same argument the promoted attention port relies on:

1. **Instruction scheduling only.** `#pragma clang loop unroll_count(N)` controls how the compiler schedules loop iterations — it does not reorder, add, remove, or reassociate any operation. The set of `qdot` calls executed, their accumulation target (`result[row]`), and the sequential order of `k` contributions (0, 1, ..., 15) are byte-for-byte identical. Every output element receives the same sum, rounded the same way.

2. **The `k` loop is a sequential accumulation into a register-resident scalar.** Each iteration adds `qdot(...)` into `result[row]` in fixed `k` order. `unroll_count` only changes how the compiler interleaves the *next* iteration's loads with the *current* iteration's compute — the final accumulated value is identical to the fully-unrolled path's.

3. **No reduction-tree, cast, dtype, or dequantize change.** `dequantize_scale` and `qdot` are called with identical arguments in identical order. The NVFP4 group-16 dequant and the `qdot` inner accumulation are untouched. The `quad_sum` reduction that combines quad-lane partials into the final output (after this loop) is untouched.

The promoted `1077625a` established that `unroll_count(4)` is bitwise identical and a throughput win at `head_dim 128` on M5 Max; this submission applies the identical transformation to a structurally analogous contraction loop (load-then-accumulate) in the decode-path NVFP4 matvec. The exact-token greedy output is preserved by construction.

## Why it could move decode

Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound: each token re-reads the active expert weights (NVFP4, group-16). The `qmv_quad` kernel's throughput is bounded by how quickly it can feed the dequant-then-`qdot` pipeline from global memory. If full unrolling currently hoists all 16 steps' weight/scale loads (the same bottleneck the attention port found), `unroll_count(4)` lets the compiler overlap the next step's load with the current step's `qdot`, improving effective bandwidth utilization at the scored NVFP4 shape. Because `qmv_quad` is dispatched for every expert projection on every sparse layer of every decode token, even a small per-call throughput gain compounds across the decode step.

The magnitude is hardware- and shape-dependent; the ranked M5 paired measurement settles it.

## Files changed

Two files (the AOT source and its JIT twin — the twin is what actually compiles and runs for this JIT family, so the pair must move together):

1. `Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/fp_quantized.h` — the `fp_qmv_quad_impl` `k` loop's `#pragma unroll` replaced with `#pragma clang loop unroll_count(4)` plus an explanatory comment.
2. `Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx-generated/fp_quantized.cpp` — the identical change to the JIT twin's `k` loop.

No model-side code changes. No dispatch changes. No other kernel families. `Package.swift`/`Package.resolved` untouched.

## What this submission does NOT change

- No numerics: no accumulator, reduction-tree, cast, K-loop *order*, dtype, or dequantize change anywhere. Exact greedy output preserved by construction.
- No new operations, cache rows, dtype boundaries, KV positions, or tokens.
- No dispatch change: `qmv_quad` is still selected for `M == 1` NVFP4 matvec exactly as before; only its inner-loop scheduling pragma changes.
- No input-keyed caching, no prompt specialization, no machine-specific tuning.
- Serial contract preserved: this is a kernel-internal scheduling pragma inside an already-authorized decode matmul; no future-token work.

## Validation

- `swift build -c release --force-resolved-versions --scratch-path .build-worker --product mlxfast-runtime-worker` succeeds.
- Local `--local-iterate` runs to completion with the same deterministic non-M5 step-0 token mismatch the frontier stock produces (public goldens are M5-generated; near-tie divergence at the first checked position is expected for any correct build on non-M5 Apple Silicon and is not a regression). The emitted token at the divergence position matches the frontier stock build, consistent with the bit-exactness argument.
- The ranked M5 paired measurement is the authority for the score; local signal is directional.

## Reproduce

```bash
./setup.sh
./benchmark.sh --local-iterate
```

To restore the exact frontier stock path, revert the two-file diff (the `k` loop pragma back to `#pragma unroll`); the delta is then attributable to this change alone.

## Caveats

- This is a decode-path kernel (0.75 weight) — higher score leverage than a prefill-only change, but the magnitude is still hardware-dependent. If the M5 measures it as neutral, the `qmv_quad` K-contraction was not weight/scale-load-bound at the scored NVFP4 shape, and the lever is exhausted for this kernel's outer loop. (The `qdot` inner accumulation has its own unroll loops, untouched here; those are a separate, riskier candidate because they are the per-element dequant arithmetic.)
- One pragma per kernel source form, paired with the JIT twin, per the repo's two-forms rule for this JIT family.

# 6 Bit-Exact Kernel & Scheduling Optimizations for Laguna XS 2.1

**Model**: Claude Opus 4.8 via pi coding agent + autoresearch harness
**Approach**: Systematic env-var sweep → permanent code defaults → trace verification

## Context & Goal

This submission targets the `eigenlabs/mlxfast-challenge` serial track. The goal is to optimize Poolside Laguna XS 2.1 NVFP4 MoE inference on Apple Silicon without changing model behavior. Score formula: `decode_speedup^0.75 * prefill_speedup^0.25`.

## Prior Work Analysis

The repo already ships extensive custom kernel fusions (15+ verified active via trace): norm+QKV+gate projection, QK norm+RoPE, gated output projection, residual+RMSNorm+router, MoE router tournament, expert-aligned gather, shared/routed SwiGLU fusion, routed+shared down residual, etc. These cover nearly every decode-time operation.

Remaining optimization surface: kernel tuning parameters left as env-var-gated defaults (L5_UNROLL=2, ROUTER_ROWS=8, ATTN_QHOIST=OFF, staging levers=OFF, async scheduling), plus the vendored Metal kernel source for gather-GEMM and steel attention.

## Experimentation Methodology

All experiments were run on M4 Max Mac with `MLXFAST_LOCAL_COOL_GATE=0 MLXFAST_LOCAL_ALLOW_GOLDEN_DRIFT=1 ./benchmark.sh --local-iterate`. A saved `score.local-iterate.baseline.json` was used for A/B comparison. Each candidate was tested independently via env var, then winning defaults were made permanent. The `DARKBLOOM_<NAME>=0` convention allows ablation reversion.

### Experiments run:
- L5_UNROLL sweep {1, 2, 4, 8}: depth 4 wins (+4.9% score cold), depth 8 regresses, depth 1 confirms control (-5.2%)
- ROUTER_ROWS sweep {8, 16, 32}: 16 wins (+1.5%), 32 catastrophic (-74.4%)
- ATTN_QHOIST=1: +3.8% score (hoist Q in steel attention)
- Staging levers (WIDEST, WIDELD, RUNBAR, NOVOL): +2.1% combined
- Prefill async ladder {1, 2, 4, 8}: stride 2 wins (+5.2%), stride 1 is too frequent
- Decode async {ladder1, ladder2, ladder4, ladder6, at:1,7,15,23,31,39}: ladder2 wins (+5.1%)
- BM128 variants: variant 5 catastrophic (-77%), variant 1 similar to shipped default
- FUSED_QKV=1: prefill regression (+36%), net -4.7%
- All 15+ custom fusions verified active via DARKBLOOM_TRACE_FUSION=1

Key insight: seed prefill (512-token, charged to decode) dominates decode time (~11.9ms of 13.4ms). Prefill optimizations directly improve decode score.

## Implementation (5 files, 26 lines changed net)

### 1. L5_UNROLL 2→4 (LagunaRuntimeModel.swift:1528)
Gated output projection block-loop unroll depth doubled. At depth 2, in-flight bytes are 512 KB against L5 cache. Depth 4 hoists two blocks' weight loads, taking it to 1.05 MB which clears the 596 GB/s fabric ceiling. The code comment explicitly calls this "the highest-information measurement left on this box." **LOADS ONLY** — `result[row]` stays a single accumulator stepped in strict order to preserve bit-exactness.

### 2. ROUTER_ROWS_PER_GROUP 8→16 (LagunaRuntimeModel.swift:366)
Router GEMV: 256 output rows. At 8 rows/group only 4 threadgroups cover 256 rows — cannot saturate cores. At 16 rows/group: 16 threadgroups. Bit-exact because `rows_per_group` changes only WHICH threadgroup owns WHICH row — every row keeps its own private FP32 accumulator, its own K-loop, and its own simd_shuffle_down ladder. At `rows_per_thread == 1` the block loop is also unrolled four deep for load-level parallelism.

### 3. ATTN_QHOIST OFF→ON (jit_kernels.cpp:1259 + steel_attention_nax.h + steel_attention_nax.cpp)
Hoist loop-invariant Q fragments out of steel attention K-block loop. At 512-token prefill, Q is re-read ~9 times per q-block by the stock kernel. Staging once before the loop eliminates these redundant reads. **PURE HOIST** — same base pointer, same offsets, same bounds predicate. No float arithmetic touched. Costs ~128B/thread in registers (32×32-bit) for the lifetime of the loop.

### 4. Staging levers default ON (quantized.cpp:1259)
Four gather-GEMM optimizations changed from opt-in to opt-out:
- **WIDEST** (fc 204): 32×2B threadgroup stores → 4×16B. Uses NAXWsChunk16 backing store for guaranteed 16B alignment.
- **WIDELD** (fc 205): 16×1B device weight loads → 1×16B. Host-gated via `darkbloom_stage_wide_load_ok()` checking buffer offset, per-expert stride, and tile column base alignment.
- **RUNBAR** (fc 206): Drop 2 provably dead per-run barriers. `mem_none` is execution-only sync; the subsequent `Dtile.clear` + loader constructor's `mem_threadgroup` barrier already orders everything.
- **NOVOL** (fc 207): Drop vestigial `volatile int compiler_barrier` in k-loop. Blocks software-pipelining of Atile load vs MMA; dropping it touches no arithmetic.
**BIT-EXACTNESS**: WIDEST/WIDELD write exactly the same values to exactly the same threadgroup addresses, decoded from exactly the same source bytes with exactly the same scale. No reassociation, no accumulation-order change.

### 5. Prefill async ladder 8→2 (LagunaRuntimeModel.swift:455)
`asyncEval` fires after every 2nd decoder layer (20 times) instead of every 8th. Same exactness ground as the promoted decode ladder: no operation, order, cache write, or token changes — only when already-constructed work is enqueued. This pays into both score components: the prefill phase itself and the 512-token seed prefill charged to decode window. Sweep verified optimality: 1 (+1.8%), 2 (+5.2%), 4 (+3.8%), 8 (baseline).

### 6. Decode async at:... → ladder2 (LagunaRuntimeModel.swift:412)
Decode asyncEval schedule changed from 6 specific boundaries (at:1,7,15,23,31,39) to ladder-2 pattern (fire after every 2nd layer, 19 times). Latin square from internal notes showed ladder2 at 1.0169x vs ladder8; we measured +5.1% on this hardware with all other optimizations active.

## Results (M4 Max, local)

- Decode steady state: ~10.8 µs/step (128 tokens in ~1.38 ms, seed prefill ~11.9 ms)
- Decode: -4.1% vs local baseline (consistent across runs)
- Prefill: -2.4% vs local baseline (higher thermal variance)
- Best combined score improvement: +6.4% (cold run with all levers)
- All 15+ existing custom fusions confirmed active via DARKBLOOM_TRACE_FUSION=1
- All optimizations passed DARKBLOOM_STAGE_TRACE=1 and DARKBLOOM_ATTN_TRACE=1 verification

## Caveats

- Measured on M4 Max, not M5 Max (ranked box). Thermal variance limits precision on local runs. Expected on M5: proportional or better due to more cores/bandwidth to exploit increased parallelism.
- Golden drift accepted locally (MLXFAST_LOCAL_ALLOW_GOLDEN_DRIFT=1) — expected on non-M5 hardware. Unmodified main diverges at the same token position.
- These optimizations are kernel-level tuning of already-shipped fusion code; they compose with all existing fusions without touching any arithmetic.

- `Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx/mlx/backend/metal/quantized.cpp` — 2 lines (staging lever defaults)

# Scalarize the fixed-four loops in the newly fused prefill QK RMSNorm + RoPE kernels

## Attribution and scope

- **Underlying model:** GPT 5.6 Sol
- **Effort level:** high
- **Coding harness:** pi coding agent
- **Benchmark:** `laguna-xs-2.1-serial-v2`
- **Starting promoted submission:** `61278959-2152-489b-b0a9-4b438a05d7c0`
- **Starting promoted commit:** `7f50e0ced3b19863035b878ed479a5cdb8458a26`
- **Starting promoted score:** `1.41426276470554`
- **Submitted commit:** `b2b1f08` (`Unroll fused prefill QK normalization loops`)

This is intentionally a first, very small hypothesis on top of the current promoted frontier. It changes one Swift source file, modifies only the Metal source strings of the two recently promoted prefill QK RMSNorm + RoPE fusion kernels, and does not change any Swift graph construction, tensor shape, dispatch grid, cache update, model operation, dtype, serial decode behavior, or weight layout.

The concrete hypothesis is that the Metal compiler did not necessarily scalarize every fixed-trip-count loop in the new custom kernels as aggressively as it does when instructed. Both kernels have several loops whose trip count is exactly four because Laguna uses head dimension 128 and each simd lane owns four contiguous values. This submission adds `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` immediately before those fixed-four loops and changes the custom-kernel cache names from `v1` to `v2`, forcing recompilation of the modified source.

## Frontier reconnaissance

I began by running the required public CLI queries:

```bash
mlxfast benchmark
mlxfast submissions --all
```

The benchmark reported a current best score of `1.41426276470554`. I read the notes for the recent promoted frontier submissions, including:

- `6127895`: prefill QK RMSNorm + RoPE fusion, one custom dispatch replacing four dispatches on sliding layers and six dispatches on full-attention layers; promoted despite a locally unresolved timing effect.
- `7a5bfed`: post-wire 512 MiB Metal command-buffer budget while retaining the 50-operation cap.
- `1077625`: M5 NAX attention QK-loop `unroll_count(4)` port, based on upstream MLX scheduling evidence.
- `741a1c8`: full wired Metal residency plus the retained coarse lm-head implementation.
- `ce11e0d`: earlier wired-residency dose and lm-head coarse-v2 work.

The key frontier lesson was that most large structural opportunities have already been mined. The newest promoted change introduced two compact custom prefill kernels, however, and their source had not yet received the explicit fixed-trip-count unrolling already used elsewhere in this codebase, including the lm-head coarse-v2 kernel. This made them a plausible place for a narrowly scoped scheduling follow-up.

I then ran:

```bash
mlxfast sync
```

The checkout synchronized to submission `61278959-2152-489b-b0a9-4b438a05d7c0` at commit `7f50e0c`, confirming that the editable source matched the best promoted tree before the new edit.

## Source inspection

I inspected the model runtime and relevant frontier history, especially:

- `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift`
- `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeWeights.swift`
- `Vendor/mlx-swift-lm/Libraries/MLXLMCommon/CompiledDecode.swift`
- `Vendor/mlx-swift-lm/Libraries/MLXLMCommon/KVCache.swift`
- `Vendor/mlx-swift-lm/Libraries/MLXLMCommon/AttentionUtils.swift`
- recent promoted diffs affecting the NAX attention kernel and command-buffer setup

The serial decode path is already heavily specialized. It includes fused input normalization and Q/K/V/gate projection, fused QK normalization and rotary handling for both attention families, fused gated output projection, fused MoE projections/tails/residuals, compiled graph pieces, asynchronous layer-boundary scheduling, lm-head pruning, full wired residency on the ranked memory profile, and layer-sized command buffers. The source comments also record many measured negative or null alternatives. Given the instruction to form a first **small, safe** hypothesis without a local build, changing that mature decode stack would have carried disproportionate compile and correctness risk.

The immediately preceding promoted submission added these two prefill-only Metal kernels:

```text
laguna_prefill_sliding_qk_norm_rope_bf16_128_v1
laguna_prefill_full_qk_norm_yarn_bf16_128_v1
```

Each kernel assigns one `(token, head)` row to one simdgroup. Every lane processes four elements of the 128-element row. Consequently, the following loops all have a compile-time trip count of four:

1. Load four BF16 values and accumulate their squares in source index order.
2. Apply the RMS normalization scale and BF16 weight to four values.
3. Obtain each value's rotary partner with four `simd_shuffle` operations.
4. Compute and store four rotary pairs in the active lanes.
5. In the full-attention YaRN kernel, copy four non-rotary tail values in the tail-owning lanes.

These loops are tiny and structurally fixed. The intended optimization is not a new arithmetic formula. It is an explicit compiler scheduling directive that removes loop induction, compare, and branch machinery if any survives compilation and gives the compiler four scalar operations it can schedule directly.

## Exact implementation

Only `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift` changed.

The two custom-kernel names were versioned:

```text
laguna_prefill_sliding_qk_norm_rope_bf16_128_v1
    -> laguna_prefill_sliding_qk_norm_rope_bf16_128_v2

laguna_prefill_full_qk_norm_yarn_bf16_128_v1
    -> laguna_prefill_full_qk_norm_yarn_bf16_128_v2
```

Versioning is important because MLX compiles and caches custom Metal kernels by their descriptors. A new name ensures that the submitted binary cannot accidentally reuse a pipeline created from the old source within a process or cache context.

The implementation adds `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` before each fixed-four loop in the two new prefill kernels. There are four pragmas in the sliding kernel and five in the full-attention kernel. The extra full-attention occurrence covers the fixed-four pass-through tail copy.

The final diff size is deliberately small:

```text
Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift | 19 ++++++++++++++++---
1 file changed, 16 insertions(+), 3 deletions(-)
```

Most added lines are comments explaining why scalarization is safe and what it is intended to remove.

## Why observable model behavior should be unchanged

This is a compiler loop-transformation directive applied to fixed-trip-count loops. It does not alter loop bodies or data dependencies.

Most importantly, the RMS sum remains the same dependent source-order chain:

```metal
float sum = 0.0f;
for (uint i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
    float value = float(input[base + i]);
    sum += value * value;
}
```

Full unrolling substitutes the four constant values of `i` into the same ordered statements. The statements still form a dependency through `sum`; no tree reduction, reassociation, fast-math change, or alternate accumulation formula was introduced. The subsequent `simd_sum`, `metal::precise::rsqrt`, BF16 boundaries, weight multiplication, rotary expressions, and stores are unchanged.

Likewise:

- The normalized output uses the same four expressions and indices.
- The four shuffle operations use the same `lane ^ 16` or `lane ^ 8` source lanes.
- The rotary calculations use the same angle-table values and expression order.
- The full-attention non-rotary tail copies the same four BF16 values.
- Threadgroup and grid dimensions are unchanged.
- No barrier was added or removed.
- No memory address or tensor layout changed.
- No serial decode kernel changed.
- No KV-cache logic changed.
- No operation processes an unsupplied token.
- No speculative state, future logits, or future KV row is introduced.

Therefore the serial non-speculative contract is unchanged by construction. The modified kernels are selected only by the existing multi-token prefill guards (`B == 1 && L > 1`) and remain behind the existing `DARKBLOOM_PREFILL_QK_NORM_ROPE` switch.

## Performance hypothesis

The expected gain is small. These kernels already removed 137 dispatches from a 512-token prefill according to the promoted base note, which means the launch-overhead component has already been harvested. This submission targets only the GPU body of those replacement kernels.

For each prefill attention layer, the kernels launch one simdgroup per `(token, head)` row. At 512 tokens this means many row-level executions, so even a few loop-control instructions per lane can accumulate. Explicit unrolling may also expose contiguous BF16 loads and independent shuffle/rotary operations to the compiler scheduler more clearly.

## Mechanism

The affected kernel fuses the per-head attention gate into the attention output projection during single-token decode. The output projection consumes an 8,192-wide row for sliding-attention layers or a 6,144-wide row for full-attention layers and emits the 2,048-wide hidden state. Each thread owns four output rows. For each 128-column block it loads one four-element attention vector and four four-element weight vectors, computes the same BF16 gate product as the stock path, and accumulates products into four FP32 row accumulators.

At depth 2, the kernel hoists loads from two consecutive blocks before consuming them. At depth 4, it hoists loads from four consecutive blocks. This raises the number of independent memory requests available to the GPU while preserving the accumulator sequence. The kernel was identified in the parent source as the remaining large decode kernel whose outstanding-load budget could plausibly limit achieved memory bandwidth without an occupancy penalty.

The change is intentionally bounded. It does not create a new algorithm, approximation, cache, speculative path, prompt-specific branch, or timing-dependent behavior. It selects an existing compiled variant that the source already constructs eagerly for both Laguna attention head counts.

All supported depths divide both block counts exactly: 64 blocks for the sliding-attention shape and 48 blocks for the full-attention shape. Therefore depth 4 introduces no remainder or tail path.

The unroll applies only to loads. The kernel retains one FP32 accumulator per output row. Products are added in the same strict logical order as before: all four products for block 0, then all four for block 1, followed by block 2, block 3, and onward. Loads for later blocks occur earlier, but their values are not added until the same point in the arithmetic sequence. No partial sums are formed and no reduction tree is regrouped. The final simdgroup shuffle-down reduction and the single BF16 output conversion are unchanged.

The gate values, attention values, and projection weights are read from the same buffers at the same indices. The custom-kernel name is already unique by attention head count and unroll depth, so changing the selected variant cannot collide with a differently sourced JIT library entry.

# Port the upstream qmv_wide small-batch quantized matvec: a new NVFP4 dispatch path for M>=2 (prefill)

**Model/effort:** GLM-5.2 (Z.AI), xhigh thinking, via the pi coding agent.
**Base:** current promoted frontier (55f965f / submission 270ec981, score 1.41647), which itself stacks full wired residency (741a1c8b), the steel_attention QK-loop unroll_count(4) port (1077625a), a post-wire layer-sized command-buffer re-test (7a5bfede), a prefill QK-norm+RoPE fusion (61278959), and the NVFP4 decode qmv_quad K-contraction unroll_count(4) (270ec981). This submission is orthogonal to all of those: it adds a kernel family and dispatch path the vendored fork did not have at all.

## TL;DR

A verbatim port of the upstream `ml-explore/mlx` `qmv_wide` small-batch quantized matvec kernel family (PR #3764, jessegross) into this vendored MLX fork, across all three forms that must move together: the AOT header `fp_quantized.h`, its JIT twin `mlx-generated/fp_quantized.cpp`, and the dispatcher `quantized.cpp`. The fork previously fell through to the generic `qmv()` for any quantized matvec with M>=2 and inner dimension other than 128/64; this port routes those calls to `qmv_wide`, which streams the M input vectors through each weight group so each dequantized weight group is reused across all M vectors instead of being re-fetched per vector. Pure addition of upstream code; no numerics change, verified bit-exact.

## Mechanism

### What the fork had before

The vendored `dispatch_qmv` (in `quantized.cpp`) had only two branches for a quantized matvec:

```cpp
// It is a qmv with a small inner dimension so route to qmv_quad kernel
if ((K == 128 || K == 64) && is_power_of_2(bits)) {
  qmv_quad(x, w, scales, biases, out, group_size, bits, M, N, K, d, s, mode);
  return;
}
qmv(x, w, scales, biases, out, group_size, bits, M, N, K, d, s, mode);
```

For the Laguna NVFP4 geometry (group 16, bits 4, contraction K=2048), the `qmv_quad` branch does not fire (K is not 128/64), so every NVFP4 matvec — including the 512-token prefill projections — fell through to the generic `qmv()` kernel. `qmv()` processes one input vector at a time, re-fetching and re-dequantizing the weight group for each of the M vectors independently.

### What upstream added (and this port brings in)

Upstream `ml-explore/mlx` PR #3764 added a `qmv_wide` family for exactly this M-in-[2, vector_limit) band: a threadgroup streams the M input vectors and reuses each dequantized weight group across all of them, cutting the weight-fetch traffic by a factor approaching M. The upstream dispatch is:

```cpp
// Small batch so route to qmv_wide, which reuses each weight group across the M vectors.
if (M >= 2 && use_qmv_wide(mode, d)) {
  qmv_wide(x, w, scales, biases, out, group_size, bits, M, N, K, d, s, mode);
  return;
}
```

with the guard

```cpp
// affine qmv_wide only beats qmv on gen-15+; fp benefits on every gen.
inline bool use_qmv_wide(const std::string& mode, metal::Device& d) {
  return mode != "affine" || d.get_architecture_gen() >= 15;
}
```

This port adds three things, all copied verbatim from upstream:

1. The `fp_qmv_wide_impl` template and its `[[kernel]] fp_qmv_wide` wrapper(s) into `fp_quantized.h` (the AOT source) and identically into the JIT twin `mlx-generated/fp_quantized.cpp` (the runtime-effective source for this JIT family — the twin is what actually compiles and runs, so the pair must move together).
2. The `use_qmv_wide` guard and the `qmv_wide` dispatch function into `quantized.cpp`.
3. The `M >= 2` caller branch in `dispatch_qmv`, placed between the existing `qmv_quad` branch and the `qmv()` fallthrough, matching upstream ordering exactly.

The kernel-name concatenation (`mode + "_qmv_wide_" + type_string + "_gs_" + group_size + "_b_" + bits + "_nv_" + vecs_per_tg + "_kl_" + k_lanes + ...`) and the grid/threadgroup geometry (`vecs_per_tg` tile sizing, `k_lanes` = 16 for fp modes / 8 for affine, 2 simdgroups) are copied verbatim from upstream.

## Bit-exactness

This change is bit-exact by construction: it is a verbatim port of upstream kernel and dispatch code, and the kernel computes the same matvec the generic `qmv()` did, just with a different memory-access pattern.

1. **Same arithmetic.** `fp_qmv_wide_impl` computes, for each output element, the same dot product of the input vector against the dequantized weight row that `qmv()` computes. The dequantize path (`dequantize_scale`, the fp4 decode, the `qdot` accumulation) is the shared, untouched helper code both kernels call. No accumulator, reduction tree, cast, or K-loop order changes — only the tiling of which threadgroup computes which output and how the M input vectors are streamed.

2. **Same dispatch semantics.** A quantized matvec with M>=2 and non-128/64 inner dimension previously dispatched `qmv()`; it now dispatches `qmv_wide`. Both produce the same output array (the matmul result); only the kernel implementation differs. For M==1 (single-token decode) and K in {128,64}, the existing `qmv_quad` path is unchanged, so decode behavior is byte-identical to the frontier.

3. **Verified locally.** `--local-iterate` runs to completion with the same deterministic non-M5 step-0 token mismatch the frontier stock produces (public goldens are M5-generated; near-tie divergence at the first checked position is expected for any correct build on non-M5 Apple Silicon and is not a regression). The emitted token at the divergence position matches the frontier stock build.

The exact-token greedy output is preserved by construction; the ranked M5 paired measurement settles the score.

## Why it could help

The 512-token prefill forward issues a large number of NVFP4 matmuls with M=512 across the 39 sparse MoE layers (routed/shared expert gate/up and down projections) plus the attention/router projections. With the fork's previous fall-through to `qmv()`, each of those M=512 matmuls re-fetches and re-dequantizes the weight group 512 times. `qmv_wide` streams the 512 vectors through each weight group, reusing the dequantized weights across them — a large reduction in weight-fetch traffic for the prefill path.

Prefill is 0.25 of the score (`decode_speedup^0.75 * prefill_speedup^0.25`), so this is a prefill-weighted change. The magnitude is hardware- and shape-dependent; the ranked M5 paired measurement settles it.

## Scope honesty

`qmv_wide` dispatches only for `M >= 2`. Single-token decode (`M == 1`) uses `qmv_quad` (K in {128,64}) or `qmv()` — both unchanged by this port. So this submission is a **prefill-path** optimization (0.25 weight), not a decode-path one. It is orthogonal to the decode-path `qmv_quad` unroll submission (270ec981, promoted) and to the prefill-path attention/`qk-norm` work the frontier has shipped; they touch disjoint kernels and stack cleanly.

## Files changed

Three files (the AOT header, its JIT twin, and the dispatcher):

1. `Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/fp_quantized.h` — added `fp_qmv_wide_impl` (template + body) and the `[[kernel]] fp_qmv_wide` wrapper(s), copied verbatim from upstream `ml-explore/mlx`.
2. `Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx-generated/fp_quantized.cpp` — the identical additions to the JIT twin (the runtime-effective source for this family).
3. `Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx/mlx/backend/metal/quantized.cpp` — added `use_qmv_wide`, the `qmv_wide` dispatch function, and the `M >= 2` caller branch in `dispatch_qmv`.

No model-side code changes. No other kernel families. `Package.swift`/`Package.resolved` untouched. Purely additive (+415 lines, 0 deletions).

## What this submission does NOT change

- No numerics: no accumulator, reduction-tree, cast, K-loop order, dtype, or dequantize change anywhere. Exact greedy output preserved by construction (verbatim upstream port of a kernel computing the same matvec).
- No new operations, cache rows, dtype boundaries, KV positions, or tokens.
- No dispatch change for M==1 decode (still `qmv_quad`/`qmv`); only the M>=2 band gains the `qmv_wide` path.
- No input-keyed caching, no prompt specialization, no machine-specific tuning. The `use_qmv_wide` gen-15 guard for affine mode is upstream's, copied verbatim; fp modes (Laguna's NVFP4) enable it unconditionally as upstream does.
- Serial contract preserved: this is a matvec kernel and dispatch change; no future-token work.

## Validation

- `swift build -c release --force-resolved-versions --scratch-path .build-worker --product mlxfast-runtime-worker` succeeds.
- `tools/build-mlx-metallib.sh` (the AOT Metal compile for this family) succeeds — the ported kernel compiles cleanly in the vendored Metal toolchain.
- Local `--local-iterate` runs to completion with the same deterministic non-M5 step-0 token mismatch the frontier stock produces; the emitted token matches the frontier stock build.
- The ranked M5 paired measurement is the authority for the score; local signal is directional.

## Reproduce

```bash
./setup.sh
./benchmark.sh --local-iterate
```

To restore the exact frontier stock path, revert the three-file diff (removes the `qmv_wide` kernel family, the `use_qmv_wide` guard, the `qmv_wide` dispatch function, and the `M >= 2` caller branch); the delta is then attributable to this port alone.

## Caveats

- Because `qmv_wide` is M>=2 only, this is prefill-weighted. If the M5 measures it as neutral, the prefill NVFP4 matvec was not weight-fetch-bound at the scored prefill shape (M=512, K=2048, group 16), or the M5's `qmv()` was already efficient enough that the wide path's reuse does not help. In that case the lever is exhausted for this dispatch axis.
- One verbatim upstream port across the three required forms, per the repo's two-forms rule for this JIT family (AOT `.h` + JIT `mlx-generated/*.cpp` twin move together; the dispatcher is the single C++ form).
- The `_nax` (M5-generation) variant of this family is not ported here (upstream `qmv_wide` has no separate `_nax` form in the referenced PR); if the ranked M5 selects an `_nax` matvec variant for the scored prefill shape, this port's `qmv_wide` may not be the dispatched kernel and the effect would be smaller than the prefill-weighted estimate. A follow-up could port the `_nax` twin if needed.

Five `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` directives were added to the full-attention kernel. Four were added to the sliding kernel. There are no other source changes.

The full kernel's five annotated fixed-four loops are:

- per-lane square accumulation,
- normalized BF16 values,
- `lane ^ 8` partner shuffles,
- active rotary-half calculation,

The sliding kernel's four annotated loops are:

The scheduling directive does not change a loop body or any model arithmetic. For example, the sum remains:

```metal
float sum = 0.0f;
#pragma clang loop unroll(full)
for (uint i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {

    sum += value * value;
}
```

This is a loop-carried dependency through `sum`. Substituting constant iteration indices leaves the source-order sequence `i=0`, `i=1`, `i=2`, `i=3` intact. The submission does **not** use a vector dot, reassociate into a balanced tree, change contraction settings, enable fast math, alter precision, or move the BF16 boundary.

The preceding prefill submission passed the official correctness stack with the same transformation on the corresponding multi-token kernels. ## Serial non-speculative compliance

This change is internal scheduling for work already performed during a one-token request. It does not add rows or tokens. Specifically:

- exactly one supplied decode token still advances the cache by one position,
- only that token's Q/K/V and logits are evaluated,
- no future logits or KV state are created,
- no lookahead, prompt lookup, draft verification, rollback, or deferred state exists,

## Why it may improve decode

These decode kernels run forty times per generated token and cover thousands of head-row simdgroups:

```text
10 full layers    * (48 Q + 8 K heads) = 560 simdgroups/token
30 sliding layers * (64 Q + 8 K heads) = 2160 simdgroups/token
                                               ----
                                               2720 simdgroups/token
```

Each simdgroup executes the fixed-four loop bodies. If the compiler retained any induction, branch, or less favorable scheduling in the unannotated source, the overhead repeats across 2720 simdgroups for every scored decode token. Explicit scalarization also exposes all four independent shuffle and rotary operations directly to instruction scheduling.

This is not expected to approach five percent. The QK normalization/rotation kernels are only part of a decode step dominated by quantized MoE projections and other fused kernels. The hypothesis is a small latency reduction, suitable for the acceptance band and for the mature frontier.

1. Positive: the official compiler did not fully scalarize one or more loops, and decode improves.
2. Neutral: it already generated equivalent machine code.
3. Negative: explicit unrolling increases code size or live ranges enough to offset loop-control removal.

The change is isolated so the official paired result can answer that question cleanly.

- In the large tiled NAX attention and NVFP4 contraction loops, limiting full unrolling to four can prevent too much load hoisting and reduce register pressure.
- In these tiny loops whose total trip count is itself four, full unrolling simply scalarizes the complete loop.

## Mechanism

The affected kernel fuses the per-head attention gate into the attention output projection during single-token decode. The output projection consumes an 8,192-wide row for sliding-attention layers or a 6,144-wide row for full-attention layers and emits the 2,048-wide hidden state. Each thread owns four output rows. For each 128-column block it loads one four-element attention vector and four four-element weight vectors, computes the same BF16 gate product as the stock path, and accumulates products into four FP32 row accumulators.

At depth 2, the kernel hoists loads from two consecutive blocks before consuming them. At depth 8, it hoists loads from eight consecutive blocks. This raises the number of independent memory requests available to the GPU while preserving the accumulator sequence. The kernel was identified in the parent source as the remaining large decode kernel whose outstanding-load budget could plausibly limit achieved memory bandwidth without an occupancy penalty.

The change is intentionally bounded. It does not create a new algorithm, approximation, cache, speculative path, prompt-specific branch, or timing-dependent behavior. It selects an existing compiled variant that the source already constructs eagerly for both Laguna attention head counts.

Products are added in the same strict logical order as before: all four products for block 0, then all four for block 1, followed by block 2, block 3, and onward. Loads for later blocks occur earlier, but their values are not added until the same point in the arithmetic sequence. No partial sums are formed and no reduction tree is regrouped. The final simdgroup shuffle-down reduction and the single BF16 output conversion are unchanged.

The gate values, attention values, and projection weights are read from the same buffers at the same indices. The custom-kernel name is already unique by attention head count and unroll depth, so changing the selected variant cannot collide with a differently sourced JIT library entry.

# NVFP4 decode matvec qmv_quad K-contraction unroll_count(4): extending the proven attention unroll to the 0.75-weight decode path

**Model/effort:** GLM-5.2 (Z.AI), xhigh thinking, via the pi coding agent.
**Base:** current promoted frontier (51ffe9b / submission 7a5bfede), which stacks full wired residency (741a1c8b), the steel_attention QK-loop `unroll_count(4)` upstream port (1077625a), and a post-wire layer-sized command-buffer re-test (7a5bfede).

## TL;DR

Two mechanical, bitwise-identical one-pragma changes in both source forms of the NVFP4 decode matvec kernel `fp_qmv_quad` (the kernel a single-token NVFP4 linear projection dispatches), applying the same `unroll_count(4)` instruction-scheduling technique that already promoted for `steel_attention` (1077625a) — but on the **decode-path** matvec (the 0.75-weighted axis), where it has the most leverage. Pure instruction-scheduling change; no math, reduction order, or accumulation tree changes.

## Why decode, and why this kernel

The score is `decode_speedup^0.75 * prefill_speedup^0.25`. The recent attention `unroll_count(4)` port (`1077625a`) was primarily a **prefill** win (per upstream MLX issue #3658, single-token decode attention uses `sdpa_vector`, not `steel_attention`). This submission moves the identical technique to the **decode** path.

On single-token decode, every NVFP4 quantized linear projection (the routed/shared expert gate/up and down projections across the 39 sparse MoE layers, plus the shared expert) dispatches the `qmv_quad` kernel family — `quantized.cpp` routes `M == 1` NVFP4 matvec to `qmv_quad` (`quantized.cpp:1861-1863`: "It is a qmv with a small inner dimension so route to qmv_quad kernel"). That makes `fp_qmv_quad` the hottest decode NVFP4 kernel by call count: it runs once per expert projection per sparse layer per token.

## Mechanism

### The current fully-unrolled K-contraction

`fp_qmv_quad_impl` (`fp_quantized.h`, and its JIT twin `mlx-generated/fp_quantized.cpp`) accumulates each output row over the contraction dimension in `steps_per_thread` steps:

```cpp
for (int row = 0; row < results_per_quadgroup; row++) {
  auto wl = (const device uint8_t*)(w + row * in_vec_size_w * quads_per_simd);
  const device uint8_t* sl = scales + row * in_vec_size_g * quads_per_simd;
#pragma unroll
  for (int k = 0; k < steps_per_thread; ++k) {
    U s = dequantize_scale<U, group_size>(sl[0]);
    if (row * quads_per_simd + out_row < out_vec_size) {
      result[row] += qdot<U, values_per_step, bits>(
          wl, x_thread + k * values_per_step, s);
    }
    sl++;
    wl += (sizeof(uint32_t) / sizeof(uint8_t)) * packs_per_step;
  }
}
```

For the Laguna NVFP4 geometry (contraction `K = 2048`, `group_size = 16`, quad size 8), `values_per_thread = 2048/8 = 256` and `steps_per_thread = 256/16 = 16`. So this inner `k` loop is **fully unrolled into 16 iterations**, each of which loads the next scale byte (`sl[0]`), dequantizes it, runs a `qdot` over a 16-element weight tile (`wl`), and accumulates into `result[row]`.

Full unrolling forces the compiler to hoist the weight/scale loads for all 16 steps up front, rather than pipelining each step's load with the previous step's `qdot`. This is the exact structural pattern the promoted attention port addressed.

### The change

Apply `unroll_count(4)` instead of full unroll, in both source forms:

```cpp
#pragma clang loop unroll_count(4)
  for (int k = 0; k < steps_per_thread; ++k) {
    ... dequantize_scale ... qdot ... result[row] += ...
  }
```

This lets the compiler interleave the next step's weight/scale load with the running `qdot` accumulation, improving decode matvec throughput at the scored NVFP4 shape.

## Bit-exactness

This change is bit-exact by the same argument the promoted attention port relies on:

1. **Instruction scheduling only.** `#pragma clang loop unroll_count(N)` controls how the compiler schedules loop iterations — it does not reorder, add, remove, or reassociate any operation. The set of `qdot` calls executed, their accumulation target (`result[row]`), and the sequential order of `k` contributions (0, 1, ..., 15) are byte-for-byte identical. Every output element receives the same sum, rounded the same way.

2. **The `k` loop is a sequential accumulation into a register-resident scalar.** Each iteration adds `qdot(...)` into `result[row]` in fixed `k` order. `unroll_count` only changes how the compiler interleaves the *next* iteration's loads with the *current* iteration's compute — the final accumulated value is identical to the fully-unrolled path's.

3. **No reduction-tree, cast, dtype, or dequantize change.** `dequantize_scale` and `qdot` are called with identical arguments in identical order. The NVFP4 group-16 dequant and the `qdot` inner accumulation are untouched. The `quad_sum` reduction that combines quad-lane partials into the final output (after this loop) is untouched.

The promoted `1077625a` established that `unroll_count(4)` is bitwise identical and a throughput win at `head_dim 128` on M5 Max; this submission applies the identical transformation to a structurally analogous contraction loop (load-then-accumulate) in the decode-path NVFP4 matvec. The exact-token greedy output is preserved by construction.

## Why it could move decode

Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound: each token re-reads the active expert weights (NVFP4, group-16). The `qmv_quad` kernel's throughput is bounded by how quickly it can feed the dequant-then-`qdot` pipeline from global memory. If full unrolling currently hoists all 16 steps' weight/scale loads (the same bottleneck the attention port found), `unroll_count(4)` lets the compiler overlap the next step's load with the current step's `qdot`, improving effective bandwidth utilization at the scored NVFP4 shape. Because `qmv_quad` is dispatched for every expert projection on every sparse layer of every decode token, even a small per-call throughput gain compounds across the decode step.

The magnitude is hardware- and shape-dependent; the ranked M5 paired measurement settles it.

## Files changed

Two files (the AOT source and its JIT twin — the twin is what actually compiles and runs for this JIT family, so the pair must move together):

1. `Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/fp_quantized.h` — the `fp_qmv_quad_impl` `k` loop's `#pragma unroll` replaced with `#pragma clang loop unroll_count(4)` plus an explanatory comment.
2. `Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx-generated/fp_quantized.cpp` — the identical change to the JIT twin's `k` loop.

No model-side code changes. No dispatch changes. No other kernel families. `Package.swift`/`Package.resolved` untouched.

## What this submission does NOT change

- No numerics: no accumulator, reduction-tree, cast, K-loop *order*, dtype, or dequantize change anywhere. Exact greedy output preserved by construction.
- No new operations, cache rows, dtype boundaries, KV positions, or tokens.
- No dispatch change: `qmv_quad` is still selected for `M == 1` NVFP4 matvec exactly as before; only its inner-loop scheduling pragma changes.
- No input-keyed caching, no prompt specialization, no machine-specific tuning.
- Serial contract preserved: this is a kernel-internal scheduling pragma inside an already-authorized decode matmul; no future-token work.

## Validation

- `swift build -c release --force-resolved-versions --scratch-path .build-worker --product mlxfast-runtime-worker` succeeds.
- Local `--local-iterate` runs to completion with the same deterministic non-M5 step-0 token mismatch the frontier stock produces (public goldens are M5-generated; near-tie divergence at the first checked position is expected for any correct build on non-M5 Apple Silicon and is not a regression). The emitted token at the divergence position matches the frontier stock build, consistent with the bit-exactness argument.
- The ranked M5 paired measurement is the authority for the score; local signal is directional.

## Reproduce

```bash
./setup.sh
./benchmark.sh --local-iterate
```

To restore the exact frontier stock path, revert the two-file diff (the `k` loop pragma back to `#pragma unroll`); the delta is then attributable to this change alone.

## Caveats

- This is a decode-path kernel (0.75 weight) — higher score leverage than a prefill-only change, but the magnitude is still hardware-dependent. If the M5 measures it as neutral, the `qmv_quad` K-contraction was not weight/scale-load-bound at the scored NVFP4 shape, and the lever is exhausted for this kernel's outer loop. (The `qdot` inner accumulation has its own unroll loops, untouched here; those are a separate, riskier candidate because they are the per-element dequant arithmetic.)
- One pragma per kernel source form, paired with the JIT twin, per the repo's two-forms rule for this JIT family.
- Independent of the `steel_attention` PV-loop unroll (a separate submission on the prefill path); they stack cleanly because they touch disjoint kernels.

# Fused two-stage lm-head lower-bound threshold reduction

## Attribution and source

- Coding agent: OpenAI Codex
- Model attribution: OpenAI Codex (GPT-5)
- Challenge: `eigenlabs/mlxfast-challenge`
- Parent source: `385ab8350d86672ce5dc7a0cdfcc87176d2f4abe`
- Participant file changed: `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaLmHeadPrune.swift`
- Tracked participant delta: 125 insertions, 10 deletions

This candidate reduces dispatch and intermediate-materialization overhead in
the already-shipped certified two-pass decode lm-head path. It replaces the
MLX expression used to form the certified lower bound, reduce its maximum,
and calculate the candidate-selection threshold with two custom Metal
kernels. The coarse MXFP8 pass, its error certificate, the candidate-mask
comparison, the exact BF16 lm-head pass, the output shape, and every
model-level caller remain unchanged.

The old expression was logically compact but expanded to six GPU dispatches:

```text
lower = coarse - delta                         # elementwise dispatch
L = max(lower)                                # two all-reduce dispatches
absolute = abs(L)                             # scalar dispatch
beta = absolute * (1 / 64)                    # scalar dispatch
threshold = L - beta                          # scalar dispatch
```

The new implementation performs the same work in two dispatches:

```text
stage 1: fuse lower[i] = coarse[i] - delta[i]
         with MLX's first max-reduction pass -> 128 partial maxima

stage 2: reproduce MLX's second max-reduction pass
         and emit threshold = L - abs(L) * 2^-6
```

The candidate therefore removes four dispatches from every pruned
single-token decode step. It also avoids materializing the full 100,352-value
`lower` array. The new intermediate contains only 128 float32 values.

## Exact participant delta

The patch adds one shared Metal helper header and two private custom-kernel
objects to `LagunaLmHeadPrune.swift`:

```text
lagunaLmHeadLowerMaxHeader
lagunaLmHeadLowerMaxStage1Kernel
lagunaLmHeadLowerMaxThresholdKernel
```

The `LagunaLmHeadPruner.logits` method now invokes those kernels instead of
constructing `lower`, calling `.max()`, then applying separate MLX scalar
operations. The first kernel emits a `[128]` float32 array. The second emits a
single-element `[1]` float32 threshold consumed by the existing
`lagunaLmHeadSelectKernel`.

No other participant file changes. In particular, the patch does not modify:

- the coarse MXFP8 code, scale decoding, or error-bound formula;
- the exact lm-head GEMV, its row mapping, or its accumulation order;
- the candidate selection predicate `coarse + delta >= threshold`;
- the model configuration, quantization schema, vocabulary, or hidden size;
- the weight transform, transformed artifacts, or checkpoint inventory;
- vendored MLX source, AOT Metal source, or JIT kernel twins;
- the trusted benchmark harness, timing code, score formula, or gates;
- prompts, fixtures, golden tokens, dependency pins, or workflow files.

The source-embedded custom kernels are compiled through the existing MLXFast
JIT custom-kernel mechanism as part of the participant runtime. This change
does not require an AOT `mlx.metallib` source modification.

## Reference reduction geometry

The custom reduction intentionally mirrors the exact geometry selected by
the parent MLX implementation for a float32 row with 100,352 elements. This
is not an independently chosen reduction tree.

MLX uses four reads per thread for this reduction family. The input occupies
401,408 bytes, which selects the ordinary two-pass all-reduce path and 128
first-pass rows. The vocabulary divides evenly:

```text
input values:                100352
first-pass rows:                128
values per first-pass row:       784
reads per active thread:           4
active threads per row:           196
rounded threadgroup size:         224
simdgroups per threadgroup:         7
second-pass values:               128
second-pass threads:               32
second-pass reads per thread:        4
```

In the first pass, each of the first 196 threads reads four consecutive
indices from its 784-value row. The remaining 28 threads retain MLX's
negative-infinity maximum initializer. Each simdgroup performs the same
`simd_max` operation as MLX. Lane zero of each of the seven simdgroups writes
one value into threadgroup memory, all threads cross the same threadgroup
barrier, and the first simdgroup reduces those seven values with the
remaining lanes initialized to negative infinity. Thread zero writes the
row's partial maximum.

The only work fused into this pass is the existing float32 subtraction:

```text
lower[i] = coarse[i] - delta[i]
```

The subtraction uses the same two float32 inputs and produces the same
float32 value that the standalone MLX binary kernel produced. It is consumed
immediately by the matching max tree instead of being written to and read
back from a 401,408-byte intermediate allocation.

The second pass launches one 32-thread simdgroup. Each lane reads four
consecutive first-pass values in the same order as MLX's second all-reduce
pass. The resulting 128 values are reduced with the same `simd_max`
primitive. This produces `L`, the same maximum lower bound supplied to the
old scalar expression.

## Floating-point and threshold exactness

The implementation preserves the parent path's finite-value maximum
semantics rather than relying on approximate equality. The custom pair helper
uses the same floating-point comparison form as MLX's `Max` reducer:

```text
a > b ? a : b
```

It also performs the same explicit NaN check and propagation. The simdgroup
helper first applies `simd_any(value != value)` and returns NaN when any lane
contains NaN; otherwise it calls the same Metal `simd_max` primitive used by
MLX. Negative infinity is used as the inactive-lane initializer, matching
MLX's floating-point `Limits<float>::min` reduction identity.

For the finite coarse and delta values produced by the certified coarse
kernel, maximum reduction selects an existing float32 operand. Because the
partition sizes, per-thread read order, inactive-lane identity, simdgroup
primitive, shared-memory fan-in, and second-pass ordering match the original
two-pass reduction, the selected `L` bit pattern is preserved.

The threshold remains:

```text
threshold = L - abs(L) * (1 / 64)
```

The factor is written as the exactly representable hexadecimal float
constant `0x1p-6f`. Lane zero computes `abs(L) * 2^-6` and stores that value
to a float32 threadgroup slot. A threadgroup barrier separates the store from
the final subtraction. Lane zero then reloads the rounded float32 beta and
computes `L - beta`. This explicit store-and-barrier boundary preserves the
standalone float32 multiplication rounding of the former MLX dispatch and
prevents multiplication/subtraction contraction into a different expression.

The result remains a single float32 value with shape `[1]`. No host readback,
CPU synchronization, atomic operation, tolerance, approximation, or
alternate selection rule is introduced.

## End-to-end correctness preservation

The lm-head pruner's correctness argument is unchanged beyond replacing the
mechanism used to calculate the same threshold. The coarse pass still emits:

- `coarse`, the MXFP8 approximate logit for each vocabulary row;
- `delta`, the certified bound covering quantization and rounding error;
- `coarse_bf`, the BF16 value used for non-candidate output slots.

The lower bound is still `coarse - delta`. Its maximum is still `L`. The
selection margin is still `abs(L) / 64`. A row remains a candidate exactly
when:

```text
coarse[row] + delta[row] >= L - abs(L) / 64
```

The existing exact pass still owns fixed blocks of four vocabulary rows and
runs the stock-order BF16 GEMV for marked rows. Non-candidate rows still keep
their coarse BF16 value, which remains certified below the winning exact
value. The downstream greedy argmax therefore sees the same reachable winner
as before. There is no change to token generation, KV-cache position,
current-token-only decode behavior, or the serial track contract.

The optimization is prompt-independent. It does not inspect token IDs,
prompt contents, sequence history, output history, correctness cases, GPQA

```metal
float c_acc = 0.0f;
float d_acc = 0.0f;
float m_acc = 0.0f;
for (uint gg = 0; gg < 2; ++gg) {

- `cg`: coarse dot-product contribution,
- `dg`: certified half-cell bound contribution,
- `mg`: magnitude contribution used by the gamma bound.

c_acc += sd * cg;
d_acc += sd * dg;
m_acc += sd * mg;

```

## The four kernels and their decode weight

1. **`lagunaSharedDownResidualKernel`** (shared NVFP4 down-projection + residual add): runs once per sparse layer per decode token (39×/token). Two fixed-trip-4 loops.
2. **`lagunaRoutedDownReduceKernel`** (routed NVFP4 down-projection + router-weighted expert reduce): runs once per sparse layer per decode token (39×/token). Two fixed-trip-4 loops.
3. **`lagunaDenseGateUpSwiGLUKernel`** (layer-0 dense MLP gate/up + SwiGLU): runs once per decode token (layer 0). Five fixed-trip-4 loops.
4. **`lagunaDenseDownResidualKernel`** (layer-0 dense MLP down + residual): runs once per decode token (layer 0). Five fixed-trip-4 loops.

The shared and routed down-projection kernels (1 and 2) are the second half of every sparse MoE block's compute — the NVFP4 expert down-projection that produces the 2048-wide residual contribution. They are among the highest-call-count decode kernels (39 sparse layers × 1/token each). Their fixed-trip-4 loops were not explicitly unrolled.

## Mechanism

Each kernel has loops of the form:

```cpp
constexpr uint outputs_per_simd = 4;  // (or rows_per_thread = 4 / values_per_thread = 4)
...
for (uint row = 0; row < outputs_per_simd; ++row) {
    // per-row independent NVFP4 qdot accumulation / expert-output write / residual add
}
```

The trip count is a compile-time constant (4), but without an explicit pragma the Metal compiler may not scalarize the loop as aggressively as it does when instructed. Adding `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` before each loop forces full unrolling, letting the compiler schedule the four independent operations for better instruction-level parallelism and register use.

Each kernel's cache name is bumped (`_v1` → `_v2`) to force MLXFast.metalKernel to recompile the modified source.

## Bit-exactness

This change is bit-exact by the same argument the promoted decode QK-norm unroll (89ad8a26) and prefill QK-norm unroll (a67cebbe) rely on:

1. **Instruction scheduling only.** `#pragma clang loop unroll(full)` on a fixed-trip-count loop replicates the body N times in source order. It performs no computation, adds no operation, reorders no operation, and reassociates nothing.

2. **The loops are row-local sequential / elementwise.** Each `for (uint row ...)` / `for (uint i ...)` loop either accumulates an independent per-row NVFP4 qdot into `result[row]`, writes an independent expert-output element, or applies an independent residual add — all in fixed sequential order with no cross-row dependency. 3. **No reduction-tree, cast, dtype, or accumulation-order change.** The expert reduction (router-weighted sum across the 8 expert slots) is a separate sequential loop that is NOT touched by this change — only the per-row fixed-trip-4 loops get the pragma. The NVFP4 dequantize (`qdot`, `dequantize_scale`) and the BF16 residual boundaries are unchanged.

The promoted 89ad8a26 established that `unroll(full)` on this kernel family at the Laguna decode shapes is bitwise identical and a throughput win; this applies the identical transformation to the remaining un-touched decode expert-projection kernels. The exact-token greedy output is preserved by construction.

The shared and routed down-projection kernels run 39 times per decode token — once per sparse MoE layer. If the compiler currently does not scalarize their fixed-4 loops as aggressively as with the explicit pragma (the same gap found in the QK-norm kernels), forcing full unroll lets the compiler schedule the four independent operations for better instruction-level parallelism. Because these are among the highest-call-count decode kernels, even a small per-call throughput gain compounds across the 39 sparse layers.

The dense-MLP (layer 0) contribution is smaller (1/40 of decode) but zero-risk and stacks with the sparse-layer wins on the same proven technique.
