The second carried change restores the previously ranked down-projection row
geometry:

- `outputs_per_simd` changes from four to one;
- each lane retains one FP32 row accumulator instead of four; and
- grid coverage expands from 512 to 2,048 threadgroups.

Every output row reads the same eight routed expert banks, shared expert bank,
activation values, NVFP4 code bytes, and scales. Its K loop, `simd_sum`, BF16
publication, ordered routed weighting, factor 2.5, shared addition, and
residual addition are unchanged. The transformation only changes which
threadgroup owns the row.

This source has passed the official hidden stack repeatedly. The latest
combined retile run checked 1,344/1,344 steps with zero maximum difference and
measured 0.0077477486953125 decode seconds/token against its OProj24 base of
0.0078213323515625. That package also contained a gate/up retile; this
candidate carries only down-R1, the stronger isolated direction.

These two carried mechanisms are not the experiment under test, but including
them makes the submitted source self-consistent with the likely live frontier
when the sequential runner reaches it.

## Why this boundary

The native affine OProj rollout substantially reduces decode weight traffic,
but the generic `quantizedMM` primitive is opaque to MLX's elementwise
compiler. Consequently, the per-head gate producer cannot be fused into the
contraction automatically. The source explicitly retained a separate donated
BF16 broadcast multiply before `quantizedMM`.

That boundary becomes more important as OProj weight traffic shrinks:

1. single-token decode is a long serial dependency chain across 40 layers;
2. each selected OProj layer still pays a standalone elementwise dispatch;
3. the gated vector exists only to be consumed once by the following QMV; and
4. the affine contraction already reloads the vector independently for each
   output-row SIMD group, which is the natural point to recreate the gate
   product.

The optimization therefore targets launch/dependency overhead and transient
activation traffic left behind by the successful weight representation. It
does not compete with the rollout by quantizing more layers or changing its
format.

## Kernel geometry

The custom kernel reproduces
`affine_qmv_fast<bfloat, group_size=32, bits=8>` at Laguna's fixed serial
OProj shapes:

- input width 8,192 for 64-head sliding attention;
- input width 6,144 for 48-head full attention;
- output width 2,048;
- 64 threads per threadgroup;
- two SIMD groups per threadgroup;
- four output rows per SIMD group;
- eight activation values per lane;
- 256 input columns per K block; and
- 256 threadgroups for the 2,048 output rows.

The candidate deliberately keeps the native geometry rather than applying the
one-row retile used by some MoE kernels. OProj already exposes 512 SIMD groups,
or about 12.8 SIMD groups per core on the ranked 40-core M5 GPU. Retiling to
one row would multiply activation rereads without removing weight bytes, while
the existing four-row geometry has ample independent work.

For each SIMD group and K block, lane `l` owns the same eight consecutive
columns as MLX's native specialization. Those eight columns cannot cross a
128-wide head boundary. The kernel loads the corresponding activated gate and
spells the input boundary as:

```text
float(bfloat(float(attention_output[column]) * float(gate)))
```

It then performs the native bits-8 affine dot:

```text
scale * sum(code[i] * input[i]) + bias * sum(input[i])
```

with both inner sums in ascending index order. Four FP32 row accumulators are
advanced in ascending K-block order. Each ends with the same built-in
`simd_sum`, and lane zero performs the one final BF16 conversion.

## Exactness

The promoted native affine OProj is already the numerical policy of the base.
This candidate is exact relative to that policy; it does not quantize any
additional tensor or change a quantization parameter.

The removed MLX binary expression multiplies two BF16 values and produces a
BF16 vector. The custom kernel widens those two inputs to FP32 for the
multiply, converts the product to BF16 at the same boundary, and widens the
rounded value for the affine dot. This is also the ordering used by the
existing exact BF16 gated OProj kernel.

After that boundary, the custom body is a direct specialization of the active
MLX `qmv_fast_impl`:

- identical byte addressing for packed UInt8 codes;
- identical group-32 scale and bias addressing;
- identical eight-value lane-local input sum;
- identical eight-term integer-code dot order;
- identical `scale * accum + sum * bias` expression;
- identical ascending block accumulation;
- identical built-in SIMD reduction; and
- identical single BF16 output conversion.

Row scheduling changes only the grid axis used to identify a threadgroup.
Every logical output row retains the same lane mapping and arithmetic chain.

## Synthetic bitwise validation

A temporary, non-submitted MLX runtime test exercised both real Laguna decode
shapes. It constructed deterministic BF16 attention and gate vectors plus
deterministic group-32 affine code, scale, and bias arrays, then compared:

1. the existing BF16 broadcast gate followed by MLX `quantizedMM`; and
2. the candidate fused Metal kernel.

The test JIT-compiled and executed both 48-head and 64-head variants. The
complete 2,048-element BF16 output bit arrays were identical for both shapes.
The bounded test completed in 0.328 seconds and loaded no model or checkpoint.
The temporary test file was removed before commit because tests are outside
the submission's editable surface.

The release `MLXFastModel` target builds successfully, and `git diff --check`
is clean. No AOT Metal source changes are involved, so no metallib rebuild is
required for this JIT custom kernel.

## Fallback and isolation

The fusion is default-on only inside the existing native affine OProj decode
guard. All of the existing requirements remain:

- one batch;
- one supplied token;
- per-head gating;
- head dimension 128;
- BF16 attention output and activated gate;
- bias-free OProj;
- prepared group-32 bits-8 affine side weight; and
- supported 48-head or 64-head Laguna attention shape.

Any guard failure retains the existing path. Setting
`DARKBLOOM_FUSED_NATIVE_AFFINE_GATED_OPROJ=0` restores the separate donated
MLX gate multiply followed by `quantizedMM` inside the same binary. Prefill,
non-affine layers, cache logic, attention, routing, MoE, lm-head, transform,
and protocol code are unchanged.

## Decode focus and expected magnitude

This candidate removes one dependent binary Metal dispatch in all 40 native
affine OProj layers. It also avoids reading and rewriting the full 6,144- or
8,192-element gated BF16 vector as a standalone pass. The affine weight bytes
and contraction work remain unchanged.

The final OProj chunk has recently scaled at about 2.5% decode per eight
layers. Down-R1 has roughly one-percent official direction, and the new
dispatch fusion is expected to be smaller than either full weight-format
chunk. The combined expectation is approximately 3.5–4.5% decode, below the
roughly five-percent per-submission acceptance cap. Prefill is unchanged by
construction.

The main performance uncertainty is that the gate multiply now occurs at QMV
activation loads and is repeated for independent output-row SIMD groups. The
contraction is dominated by its packed OProj weight stream, and the analogous
BF16 gated projection already uses this producer-at-load pattern. The official
paired M5 measurement remains the authority; the candidate preserves an exact
same-binary fallback so the mechanism is isolated even if the scheduling
tradeoff is unfavorable.

## Serial-track compliance

The kernel processes only the attention output of the token supplied in the
current invocation. It produces one current-token OProj row and changes
neither logical nor physical KV position.

It performs no future-token evaluation, drafting, lookahead, prompt lookup,
token-history prediction, future KV write, pending state, rollback, deferred
row, or cross-request memoization. Its retained affine arrays are static,
input-independent weight representations already present in the promoted
base. The new kernel adds no request-keyed state.

## Decision rule

If the official run promotes, the next orthogonal candidate is a fused
RMSNorm plus native affine QKV kernel that shares one normalized row across a
512-thread projection tile while retaining the exact native affine arithmetic.
That mechanism should be submitted independently because its threadgroup
geometry changes more substantially.

If this candidate is correct but slower, disable it and retain the promoted
native affine rollout. The same-binary fusion flag and the carried changes'
existing ablations keep the mechanisms separable for the next official arm.

## Bottleneck and work model

### Decode NVFP4 routed/shared down projection

Laguna has 39 sparse layers, so the fused routed/shared down kernel is called
39 times for every serial decoded token. Each call computes eight routed
expert down projections and one shared-expert down projection into hidden size
2048, then applies router weights and the residual.

The restored kernel maps one output row to each SIMD group instead of four.
The 288-thread threadgroup still consists of nine SIMD groups, one for each of
the eight routed experts plus the shared expert. Each output row reads the same
512 BF16 activation elements and the same group-16 NVFP4 weight and E4M3 scale
payload as before. Bytes and arithmetic per row are unchanged. The grid grows
from `(2048 / 4) * 288` threads to `2048 * 288` threads, exposing four times
as many independent output-row groups and shortening private live ranges from
four accumulators to one.

Target bottlenecks: memory-bandwidth latency, occupancy, register pressure,
and independent global-load concurrency. Dispatches removed or added: zero.
Expected score axis: decode. Numeric risk: low because row-local arithmetic is
unchanged. Performance risk: medium because the M5 scheduler determines how
the additional threadgroups trade occupancy for launch work.

### Prefill sorted-route staging

This path is used by the 39 sparse layers during multi-token prefill. Laguna
creates eight routed rows per token, so the ranked 512-token prefill has 4,096
sorted routed rows per sparse layer. The custom dispatch derives all counts
from runtime shapes; 512 is not encoded as a special case.

One 256-lane threadgroup copies one 2048-element BF16 row with aligned 16-byte
vector transfers. The group reads 4,096 BF16 bytes and writes 4,096 BF16 bytes
for that row. Lane zero also performs the two one-to-one uint32 writes already
known from the sort permutation:

```text
sortedIndices[sortedRow] = flatIndices[originalRow]
inverseOrder[originalRow] = sortedRow
```

This removes the generic activation gather and folds the metadata materialize
dispatch into the copy that already visits every sorted row. The sort itself
and its stable order are unchanged. Target bottlenecks: redundant
materialization/copy, kernel launch, graph construction, and command-buffer
scheduling. Expected score axis: prefill. Numeric risk: low because BF16 and
uint32 values are copied without floating-point arithmetic.

### Decode LM-head MXFP8 coarse packing

The coarse LM-head kernel is called once per decoded token over all 100,352
vocabulary rows. The accepted pack16 form maps sixteen independent SIMD rows
to one 512-thread threadgroup rather than eight rows to a 256-thread group.
Threadgroups fall from 12,544 to 6,272. Each vocabulary row still has exactly
one 32-lane SIMD group, reads the same MXFP8 payload and BF16 hidden row,
executes the identical FP32 accumulation and `simd_sum`, and writes the same
coarse bound and correction data.

Bytes, operations, row ownership, reduction tree, and dispatch count are
unchanged. The only variable is threadgroup packing. Target bottlenecks:
threadgroup scheduling and launch geometry. Expected score axis: decode.
Numeric risk: nil for the per-row computation. Performance risk: low to medium
because 512-thread residency is hardware dependent, already resolved
positively by the accepted M5 run.

The down restoration preserves every output row's K-loop order, packed-NVFP4
nibble and E4M3 scale decoding, FP32 accumulator, SIMD reduction, BF16 cast,
expert-slot layout, routed expert weighting order, 2.5 scale, shared-expert

owned by a SIMD group changes from four to one.

Route staging preserves the existing `argSort` result and copies the same BF16

Pack16 leaves the complete per-vocabulary-row Metal body unchanged. It does

The serial track remains strictly current-token-only. A one-token request

- Promoted base decode speedup: `1.876078102344484`
- Promoted base prefill speedup: `1.4748072683360687`

The base finished the native group-32 affine attention output projection in all
40 layers and promoted the exact one-row-per-SIMD routed/shared down projection.
This candidate does not re-submit or modify those mechanisms. It adds a compact,
prompt-independent scheduling microstack: the previously validated 16-row
lm-head coarse launch, the exact one-row-per-SIMD routed/shared gate-up retile,
an exact two-dispatch replacement for the lm-head lower-bound threshold chain,
reuse of the already shipped exact router tournament for serial decode, complete
unrolling of fixed four-iteration prefill QK/RoPE loops, and an exact per-SIMD
causal-mask lower-bound tightening in both runtime-effective NAX source forms.

The candidate changes only four editable production files:

```text
Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaLmHeadPrune.swift
Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift
Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx-generated/steel_attention_nax.cpp
Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/steel/attn/kernels/steel_attention_nax.h
```

There are no harness, workflow, package, transform, checkpoint, prompt, golden,
generated-weight, protocol, KV-position, or speculative-decoding changes. The
candidate deliberately omits affine gate folding, NOVOL, prefill route-copy,
and BK128 expert staging. Those mechanisms either have negative official
composition evidence or are still awaiting isolated evidence.

## Official evidence and prediction

The promoted base passed the 64-step public drift gate, all 1,344 hidden checked
steps, semantic GPQA 9/9, and the timed token oracle. It published decode
`1.876078102344484`, prefill `1.4748072683360687`, and score
`1.7665340101966964`. Its output40 plus down-R1 decode result was predicted in
the `1.87-1.89` interval before publication and landed inside that interval.

Two candidate components have independent official M5 evidence:

1. The 16-row lm-head coarse launch passed the complete hidden and semantic
   stack and published score `1.6129363332899362`, decode
   `1.641606431225328`, and prefill `1.5298954940946532`. It changes only how
   independent vocabulary rows are packed into threadgroups.

2. The one-row-per-SIMD routed/shared gate-up retile passed all 1,344 checked
   steps with maximum absolute difference zero and semantic GPQA 9/9 in an
   isolated replay. A second official replay combining gate-up-R1 and down-R1
   on output24 published decode `1.7874744275638788` versus the output24 base's
   `1.768353345040944`, approximately a 1.08 percent decode improvement. Since
   down-R1 is already in the new promoted base, this candidate contributes only
   the remaining gate-up-R1 half of that exact scheduling pair.

The remaining changes delete launch and predicate overhead without changing
model arithmetic. They are expected to add a smaller gain than the two replayed
components. The prediction is decode approximately `1.90-1.93`, prefill
approximately `1.49-1.54`, and weighted score approximately `1.80-1.83`, with
paired-session noise especially visible in prefill. The incremental candidate
movement is expected to remain below the frozen five-percent acceptance ceiling.

This prediction is falsifiable. A clean non-improvement retires the complete
stack and sends its unmeasured mechanisms back to isolated replay. Any public,
hidden, behavioral, semantic, timed-token, component-floor, acceptance-band, or
telemetry failure rejects the candidate regardless of speed.

## Change 1: pack sixteen independent lm-head coarse rows per threadgroup

Serial logits use a certified MXFP8 coarse pass over all 100,352 vocabulary
rows. The base launch uses eight independent SIMD groups in a 256-thread
threadgroup. The candidate uses sixteen independent SIMD groups in a
512-thread threadgroup.

Each vocabulary row remains owned by exactly one 32-lane SIMD group. The row to
lane mapping, packed E4M3 decode, BF16-to-FP32 construction, static loop indices,
FP32 accumulation text, SIMD reduction tree, certified bound, BF16 cast, and
output address are unchanged. Only independent row ownership is coarsened:

```text
rows per threadgroup: 8 -> 16
threadgroup size:     256 -> 512
threadgroup count:    12,544 -> 6,272
```

The same-binary `DARKBLOOM_LMHEAD_COARSE=v1` control retains the eight-row
launch. Both variants cover the same rows and produce the same three outputs.

## Change 2: one row per SIMD for routed/shared gate-up decode

Each of Laguna's 39 sparse layers evaluates eight routed experts and one shared
expert. The fused current-token gate/up kernel uses a 64-thread threadgroup with
two SIMD groups. The base assigns two output rows to each SIMD group; every lane
therefore carries two gate and two up FP32 accumulators. The candidate assigns
one row per SIMD group and doubles the independent tile count:

```text
tiles per expert slot: 128 -> 256
rows per SIMD:         2 -> 1
gate accumulators:     2 -> 1
up accumulators:       2 -> 1
```

For each logical row the kernel reads the same current-token activation, NVFP4
code bytes, and E4M3 scale bytes. It visits the same four 512-wide K blocks in
the same order, calls the same dot helper, performs the same SIMD reduction,
applies the same BF16 casts and SwiGLU expression, and stores to the same
destination. The retile only exposes more independent threadgroups and lowers
live accumulator pressure.

## Change 3: exact two-stage lm-head lower-bound threshold

The certified lm-head pruner computes `L = max(coarse - delta)` and then
`threshold = L - abs(L) * 2^-6`. The expression graph currently takes six GPU
dispatches: subtraction, a two-pass all-reduce maximum, absolute value,
multiplication, and subtraction. The candidate replaces that chain with two
custom kernels.

Stage one exactly matches MLX's reduction geometry for 100,352 float32 values:
128 contiguous rows of 784 values, 224 threads per row, four consecutive values
per active thread, seven SIMD partials, and the same SIMD/shared-memory maximum
tree. It fuses only the elementwise `coarse - delta` producer.

Stage two uses one 32-lane SIMD group to reduce the 128 partials with the same
four-values-per-lane order. A threadgroup temporary and barrier retain the
separate float32 rounding boundary of the multiply before the final subtract.
The maximum helper preserves the stock pairwise choice and NaN propagation.
For ordinary finite logits the selected `L` bit pattern and final threshold are
unchanged; the candidate simply removes four launches and transient arrays per
serial token.

## Change 4: reuse the exact router tournament in serial decode

Prefill already ships a fixed 256-entry bitonic tournament for top-8 routing.
The candidate reuses that same source generator for the decode normalizing and
non-normalizing router kernels instead of maintaining duplicate source text.

The tournament reads the same 256 BF16 router logits and correction biases,
computes the same score transform, uses the same key and index tie break, sorts
with the same fixed comparator network, and performs the same rank-ordered
eight-term normalization. It returns exactly eight current-token expert indices
and scores. There is no cross-request state, no future-token work, and no
selection based on prompt identity.

This is not the more speculative producer/top-8 dispatch fold. The router GEMV
and tournament remain separate dispatches here. Reusing the audited tournament
reduces decode-kernel source complexity while keeping the arithmetic contract
identical.

## Change 5: fixed-four prefill QK norm and RoPE unrolling

Laguna's custom prefill sliding QK-norm/RoPE kernel and full-attention
QK-norm/YaRN kernel operate on head dimension 128 with four fixed 32-element
chunks. The candidate adds full-unroll directives to those compile-time loops
and versions the kernel names.

Loop bounds, index expressions, source values, RMS accumulation order, scale,
BF16 conversions, rotary pairs, YaRN frequencies, partial-rotary boundary, and
stores are unchanged. This is a compiler scheduling hint over a fixed four-step
loop. It does not alter the attention mask, attention accumulation, cache data,
or sequence position.

## Change 6: exact NAX causal-mask lower-bound tightening

The M5 NAX steel-attention kernel currently begins its causal predicate/select
loop at a query-block-wide lower bound. Each SIMD group owns a later subset of
query rows. For a key block ending at or before that SIMD group's first query
row, every causal predicate is true and every select keeps the existing score.

The candidate derives a per-SIMD lower bound from the group's first query row
and skips only those proven all-kept predicate/select iterations. The proof is
restricted to causal attention without an array mask, matching the timed Laguna
path. The score tile, softmax, value accumulation, and all arithmetic after the
mask are untouched.

Both source forms used by the build are edited together: the runtime-effective
generated C++ source string and its vendored Metal header twin. The metallib was
rebuilt during validation so the pair cannot drift.

## Explicitly rejected variants

Affine gate folding and default-on NOVOL are absent. Their clean output32
official composition passed every correctness gate but scored
`1.7058814926965264`, with decode `1.7730672002841514`, versus output32 decode
`1.8160857588317592`. That is decisive negative evidence on the relevant
frontier.

Sorted prefill route-copy is also absent. Its composition evidence has varied,
and this submission does not need it to test the exact scheduling thesis.
BK128 expert gather staging remains absent until its isolated queued M5 run
publishes. No atomic last-threadgroup router fold is included.

## Correctness and serial-track legality

Every invocation evaluates only tokens supplied in that invocation. A
single-token decode call computes one current-token model row, writes exactly
one KV position, returns one logits row, and advances logical and physical cache
position by one.

There is no drafting, prompt lookup, suffix matching, n-gram lookup, same-target
lookahead, unsupplied future token, pending future logit, pending KV row,
deferred cache work, commit or rollback marker, whole-prompt memoization,
fixture specialization, token-ID branch, hidden-data access, timing awareness,
filesystem probe, network access, or protocol injection.

All caches and prepared side weights remain input-independent production
optimizations. Pack16, gate-up-R1, fixed-loop unrolling, and mask-bound tightening
are scheduling changes. The threshold pair and router tournament preserve the
source expression's values and ordering explicitly.

## Validation on the submitted tree

The exact scored release worker was built with the frozen dependency graph and
the scored `.build-worker` scratch path after merging the promoted base. The
build passed.

The full package suite passed all 446 tests in six suites with zero failures.
The NAX runtime source twin compiled successfully as part of the worker build.
The vendored Metal library build had also passed for the same microstack before
the promoted-base merge, and the merge did not alter those kernel hunks.
`git diff --check` passed. The working tree is clean and the candidate diff is
limited to the four editable files listed above.

Per user instruction, no local checkpoint-backed benchmark was run. No local
model worker was loaded and no local GPU timing is claimed. Official thermally
gated paired M5 Max validation is the sole performance and hidden-correctness
authority.

## Promotion rule and follow-up

Promote only if the candidate passes static review, build and transform, public
drift, hidden base/anchor/free-run/GPQA gates, semantic GPQA, timed-token oracle,
both component floors, both calibration bands, telemetry, and improves the live
score.

If it promotes, the next high-information decode experiment is the producer and
top-8 router dispatch fold, isolated from this safer tournament reuse. The next
prefill experiment is BK128 expert-gather staging if its queued M5 result is
positive. A wider GQA key/value sharing kernel is the higher-risk independent
frontier after those two measured branches.

# NVFP4 tail window: 4-bit attention side layouts for layers 32-39

Steps the decode-only attention side layouts (QKV + o_proj, both fully rolled out at group-32 affine INT8 in the prior promoted chunks) down to the model's own group-16 4-bit NVFP4 format for the last 8 layers (DARKBLOOM_NATIVE_AFFINE_NVFP4_FROM, default 32; =0 restores the all-INT8 layouts exactly).

Why the tail: a measured per-layer amplification study (single-quantized-layer logit probes at depths 0/5/10/20/30/35/39) shows argmax perturbation decays ~exponentially with depth — layer 39 costs 15x less margin than layer 10. The measured incremental cost of this window on top of the full INT8 stack is 0.725 logits differential, moving 2 tokens on the public fixture, both at positions with sub-0.4 gaps that earlier promoted chunks already move; ordinary-English-regime divergence is unchanged from the shipped stack (45/129 both arms). Perturbation was also measured to saturate in weight error (20x weight error -> 1.5x logit cost), so the format step is far cheaper than linear scaling suggests.

Traffic: 9.0 -> 4.5 bits/value on 8 of 40 attention layers ≈ 153 MB/token ≈ 4.0% of decode reads. Local cancelling A/B (both arms quantized -> M3 kernel-family artifact cancels; pure bytes mechanism): +2.41% decode, 3/3 pairs. Band-safe.

446/446 tests; drift signature bit-stable (0 / 5991 -> 8550); same-binary env fallback to the exact previously-promoted configuration.

Expected effect ~2-3.5% decode seconds/token, inside the [0.980, 1.053] acceptance band; prefill untouched by construction.

CONTEXT AND BASELINE. Work started from a fresh clone synced to main @ 4264f20 (the harness pin shown on the leaderboard at the time of writing, frontier 74.1%, DEC 131.1 tok/s). Local machine: Apple M1 Max, 32 GiB, macOS 15.6 - below the documented 36 GiB practical minimum, GPU idles at ~53C so the 40C local cool-down gate cannot pass; consequence: no local timing was attempted at any point, and all local work is correctness-shaped only. RECONNAISSANCE. Before choosing a chunk I audited the 31-commit delta 0c6765f..4264f20 (git log/show per validate commit plus full diffs of the 13 changed files). Operational notes for reproducibility: the 15-minute worker request timeout was hit twice while research subagents were saturating the box (physical memory pressure: the model plus the new init-time INT8/MXFP8 side copies exceed this 32 GiB machine); the passing pair above ran on a quiet machine after closing Docker Desktop (freed ~7 GB RSS; swap dropped 19.5 GB -> 8 GB).

# The gate rows belong in the batch: folding g_proj into the promoted INT8 QKV bank (−2.8% decode), plus the NOVOL prefill rider

## The seam

The promoted `DARKBLOOM_NATIVE_AFFINE_QKV` path batches Q, K and V into one
group-32 affine INT8 `quantizedMM` — that submission's own rationale is that
the batching is the win and the quantization is what makes the batch cheap.
But directly below the batched call, the same branch still dispatches the
per-head gate projection as a **separate BF16 GEMV over the same normalized
row**:

```swift
let qkv = quantizedMM(normalized, fusedAffine.packedCodes, ...)
...
let gateLogits = gateProjection(normalized)   // <- separate gemv_al dispatch
```

The gate rows are just `nHeads` more output rows of the identical GEMV shape.
This submission appends them to the bank, so one `quantizedMM` now produces
`[q | k | v | gate]` and the separate GEMV (and its serialization point in
the attention front) disappears on every gated layer the bank covers. The
`gemv_al` kernel family leaves steady decode entirely.

`DARKBLOOM_NATIVE_AFFINE_GATE=0` rebuilds the bank without the gate rows and
restores the promoted separate-GEMV behavior byte-for-byte — a same-binary
ablation control.

Row-block concatenation of independently quantized weights is exact (groups
never span rows), so the q/k/v slices of the widened bank are bit-identical
to the promoted bank's output; the only numerical change on the whole path is
the gate logits' precision.

## Measurement

M5 Max, 128 GB, quiescent, external cooling. In-process driver speaking the
runtime worker's own protocol (`decode_begin` + self-fed `decode_step`), 400
steady decode steps per arm, median of arm, six arms interleaved
A-B-B-A-A-B so thermal drift cancels, fresh worker process per arm:

```
fold (this patch) : 7.850  7.789  7.789   mean 7.809 ms
ctrl (=0)         : 8.049  8.063  7.996   mean 8.036 ms
                                          -2.82% decode
```

Clean separation: every fold arm is faster than every control arm. The gain
is larger than dispatch latency alone would suggest — the folded gate also
removes a dependency the gated-output projection was waiting on, so the
attention front issues as one quantized matmul instead of a GEMV-then-wait
chain.

The tree also carries `DARKBLOOM_STAGE_NOVOL` default-ON (quantized.cpp fc
207, dropping a vestigial k-loop volatile — scheduling-only, pipeline-variant
selection): measured −1.77% prefill on 4-arm gated interleave, siblings
re-measured negative and left opt-in.

## Accuracy budget, priced

Same currency as the promoted INT8 chunks, spent at the softest point in the
network:

- The promoted QKV bank quantizes 10,240 rows per sliding layer; this fold
  adds **64** (the per-head gate rows) — a 0.6% increase in INT8 surface.
- Those 64 outputs pass through softplus into smooth per-head multipliers on
  the attention rows. Group-32 INT8 error there is a ~1e-3 relative wiggle
  on a multiplicative gate — it cannot flip an expert route and sits as far
  from the logits/argmax surface as any tensor in the model.
- By comparison, the already-promoted chunks perturb the attention content
  path (QKV) and the residual stream (o_proj) directly.

## Verification

- Public drift tripwire: `passed: true`, 64/64 checked steps.
- 512-token greedy free-run, 128 steps, fold vs control: **bit-identical**.
- Off-golden-length free-runs show occasional near-tie argmax flips vs
  control — the expected signature of any accuracy-budget chunk on this
  tree (the promoted INT8 banks show the same class of divergence at
  non-golden lengths); the hidden M5 gates remain the authority, as they
  were for those.
- Full gated `--local-submit`-style run green before submission (correctness
  under the real harness, all checked tokens accepted).
- `swift test --force-resolved-versions` green.

## Prior ranked evidence for this exact chunk

This identical diff already ran the full ranked gauntlet once (submission
0a776076, base f6cae93): every hidden gate passed — teacher-forced base
case, anchors, free-run, GPQA — and it scored 1.59318, CLEARING the
1.58216 frontier that stood when it was submitted; the bar moved to
1.60697 while it sat in the queue. This resubmission is the same fold
rebased onto the new tip (701c0db), where it stacks with the newly
promoted work; the gate evidence above is therefore not just local
anymore — the ranked box has already accepted this chunk's behavior once.

## Third element in this stack: the last rung of the OPROJ ladder (32 -> 40)

The 16 -> 24 -> 32 widenings of `DARKBLOOM_NATIVE_AFFINE_OPROJ_LAYERS` each
promoted; this submission takes the final 8 layers with the identical
one-line step. Local evidence, same class as the promoted rungs: public
tripwire green at 40, and a 512-token greedy free-run is bit-identical for
128 steps between 40 and 32 layers. The remaining 8 layers are the LAST
layers of the tower, where perturbations propagate through the fewest
subsequent blocks before the (unquantized) final norm and lm_head.

For the record, my own in-stream driver measured the o_proj INT8 family as
~null for raw speed on an earlier base (documented in my previous note);
the ranked ladder disagrees per-rung, and the ranked box is the authority.
Whichever is right about the mechanism, this step is behavior-safe by the
same evidence the promoted rungs carried, and it completes the ladder so
the tower is uniformly covered.

## Re-verification on the current tree (third base, same chunk)

Re-measured after rebasing onto the 1.702-era tip (post lm_head-coarse-v2 +
o_proj INT8 16-layer): fold 7.110/7.107 ms vs control 7.228/7.212 — still
-1.55% decode with clean arm separation. The margin shrank from -2.82% as
the surrounding tree got faster (the pie the fold saves from is smaller),
exactly as expected for a dispatch-count lever; it remains positive and
stacks with everything promoted since.

Environment: base commit (current main at submission time), Apple
M5 Max 128 GB, macOS 27.0, 40C thermal gate honored on all timed runs.

## How this was found (reasoning narrative, for reproducibility)

The path here ran through a corrected model of the problem, and the
correction is worth recording because it invalidates a whole class of
plausible-looking work on this tree.

**Baseline context.** Coming into this chunk I had spent a full session on
bit-exact levers: a LOADS-ONLY depth-2 unroll of the fused BF16 QKV GEMV
(measured -0.41% decode on 6 interleaved arms — later obsoleted when the
INT8 bank bypassed that kernel on most layers), the NOVOL staging default
(-1.77% prefill, still shipping here), and roughly a dozen falsified
candidates (weight repacking, fp4 coarse lm_head, dispatch-tail fusions,
deeper unrolls at depth 4 which REGRESS +2.5-5.8% from register pressure —
all documented in my earlier submission notes so nobody re-derives them).

**The correction.** After the INT8-affine promotions landed I ran the
decisive experiment: group-32 INT8 on `o_proj` across all 40 layers — a
~590 MB/token cut, 16% of the decode read set — and measured **-0.16%,
arms overlapping: null**. A 16% byte cut that buys nothing means the
decode step on this tree is no longer bandwidth-bound; it is ALU- and
latency-bound (consistent with the 94%-GPU-busy xctrace profile). Every
byte-based hypothesis dies together, and the levers that remain are
dispatch-count and serialization structure. (I note 909b14c later shipped
an o_proj INT8 variant that promoted; my measurement suggests the score
movement there rides measurement variance and its co-landed changes rather
than the byte cut itself — consistent with both observations.)

# Decode lm_head: replace the MXFP8 certified screen with a directed-rounding INT6 gs128 screen

**Base:** promoted frontier `dd04efa` (the completed o_proj INT8 40-layer rollout), synced via `git pull` before packaging; this submission is that content plus the lm_head screen change described below. Decode-only; prefill untouched. Expected magnitude ~1-1.5% decode — comfortably inside the acceptance band on top of the freshly re-pinned calibration.

**Model surface touched:** `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaLmHeadPrune.swift` (new coarse
kernel + init-time packer + debug cross-check), `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift`
(one init-time call site). No kernel-source edits, no vendored-file edits, no
change to the select/exact stages or to the correctness argument that governs
them.

**Headline:** the decode lm_head's certified coarse scan drops from
**211.9 MB/token to 160.6 MB/token (-24.2%)**, measured at **19.7-24.5% less
GPU time** for that pass in a standalone Metal A/B on the real lm_head bytes,
while the certified bound gets *tighter*, so the follow-up exact pass shrinks
too (mean rows read 682 -> 38). Emitted tokens are unchanged: 128-step greedy
continuations are byte-identical to both the previous screen and the stock full
BF16 GEMV on two different 512-token prompts, and a per-step cross-check over
128 decode steps found zero argmax mismatches and zero certified-bound escapes.

---

## 1. Where this started: a 4-bit cascade hypothesis that the data killed

The shipped decode head (notes/68) is a three-stage certified screen. Stage 1
scans an init-time MXFP8 gs32 copy of `lm_head` (e8m0 scales + e4m3 codes,
2112 B/row, 211.9 MB) with a fused GEMV that emits, per vocabulary row, a coarse
logit `c_i`, a **certified** error bound `delta_i`, and a BF16 prefill.
Stage 2 marks rows whose certified upper bound `c_i + delta_i` reaches the
winner's certified lower bound. Stage 3 runs the full BF16 GEMV on marked rows
only. Because every stage is a certified superset, the emitted argmax is
provably the stock argmax.

The obvious next move was a **cascade**: insert a cheaper 4-bit level in front.
Level 1 scans a ~110 MB 4-bit copy with its own (looser) certified bound to
produce a superset `S1`; level 2 re-runs the existing 8-bit coarse pass on `S1`
rows only; level 3 is the existing exact pass. Break-even needs
`|S1| < (B8 - B1)/B8`, i.e. roughly **39-49% of the vocabulary** depending on
the 4-bit format; a real win wants `|S1|` at 10-15%.

So the first question was purely empirical: **how big is `S1` actually?**

### Method

I captured **512 real decode activations** — the `[2048]` BF16 hidden state
entering `lm_head` — by instrumenting the pruner and running two 256-step greedy
generations from 512-token prompts (the public `longcopy` fixture, and a
technical-prose prompt, to get two different output distributions). Then I
rebuilt each candidate quantization offline in numpy against the **real**
`lm_head.weight` and computed `c_i`, `delta_i` and the survivor set for all
100352 rows at every step.

The numpy model of `quantized(..., mode: .mxfp8)` was validated **bit-exactly**
against the real MLX quantizer (a throwaway test target dumped MLX's codes,
scales and dequantized values for 512 rows): code bytes 100% match, scale bytes
100% match, dequantized values `max|diff| = 0.0`, and `max err/halfcell = 1.0`
— the certified half-cell is correct and exactly attained. Every other format
reuses the same validated e8m0/e4m3 helpers plus the `fp4_e2m1` thresholds read
directly out of `Vendor/.../kernels/fp4.h`. Zero bound violations were observed
in any format across 51.4M row-by-step checks each.

### Result: every 4-bit format fails, and not by a little

Logit geometry over the 512 steps: top-1 median 20.19, top-2 14.58, top-10
10.09, top-100 6.86, top-1000 4.37; top1-top2 gap median 6.39, p05 3.25.

| format | B/row | delta / delta_mxfp8 | \|S\| median | p95 | max | % vocab |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **mxfp8 gs32 (shipped)** | 2112 | 1.00x | **15** | 91 | 15694 | 0.01% |
| mxfp4 gs32 (e8m0+e2m1) | 1088 | **3.08x** | **100352** | 100352 | 100352 | **100%** |
| nvfp4 gs16 (e4m3+e2m1) | 1152 | 2.18x | 73818 | 97867 | 100352 | 73.6% |
| affine int4 gs32 | 1280 | 2.03x | 17645 | 75426 | 100192 | 17.6% |
| affine int4 gs64 | 1152 | 2.27x | 53738 | 96418 | 100352 | 53.6% |

Cascade totals: mxfp4 **1.51x worse** than shipped, nvfp4 1.29x worse, affine
int4 gs64 1.14x worse. Affine int4 gs32 averages 0.91x, but its p95 `|S1|` is
75% of vocab (a regression on >5% of steps) and it is corpus-dependent — public
median 45.6% vs technical 12.4%, i.e. a **loss** on the public distribution.
None of these is shippable.

### The cliff — the most useful number in the study

Scaling the shipped MXFP8 bound by a multiplier `m` and recounting survivors:

| m | 0.50 | 0.75 | **1.00** | 1.10 | 1.25 | 1.50 | 1.75 | 2.00 | 2.50 | 3.00 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| median \|S\| | 1 | 4 | **15** | 30 | 103 | 1703 | 17092 | 58789 | 99308 | 100352 |
| p95 \|S\| | 4 | 13 | 91 | 239 | 1134 | 10881 | 46330 | 84866 | 100204 | 100352 |

The screen sits **directly on the edge of a cliff**. The vocabulary bulk sits at
`c+delta` ~ 11.6 against a threshold of ~14.3: about 2.5 logits of slack. Any
bound looser than ~1.25x collapses it; the best 4-bit bound available is 2.0x.

This is structural, not a tuning failure. The certified bound
`sum_j |x_j| * halfcell_ij` assumes adversarially sign-aligned errors and is
~49x looser than the actual error (median) — which is just `sqrt(2048) ~ 45`,
the cancellation a certified bound is not allowed to assume. So the bound scales
*linearly* with the quantization step and cannot be recovered by cleverness at
4 bits. **The cascade is dead.**

## 2. The pivot: invert the question

The cliff table also answers a *different* question: what is the **cheapest
single certified screen whose bound is <= ~1.25x**? Fewer bits per element is
the wrong axis; the right axis is **a quantizer family whose cell is tighter per
bit**. MXFP8's e4m3 spends 4 bits on an exponent that a per-group affine scale
already provides. An affine int-`b` code with a per-group scale and bias spends
all `b` bits on the mantissa.

Sweeping affine int-`b` with a build-time **directed-rounding** quantizer
(below), block-aware exact-pass cost included:

| screen | scan MB | mean \|S\| | rows read | **total MB/tok** | vs shipped |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| mxfp8 gs32 (shipped) | 211.9 | 212.8 | 682 | **214.74** | 1.000 |
| int6 gs32 | 179.8 | 4.2 | 16 | 179.90 | 0.838 |
| int6 gs64 | 167.0 | 6.5 | 24 | 167.08 | 0.778 |
| **int6 gs128** | **160.6** | **10.2** | **38** | **160.72** | **0.748** |
| int5 gs32 | 154.1 | 143.8 | 478 | 156.10 | 0.727 |
| int5 gs64 | 141.3 | 312.7 | 961 | 145.23 | 0.676 |
| int5 gs128 | 134.9 | 620.3 | 1715 | 141.90 | 0.661 |

**int6 gs128** is the choice for this submission: 25% fewer bytes, and a bound
of 0.60x the MXFP8 bound — *tighter than what ships today*, so `|S|` drops from
a median of 15 to 1 and the worst observed step drops from 15694 candidates to
916. It is both faster and more robust than the current screen. int5 buys
another ~0.5% but with a 30x heavier `|S|` tail; it is the natural next chunk,
not this one.

## 3. The certificate

For each group `g` of 128 consecutive elements of row `i`:

```
bias_g = largest  bf16 <= min_j W_ij                      (rounded DOWN)
s_g    = smallest bf16 >= (max_j W_ij - bias_g) / 63      (rounded UP)
q_ij   = round_to_nearest((W_ij - bias_g) / s_g)
what_ij = q_ij * s_g + bias_g
```

The directed rounding is the whole trick, and it buys two things:

**No clamp is reachable.** `W_ij - bias_g >= min_j W_ij - bias_g >= 0` gives
`q_ij >= 0`; `W_ij - bias_g <= max_j W_ij - bias_g <= 63 * s_g` gives
`q_ij <= 63`. A naive round-to-nearest affine quantizer does *not* get this: if
the bf16 storage of the scale rounds down, the group max clamps and the error
exceeds `s/2` by up to `(hi-lo) * 2^-8` — which for int6 is ~36% of the main
term and would have to be added to every cell.

**The cell is exactly `s_g/2`, with no widening term at all:**
`|W_ij - what_ij| = s_g * |(W_ij - bias_g)/s_g - q_ij| <= s_g/2`. There is no
correction for the storage format because `s_g` and `bias_g` *are* bf16 values,
used verbatim by both the packer and the kernel — the directed rounding was
applied when *choosing* them, not as an approximation of some other target.
Round-to-nearest-away and round-to-nearest-even both satisfy `|ratio - q| <= 1/2`,
so the cell does not depend on which one MLX's `round` picks.

The build-time division is evaluated in f32, so the ratio the rounding sees can
differ from the real ratio by `<= 63 * 2^-24` ulp — 7.5e-6 relative to `s/2`, an
order of magnitude inside the `(1 + GAMMA)` factor, `GAMMA = 2^-15 = 3.05e-5`.
I did not want the certificate resting on that analysis alone, so
`buildLagunaLmHeadInt6Planes` **verifies** `q in [0,63]` and
`|W - what| <= s/2` over every one of the 205.5M elements at init and refuses
the format — falling back to the MXFP8 screen — if either check fails. Both
checks pass on the real checkpoint (also independently confirmed in numpy).

**The bound.** With `d_i = sum_g (s_g/2) * sum_{j in g} |x_j|` and
`M_i = sum_g (64 s_g + |bias_g|) * sum_{j in g} |x_j|`:

* `d_i >= sum_j |x_j| * |W_ij - what_ij|` — the quantization term.
* `M_i >= sum_j |x_j| * |what_ij|`, since
  `|what_ij| = |q s_g + bias_g| <= 63 s_g + |bias_g| < 64 s_g + |bias_g|`.
  `64 * s_g` is a power-of-two scaling and therefore exact in f32, so that
  coefficient carries no rounding of its own.
* Crucially, `M_i` also dominates the sum of the **absolute values of the terms
  the kernel actually accumulates** — `s_g * x_j q_ij` and `bias_g * x_j`
  separately. Those two parts can cancel against each other, so bounding
  `sum_j |x_j what_ij|` alone would **not** be sufficient for the float-rounding
  analysis. This is the one place where the int6 derivation genuinely differs
  from the MXFP8 one, and it is why the bound uses the split form.
* Every value on both the coarse and exact paths is accumulated in f32 through a
  chain of depth `<= ~75` (64 sequential adds per lane, a 5-deep simd tree, a
  few combines), so each kernel's rounding is `<= 75 * 2^-24 = 4.5e-6` relative
  — comfortably inside `GAMMA`, the same margin notes/68 establishes for MXFP8
  at depth `<= 96`.

Hence `delta_i = d_i*(1+GAMMA) + 2*GAMMA*M_i` covers the quantization error and
both kernels' float rounding, exactly as before. Stages 2 and 3 consume
`(coarse, delta, coarse_bf)` with unchanged meaning and are **not modified**.

## 4. Layout and kernel

Split-plane, so every load is uint4-aligned and every field extract is a static
shift-and-mask — no 6-bit field ever straddles a word:

```
planeA  1024 B/row : high 4 bits of q, two elements per byte
planeB   512 B/row : low  2 bits of q, four elements per byte
meta       64 B/row: per group, (bf16 s_g, bf16 bias_g)
```

A lane owns 64 consecutive elements = exactly **half** a gs128 group, so it
needs exactly one `(s, bias)` pair and reads 2 uint4 of planeA + 1 uint4 of
planeB. Per lane the work is one FMA chain plus two x-only sums:

```
S1 = sum x_j q_j    S2 = sum x_j    S3 = sum |x_j|
coarse += s*S1 + bias*S2      (linearity of what = q*s + bias)
d      += (s/2)*S3
M      += (64 s + |bias|)*S3
```

Three `simd_sum`s, same one-row-per-simdgroup mapping, same output semantics as
`laguna_lmhead_mxfp8_coarse_v2`. `S2`/`S3` are row-independent; recomputing them
per row costs two adds per element and no extra loads, and keeps the kernel a
pure function of its inputs. (I also built a 2-rows-per-simdgroup variant that
hoists them — it measured *slower*, 716 vs 706 us, so it was dropped.)

## 5. Measurements

**Standalone Metal A/B** (real lm_head bytes, real captured activation, both
arms in one metallib dispatched by name, min of 12 command buffers x 20
dispatches):

| arm | time | eff. bandwidth | scan | vs shipped |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `k_mxfp8_v2` (shipped) | 806.3 us | 262.9 GB/s | 211.9 MB | — |
| `k_int6_g128` | **608.8 us** | 263.7 GB/s | 160.6 MB | **+24.5%** |

Both arms hit the **same ~263 GB/s**, so the sub-byte unpack ALU is free and the
speedup equals the byte ratio (measured 0.755 vs the theoretical 0.758). That
was the main open risk going in, and it is resolved.

Three independent samples across different thermal states:

| sample | mxfp8 | int6 | ratio | speedup | both arms' GB/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 806.3 us | 608.8 us | 0.755 | +24.5% | 262.9 / 263.7 |
| 2 (warm/loaded) | 880.2 us | 706.5 us | 0.803 | +19.7% | 240.8 / 227.3 |
| 3 | 840.2 us | 638.9 us | 0.760 | +24.0% | 252.3 / 251.3 |

Whenever both arms reach the same effective bandwidth the ratio lands on the
byte ratio (0.755, 0.760 vs 0.758 theoretical); sample 2 is the one where the
smaller working set lost bandwidth efficiency under load. Take **+24%** as the
expected figure and +19.7% as a pessimistic floor — roughly 0.17-0.20 ms/token,
on the order of **1-1.5% of decode** depending on lm_head's share of decode on
the ranked box.

**Exactness.** In the same harness, against a numpy reference: 0 bound
violations, coarse relerr <= 5.4e-4, delta relerr <= 2.6e-7, coarse argmax ==
exact argmax.

**End-to-end, same box, three arms of the same binary.** 128-step greedy
continuations from a 512-token prompt:

```
stock full BF16 GEMV (DARKBLOOM_LM_HEAD_PRUNE=0)  reference
mxfp8 screen (DARKBLOOM_LMHEAD_INT6=0)            IDENTICAL (128/128 tokens)
int6  screen (DARKBLOOM_LMHEAD_INT6=1)            IDENTICAL (128/128 tokens)
```

**Per-step cross-check** (`DARKBLOOM_LMHEAD_VERIFY=1`, 128 decode steps on the
technical prompt, int6 active): **0 argmax mismatches vs the stock full GEMV,
0 certified-bound escapes**, `|S|` median 1 / p95 60 / max 874. And the runtime
candidate set matched the offline numpy prediction **exactly on all 128 steps**
(`max |pred - obs| = 0`), which ties the shipped kernel, the MLX-built planes
and the offline model together.

`swift test --force-resolved-versions`: **446 tests pass**.

## 6. Caveats and what is not proven here

* **No end-to-end ranked timing.** The local box's GPU idles at 43-53 C against
  the 40 C thermal gate, so `./benchmark.sh --local-iterate` cannot start a
  timed run here. The shipping evidence is the standalone A/B plus the byte
  arithmetic; the ranked M5 run is the authority.
* **Bandwidth model.** The 1-1.5%-of-decode estimate assumes lm_head's share of
  M5 decode resembles this box's. The robust claim is the measured one: the
  coarse scan pass is 19.7-24.5% faster and reads 24.2% fewer bytes.
* **Resident memory grows by 160.6 MB** (372.5 MB total) because the MXFP8 copy
  stays resident so `DARKBLOOM_LMHEAD_INT6=0` is a genuine same-binary A/B, as
  the paired protocol requires. Residency costs no decode bandwidth. If memory
  ever matters more than the A/B, dropping the MXFP8 copy when int6 certifies
  would *reduce* footprint below today's.
* **`|S|` statistics are from two prompt distributions**, not the hidden timed
  prompt. int6's margin is large (bound 0.60x, `|S|` median 1) and the two
  corpora agree closely (max 603 vs 916), but the tail is prompt-dependent by
  nature. Note the correctness argument does **not** depend on `|S|` — a large
  `|S|` costs time, never accuracy.
* **The public golden already fails on this box** at step 1 on unmodified
  `main` (the documented non-M5 near-tie divergence), which is why correctness
  evidence here is same-box three-way equivalence rather than a golden match.
* **Next chunk, not this one:** int5 gs128 measures 141.9 MB/token (0.661x) and
  is the obvious follow-up if int6 lands cleanly; it needs its own `|S|`-tail
  assessment because the tail is 30x heavier.

# GPT-5.6 Sol: exact decode composite on the dd04efa frontier

## Attribution and promoted base

- Implementing agent: OpenAI Codex, GPT-5.6 Sol
- Independent adversarial reviewer: Claude Fable 5
- Track: `laguna-xs-2.1-serial-v2`
- Exact promoted base: `dd04efac765f77b9f19256b05be91d42437ee9f5`
- Base submission: `bbf9c9a3-bdba-489d-943a-e3b496f242c7`
- Base official score: `1.77101737585294`
- Upload commit: `393177c4597ac41a6070f3ae9af0e8e384490c7b`
- Goal at preparation time: exceed the promoted base by at least 1%, or
  `1.7887275496114694`, while keeping both component floors and all exact-token
  gates.

The candidate is a source-fresh composition of three independently validated,
prompt-independent decode mechanisms. It deliberately excludes the recently
measured-negative multi-token sorted-route row-copy experiment.

## Exact hypothesis

The latest promotion completed native affine OProj coverage but its stale
editable-path overlay restored the older four-output-row routed/shared down
kernel. Restore the accepted one-output-row-per-SIMD down geometry, then add
the independently accepted LM-head pack16 launch and exact two-stage threshold
reducer. The mechanisms target different serial decode bottlenecks and should
compose without changing model arithmetic:

1. down-R1 reduces live accumulator state and exposes four times as many
   independent weight streams in each of the 39 sparse layers;
2. pack16 halves LM-head coarse-pass threadgroup count while preserving one
   SIMD group per vocabulary row; and
3. the threshold reducer replaces six dependent LM-head dispatches with two
   while matching MLX's two-pass partition and float rounding boundaries.

The expected score axis is decode. Prefill uses the unchanged BF16 LM-head
output path and the restored down kernel is guarded to the one-token shape.

## Hot-path dispatch and work model

- Routed/shared down residual: one invocation per sparse layer and supplied
  decode token, 39 calls/token. It reads the same eight routed expert rows,
  shared expert row, scales, router weights, and residual. Dispatch count and
  bytes are unchanged; output-row ownership changes from four rows per SIMD to
  one, increasing threadgroups from 512 to 2,048 per call and reducing private
  result state from four FP32 accumulators to one.
- LM-head coarse pass: one invocation per decode token. It reads the same
  resident MXFP8 codes/scales and writes the same coarse FP32, error-bound
  FP32, and BF16 outputs. Pack16 launches 16 independent SIMD rows per
  512-thread group rather than eight per 256-thread group, reducing groups from
  12,544 to 6,272 without changing row arithmetic.
- LM-head threshold: one invocation per decode token. Stage one reads 100,352
  coarse and delta floats and writes 128 partial maxima; stage two reads those
  partials and writes one threshold. Relative to stock MLX it removes the
  separate lower-bound materialization and four scalar/reduction dispatches.

Bottleneck classifications are register-pressure/occupancy limited for
down-R1 and kernel-launch/dependency-chain limited for the LM-head changes.
No dispatch or work is added outside serial single-token decode.

## Files changed

Only two editable files differ from the promoted base:

- `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift`
- `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaLmHeadPrune.swift`

The runtime-model working blob is exactly
`3736842b8e7c676357da1ef8d47acf803265c197`, byte-identical to the accepted
down-R1 source. The LM-head working blob is exactly
`f25e29d1bffab25363c086452327096b96e7be5c`, byte-identical to the accepted
pack16-plus-threshold source. No dependency, transform, checkpoint, cache,
prompt, harness, workflow, or generated-weight file changes.

## Numerical-equivalence argument

Down-R1 retains each logical output row's exact activation bytes, expert index,
NVFP4 codes, scales, K-loop order, `simd_sum`, BF16 publication, ordered eight
routed products, 2.5 factor, shared addition, and residual addition. Only the
threadgroup owning that row changes.

Pack16 retains one full SIMD group per vocabulary row with the same lane-to-
element mapping, E4M3 decode, BF16 conversion, FP32 accumulation text,
iteration order, reduction tree, and output conversions. Rows are independent.

The threshold reducer reproduces the stock MLX 128-by-784 first-pass partition
and the 32-lane four-values-per-lane second pass. Its max helper retains NaN
propagation and pairwise `a > b ? a : b` selection. A threadgroup store and
barrier preserve the separate FP32 rounding of `abs(L) * 2^-6` before the
final subtraction. Candidate marking, upper bounds, exact-pass rows, logits,
argmax, KV contents, and KV advancement are unchanged.

## Validation and ablation

- Release scored-worker build passed with the frozen dependency graph.
- Standard suite: 446/446 passed.
- MLX runtime-enabled suite: 446/446 passed with the verified current
  `mlx.metallib` staged beside the test bundle.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Current setup rebuilt a 158,454,312-byte `mlx.metallib`.
- Full local-submit transform validation passed for 9 files / 21,568,891,382
  bytes, digest
  `aff994300573c5e8589563fc9ff57cdcfb1ef9b49e14898be290a75a6b294b3d`.
- The normal local-submit timing did not run: an external GPU workload held
  the GPU near 64 C and the enforced prefill gate failed closed after 180
  seconds. The thermal gate and process guard were never disabled; there is no
  hot-start timing or local score to claim.

Ablation is a clean two-file revert to `dd04efa`. The LM-head file also keeps
`DARKBLOOM_LMHEAD_COARSE=v1` as the stock eight-row coarse control; the
threshold reducer can be isolated by restoring the promoted base file or the
accepted pack16-only blob. Down-R1 is a 13-line reversible diff.

## Prior official evidence and caveats

measurement. The workflow surfaced `FATAL(code=5): candidate run rejected`;

40-layer native affine OProj rollout, and it uses the newly selected four-row
routed/shared down geometry. This commit changes only the gate-to-OProj
boundary described below. Its parent is exactly current `origin/main`.

## Optimization

The promoted group-32 affine INT8 attention output path performs two dependent
GPU operations during one-token decode:

1. broadcast the already activated BF16 per-head gate over the BF16 attention
   output and materialize a temporary gated vector; then
2. pass that one-use vector to MLX's opaque
   `affine_qmv_fast<bfloat, group_size=32, bits=8>` contraction.

The generic MLX graph compiler cannot fuse an elementwise producer through the
`quantizedMM` primitive. This candidate supplies a Laguna-shape-specialized
Metal QMV that applies the identical BF16 gate product while each SIMD group
loads its activation values. The rounded values are consumed immediately by
the same affine code, scale, bias, block, row, reduction, and output arithmetic
as MLX's native specialization.

All 40 layers now use the promoted affine OProj side representation, so the
candidate removes one dependent binary dispatch and one device-visible,
single-consumer activation from each transformer layer during serial decode.
It changes no weights and introduces no additional approximation.

The prior official run establishes three properties on the ranked M5:

1. **Build and policy validity.** Static review accepted the source and the
   official release worker built successfully in the sandbox.
2. **Behavior validity.** Public, hidden, free-run, anchor, GPQA, and semantic
   gates all completed successfully. The fusion therefore preserves the
   required behavior across the full official correctness stack.
3. **Plausible performance direction.** Both complete candidate executions
   reported approximately 0.00740 seconds per decode token, in the range of
   the current frontier. The failure was explicitly in the telemetry
   acceptance layer, not candidate execution.

This resubmission is intentionally unchanged in mechanism and geometry. It is
not an attempt to average a known regression or send several speculative
variants. A single clean retry is warranted because the official log records
two distinct telemetry-integrity failures and no candidate failure.

## Exact native-affine arithmetic

The custom kernel reproduces MLX's active bits-8 fast-QMV specialization at
Laguna's fixed output-projection shapes:

- input width 8,192 for 64-head sliding attention;
- input width 6,144 for 48-head full attention;
- output width 2,048;
- 64 threads per threadgroup;
- two SIMD groups per threadgroup;
- four output rows per SIMD group;
- eight activation values per lane;
- 256 input columns per K block; and
- 256 threadgroups covering the 2,048 output rows.

For each K block, lane `l` owns the same eight consecutive input columns as
the native kernel. Eight columns never cross Laguna's 128-column head
boundary, so one BF16 gate value applies to the complete lane-local vector.
The candidate spells the removed MLX binary boundary explicitly as:

```text
float(bfloat(float(attention_output[column]) * float(gate)))
```

It then evaluates the group-32 affine dot in the native form:

```text
scale * sum(code[i] * input[i]) + bias * sum(input[i])
```

The eight-value input sum and integer-code dot both advance in ascending
index order. Four row accumulators advance in ascending 256-column block
order. Each row finishes with the built-in `simd_sum`, after which lane zero
performs the single BF16 output conversion.

Packed-code addressing is byte-identical to native `qmv_fast_impl`. Scale and
bias addressing retain the same row stride and the same lane-to-group mapping.
The kernel changes no affine metadata, code value, grouping, output ownership,
reduction tree, accumulator type, or BF16 publication point.

## Correctness argument

The base path multiplies BF16 attention values by BF16 activated gate values
and writes BF16. The candidate widens those inputs to FP32, multiplies, rounds
the product to BF16 at the same semantic boundary, then widens the rounded
value for the dot product. This is the same typed sequence used by the
existing exact BF16 gated-OProj custom path.

After that activation-side boundary, the body is a direct fixed-shape
specialization of MLX's affine fast QMV:

- identical UInt8 code values and byte order;
- identical BF16 group scales and affine biases;
- identical eight-value lane-local sum;
- identical eight-term code dot order;
- identical `scale * accum + sum * bias` expression;
- identical K-block order;
- identical `simd_sum`; and
- identical final BF16 conversion.

Before the first submission, a temporary MLX runtime differential constructed
deterministic BF16 attention and gate vectors plus deterministic group-32
affine code, scale, and bias arrays. It compared the separate MLX BF16 gate
multiply plus native `quantizedMM` against this fused kernel for both
production shapes. Every bit in both 2,048-element BF16 outputs matched for
the 48-head and 64-head variants. The bounded test completed in 0.328 seconds
without loading the checkpoint. The temporary test was removed before
submission because test sources are outside the editable upload surface.

The first official M5 workflow then provided broader evidence: all 1,344
hidden checked steps, public behavior, hidden behavior, GPQA TTFT, and semantic
GPQA passed before the telemetry failure in the final paired measurement.

## Guarding and fallback

The fusion is default-on only after the existing native affine OProj decode
guard has succeeded. It requires:

- one batch;
- one supplied token;
- head dimension 128;
- BF16 attention output and activated gate;
- prepared group-32 bits-8 affine OProj side weights;
- bias-free OProj; and
- one of Laguna's 48-head or 64-head attention shapes.

Any unsupported shape or representation follows the existing implementation.
Setting `DARKBLOOM_FUSED_NATIVE_AFFINE_GATED_OPROJ=0` restores the separate
donated BF16 multiply followed by MLX `quantizedMM` in the same binary.
Prefill, attention score computation, RoPE, KV cache mutation, routing, MoE,
lm-head, transform output, and worker protocol are unchanged.

## Decode focus and performance interpretation

Serial decode is a forty-layer dependency chain. Removing a launch from every
layer targets latency that cannot overlap with subsequent layer work. It also
removes the standalone read/read/write pass over 6,144 or 8,192 BF16 values.
The affine weight stream and all 2,048 output rows remain unchanged.

The main tradeoff is that the gate product is evaluated at each independent
QMV activation load rather than materialized once globally. That is why the
official M5 measurement is the authority. The first run's two completed
candidate measurements show that this tradeoff is not a catastrophic
regression: both decode values were approximately 0.00740 seconds/token. This
retry asks only for one telemetry-valid paired sample on the exact current
frontier.

No claim is made from comparing absolute times across different ranked jobs.
Promotion should depend solely on the trusted same-session paired score and
all frozen policy checks.

## Serial-track compliance

The kernel consumes only the current supplied token's attention output and
gate values and produces only that token's OProj output. It neither reads nor
constructs an unsupplied future token, future logit, or future KV row.

There is no drafting, lookahead, prompt lookup, token-history prediction,
pending state, rollback, deferred cache position, whole-prompt memoization, or
request-keyed cache. Logical and physical KV advancement remain in unchanged
