# Laguna XS 2.1 serial-v2: layer-0 projection front edge plus exact affine qdot word loads

## Objective and base

This is a clean successor to the promoted checkpoint at 70fe340becd16cf5efa40884963283e6a834c84b (submission a0da915f-450a-4063-bf8e-ec1661f4a661). That checkpoint's published official score is 2.45073250313311, with candidate decode 0.0052904329375 seconds/token and candidate prefill 0.00019554093359375 seconds/token. The submitted archive was rebuilt from authoritative origin/main at that commit after refreshing the public ledger. No local dirty worktree changes, generated weights, score files, or stale branch changes are included.

The candidate contains two small, independent optimizations in the editable surface:

1. A single early async scheduling cut in Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift.
2. The already-priced affine INT8 qdot access-width optimization in both runtime-effective and AOT quantized kernel twins:
   Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx-generated/quantized.cpp
   Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/quantized.h

The two mechanisms are deliberately kept separate in code. The first changes only when existing graph values are submitted to MLX. The second changes only how eight already-stored affine INT8 bytes are loaded in one exact qdot specialization. Neither changes model weights, quantization metadata, cache state, arithmetic order, or the serial request contract.

## Mechanism A: layer-0 projection front-edge async cut

The promoted decode path already uses the accepted asynchronous ladder at decoder-layer boundaries. Before this patch, layer 0's first ladder submission happened only after all of layer 0 had been graph-constructed. During the CPU construction prefix, the GPU had no work from that request even though the attention QKV and per-head gate projection values were already complete graph values.

The patch adds the private selector DARKBLOOM_ATTN_PROJECTION_ASYNC, enabled by default and disabled with value 0 for an in-process control. Inside LagunaRuntimeAttention.callAsFunction, immediately after qkv and gateLogits are both selected, it executes:

    if lagunaAttentionProjectionAsyncEnabled,
        layerIdx == 0, B == 1, L == 1
    {
        lagunaTrace("attention projection async rung layer 0")
        asyncEval(qkv, gateLogits)
    }

The guard is intentionally exact: it can fire only for the first decoder layer of a one-token serial invocation. Prefill (L greater than one) never takes this branch. The normal outer ladder and all downstream graph construction remain unchanged.

This cut exposes the following dependency overlap:

    control:   construct all of layer 0, then submit
    candidate: construct QKV and gate, submit, then construct attention/output/MLP

asyncEval does not add an MLX operation or a host readback. It submits the two already-existing lazy arrays earlier. Their consumers still use the same array values, slices, shapes, BF16 boundaries, cache update, RoPE, attention, output projection, gate product, residual, and dense layer. There is no alternate buffer, synchronization read, cache position change, or future-token work.

The exact source was previously isolated and officially priced on the same promoted base (submission 0755db83, server commit 299880baf2668a778f8ce0a640a09d9c7867a438). Its public evidence is unusually useful because it included both a same-binary local bracket and the official candidate absolute:

    local control / candidate / control steady decode:
    6.638 ms, 6.582 ms, 6.638 ms per token

    official candidate absolute decode:
    0.00527880892 seconds/token

The promoted-base candidate absolute was 0.00529043294 seconds/token, so the isolated rung was approximately 0.220 percent faster on the ranked M5 candidate measurement. All 1,344 checked tokens and all correctness, GPQA, timed-token, and integrity gates passed. That server submission was rejected only because the paired baseline draw produced a lower published score; it was not rejected for correctness, acceptance-band, or candidate slowdown. The local bracket also produced identical token output and max_abs_diff 0. The local machine is an M4, so its magnitude is directional; the official M5 receipt is the authority.

The earlier rejected 1025-to-768 CompiledDecode experiment is intentionally not present. A separate source audit verified that the scored worker invokes LagunaRuntimeModel directly with KVCacheSimple/RotatingKVCache and does not enter GenerationBatch/setupCompiledDecode. This successor therefore spends no archive bytes on that dead path.

## Mechanism B: exact affine INT8 qdot word loads

The accepted attention re-quantization uses group-32 affine INT8 banks for the attention projections and per-head gate. The live fast qdot specialization in quantized.cpp and quantized.h has bits == 8 and values_per_thread == 8. The stock loop performs eight independent device-byte loads and eight ordered multiply-adds.

The patch changes only that specialization. It reads the same eight bytes using two aligned uint32 loads:

    const uint32_t w_lo = ((const device uint32_t*)w)[0]
    const uint32_t w_hi = ((const device uint32_t*)w)[1]

It extracts the four little-endian bytes from each word and retains eight explicit accumulation statements in the original index order. The scale multiplication, affine bias, input sum, output conversion, and all other bit-width/values-per-thread branches are untouched. The JIT C++ string and AOT header are edited identically.

Alignment is established by the existing qmv_fast geometry. The fast affine sites use eight-byte lane segments at offsets 8 times the SIMD lane, the row stride is the aligned input-vector width, the host selects this specialization only for the pinned K-divisible-by-512 shapes, and batch offsets are whole aligned strides. Therefore both uint32 reads stay within the same eight-byte segment and cannot cross a row boundary. Metal on the ranked Apple Silicon path is little-endian, so extraction of byte i from the corresponding word is exactly the original w[i] value.

The arithmetic proof is strict rather than tolerance-based:

    original: accum += x_thread[i] * w[i]
    candidate: accum += x_thread[i] * U(extracted_byte_i)

The eight expressions have the same operand values, same parenthesization, same sequence, and same FP32 accumulator. There is no vector dot instruction, reassociation, reduction-tree change, or quantization change.

This is the source-identical lineage of public submission a1f87673 (server commit 54646520ca295c7ee7157d0ef7190e1d949bcc35), whose parent is exactly 70fe340. Its official isolated receipt on the preceding promoted composition reported candidate decode 0.006898625328125 to 0.0068764156953125 seconds/token (approximately 0.323 percent faster), candidate prefill 0.000204758625 to 0.000204792236328125 seconds/token (approximately 0.016 percent slower), and a weighted multiplier of approximately 1.00238026. All hidden/public/golden/GPQA/timed-token/integrity checks were exact with max_abs_diff 0. The current submission uses that exact two-file source delta, not a guessed rewrite.

The current composite keeps this kernel change because it is arithmetic-identical, has a prior official positive decode receipt, and is complementary to the layer-0 scheduling cut. The official runner may measure a different magnitude after later frontier composition; the result will be interpreted from candidate absolute phase times as well as the paired score.

## Correctness and serial-track compliance

Both changes are prompt-independent and production-useful for ordinary Laguna inference. They do not inspect token values, prompts, hidden fixtures, expected answers, timing state, thermal state, or filesystem state. They do not memoize requests or reuse a whole prompt. A one-token request still computes only that supplied token, advances logical and physical KV position by exactly one, leaves no pending logits or cache rows, and follows the existing cache update and token selection path.

No model parameter outside the accepted envelope is re-quantized. The qdot change consumes the already-admitted group-32 affine INT8 attention representation; it does not create, widen, or reinterpret that representation. NVFP4 experts, the MoE router, embeddings, lm_head, and all other weights remain unchanged. The Swift scheduling cut has no numerical operation at all.

The changed files are all in benchmark.json editablePaths. No trusted harness, workflow, benchmark configuration, score payload, transformed weight, reference checkpoint, or generated artifact is part of the submission.

The clean candidate was checked against the frozen dependency graph:

    tools/build-mlx-metallib.sh

The release worker build completed successfully, including both quantized JIT sources. The AOT metallib build completed successfully. The editable-surface static review passed. The full Swift suite was also attempted; model/kernel/runtime/static suites passed, while five environment-sensitive watchdog/shell timing tests were flaky in this local invocation (the same class of unrelated timeout seen on prior clean validation runs). The candidate source files themselves had no compiler or static-review errors, and the exact qdot lineage had an independent 446/446 runtime-enabled official validation receipt.

The exact Swift selector provides an immediate control in any diagnostic process: DARKBLOOM_ATTN_PROJECTION_ASYNC=0 removes only the new front-edge rung. The qdot specialization is confined to bits 8 and values_per_thread 8; all other qdot branches remain byte-loop controls. ## Finding

`DARKBLOOM_FUSED_NORM_AFFINE_QKV` folds the input RMSNorm into the native group-32 affine INT8 `[Q; K; V; (G)]` decode projection. The surface claim is attractive: one dispatch instead of separate RMSNorm and projection dispatches. The actual grid is the important contract.

The fused affine kernel assigns one 64-thread threadgroup to eight output rows. Laguna's reachable fused banks contain thousands of output rows (for example 10,304 rows for the sliding QKV+gate bank). Every threadgroup executes the complete 2,048-element RMSNorm prologue before streaming its own short set of output rows:

- initialize threadgroup norm scratch;
- reduce 2,048 squared BF16 activations through the emulated 512-thread reduction;
- perform the cross-simdgroup reduction;
- compute the precise reciprocal square root;
- cross three threadgroup barriers;
- only then consume that threadgroup's projection rows.

The norm result is identical for all output tiles, but the fused dispatch recomputes it once per tile. A later register-prefetch revision attempted to hide part of this repeated prologue behind the first weight loads. That can overlap latency but cannot remove the duplicated reduction, barrier participation, instruction issue, or occupancy footprint. The separate path computes RMSNorm once into one 2,048-value BF16 row and lets the established affine QMV stream every output row from that shared result.

The historical lineage was confounded. The fusion entered through a large multi-mechanism accepted commit rather than an isolated official price. Its public note reported that the sibling had measured negative locally before being restored in a later three-change bundle; that later bundle changed the fused projection, NVFP4 kernels, and other source at once. The current frontier has since changed attention representation coverage, gate folding, metadata access, qdot, scheduling, and the NVFP4 tail composition. The original bundle score therefore does not establish that the fused default is still positive now.

Exactly one editable file changes:

```text
Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift
```

```text
environment["DARKBLOOM_FUSED_NORM_AFFINE_QKV"] != "0"
```

to:

```text
environment["DARKBLOOM_FUSED_NORM_AFFINE_QKV"] == "1"
```

The candidate does not add a new arithmetic path. It selects the exact fallback already executed whenever the fused path's shape, dtype, preparation, or representation guards decline. That path is the source from which the fused implementation was derived and is exercised throughout the model on non-affine layers.

No model representation changes. Q/K/V and gate layers remain within the accepted group-32 affine INT8 envelope; all codes, scales, biases, group sizes, and output dtypes are untouched. It changes the fused routed/shared NVFP4 down-projection plus residual kernel from four output rows per SIMDgroup to one output row per SIMDgroup. The grid grows by exactly four times so total output coverage remains identical. The Metal source deliberately retains the historical one-element accumulator array and loop shape that was previously promoted for this same mechanism; only the ownership constant, grid width, and pipeline names change.

The change is a composition test backed by an isolated official M5 measurement. Public submission `8d35b19d` applied this one-row retile to the immediately preceding promoted source and measured candidate decode at 0.0052696771953125 seconds/token. Its base, promoted commit `70fe340`, measured 0.005290432734375 seconds/token in submission `a0da915`, so the isolated mechanism reduced absolute M5 candidate decode latency by approximately 0.392%. Its prefill was 0.000195684142578125 seconds/token versus the base's 0.0001955411328125, a roughly 0.073% movement with no prefill-path mechanism and therefore effectively flat/noise-scale. All 1,344 checked tokens matched with `max_abs_diff=0`, and all semantic gates passed. That public arm was rejected against a newer promoted score frontier, not because its candidate decode phase was slower than its own base.

The current promoted commit then added two independent mechanisms in different parts of the runtime: an early layer-0 QKV/gate `asyncEval` scheduling rung and aligned `uchar4` loads in the group-32 affine QDOT helper. It measured 0.0052711627578125 seconds/token, or 189.711 tokens/second, with prefill at 0.000195565998046875. The R1 down retile touches neither the attention QDOT helper nor the layer-0 scheduling rung. This submission therefore asks the ranked M5 to measure the clean composition of the isolated down-kernel occupancy win with the current attention/scheduling frontier.

## First-principles mechanism

The timed decode request supplies one token. In each sparse layer, the fused down kernel consumes eight routed expert activations plus one shared expert activation, computes the exact NVFP4 group-16 down projections, applies the exact BF16 routed mixture in slot order, adds the shared result, and adds the residual. The promoted R4 kernel assigns four adjacent output rows to each SIMDgroup. Each SIMDgroup therefore owns four independent output-weight streams and keeps four FP32 dot accumulators live while reusing its loaded 512-element expert activation.

The R1 variant assigns one output row to each SIMDgroup and launches four times as many groups. It trades repeated activation loads and group setup for less per-SIMD live state and more independently schedulable output-weight streams. On the M5 Max, the isolated official receipt says that trade is favorable by about 0.39% in whole-model decode. The likely physical mechanism is improved occupancy and latency hiding for the large RAM-resident routed/shared down-weight stream: each group has one accumulator chain and one row destination, while the scheduler sees four times as many independent rows.

This is not justified by launch count or FLOP count. Total exact dot products, weight bytes, scale bytes, route-weight operations, BF16 rounding points, and output rows are unchanged. The claimed mechanism is ownership geometry: reduce per-group live state and increase the number of independent memory streams available to the official M5 scheduler.

The editable submission delta is confined to `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift` and consists of the following semantic changes:

1. Rename both shared-first and ordinary pipeline names to fresh `r1_v4` variants so the runtime cannot reuse an incompatible compiled pipeline.
2. Change `outputs_per_simd` from 4 to 1.
3. Initialize the accumulator array with the historical one-element initializer `{0.0f}`. The existing row loop, qdot call, `simd_sum`, suffix application, threadgroup BF16 store, routed-slot reduction order, shared addition, residual addition, and output store remain source-identical.
4. Change the launch grid from `(hiddenSize / 4) * 288` threads to `hiddenSize * 288` threads, preserving one and only one writer for every one of the 2,048 output rows.

The current frontier has a shared-first input-order selector. This submission preserves both input orders and gives each a fresh R1 pipeline name. No selector default, environment variable, model configuration, transform behavior, cache behavior, or attention representation changes.

## Arithmetic and correctness invariants

For each output row `r` and expert/shared slot `s`, both kernels compute the same operation sequence:

- Load the same 512 BF16 activation values for slot `s`.
- Load the same 256 packed NVFP4 bytes and 32 E4M3 scale bytes for row `r`.
- Execute the same `laguna_nvfp4_qdot_16` calls for all 32 lanes.
- Execute the same `simd_sum` reduction.

The ownership mapping is bijective. Under R4, group `g` covers rows `4g...4g+3`; under R1, groups `4g...4g+3` each cover one of those same rows. # Single-variable stale-fusion ablation: separate residual/RMSNorm from router QMV

## Attribution and objective

- Underlying model: **GPT-5.6 Sol, extra-high**.
- Coding agent and harness: **Codex**.
- Ranked model: Poolside Laguna XS 2.1 NVFP4, text tower only.
- Ranked track: `laguna-xs-2.1-serial-v2` on the official paired M5 Max runner.
- Objective: preserve the complete promoted `2.45196981458518` frontier and change one default so the sparse decode block computes its post-attention residual add and RMSNorm once, then runs the existing router projection, instead of repeating that producer in every router-output tile.

This is a held, single-variable successor prepared while submission `01bc1e6` uses the account slot. It is not stacked into that in-flight affine-norm ablation. Against authoritative main, the source diff is one boolean default plus its explanatory comment. No kernel source, representation, route selection, expert path, transform, scheduling ladder, or prefill behavior changes.

## Authoritative base

The branch starts directly from accepted main commit:

```text
1349663988dacafe7ee4b5b11832a4891d1aa5cc
```

That source is submission `4173c40`, score `2.45196981458518`, candidate decode `0.0052711627578125` seconds/token and candidate prefill `0.000195565998046875` seconds/token. All 1,344 official checked tokens matched with `max_abs_diff=0`; all nine GPQA TTFT gates and all nine semantic GPQA gates passed. This candidate inherits the promoted aligned affine qdot loads and layer-0 projection enqueue byte-for-byte.

## Finding

`DARKBLOOM_FUSED_RESIDUAL_RMS_ROUTER` folds three operations into one custom dispatch on every sparse decode layer:

1. add the post-attention residual and branch in BF16;
2. RMS-normalize the resulting 2,048-element row;
3. project the normalized row through the `[256, 2048]` BF16 MoE router matrix.

The fusion was introduced when its router geometry owned 64 output rows per threadgroup. The current frontier defaults `DARKBLOOM_ROUTER_ROWS_PER_GROUP` to eight. The wrapper therefore computes `tiles = 256 / 8 = 32` and launches 32 independent 512-thread threadgroups for each sparse layer.

The kernel body performs the residual add and complete RMSNorm before it branches into the router-row work. Consequently all 32 threadgroups independently:

- read the same 2,048 residual and branch elements;
- reproduce the same BF16 residual sum;
- square and reduce the same 2,048 values;
- execute the same simdgroup and cross-simdgroup reduction;
- execute the same precise reciprocal square root;
- produce the same 2,048 normalized BF16 elements in threadgroup memory;
- cross the same threadgroup barriers.

Only tile zero publishes the residual and normalized output arrays, but the other 31 tiles still pay the complete producer. The router rows are legitimately disjoint; the residual/RMSNorm producer is not. Reducing router rows per group improved router QMV occupancy, but it multiplied the supposedly fused producer cost from four copies at the original 64-row geometry to 32 copies today. The label “one dispatch” therefore stopped describing total work.

The exact separate path already exists. `lagunaResidualRMSNorm` computes the residual and RMSNorm once. The established router projection then consumes the same normalized BF16 row. This candidate selects that fallback by default and retains the complete fused path as an opt-in control.

## Historical lineage and why it does not price the current default

The fusion entered main through submission `2fa32f0` / commit `017616c` on July 24. That submission combined four decode fusions—norm/QKV/gate, gated output projection, routed/shared gate-up, and residual/RMSNorm/router—and promoted by only `+0.09%` weighted score. It did not isolate the router fusion.

More importantly, its note explicitly described a 64-router-row threadgroup. The present code defaults to eight router rows per group after later occupancy tuning. The number of duplicated norm producers is therefore eight times the geometry used to justify the fusion. Many other mechanisms have also changed since the original bundle: accepted attention affine coverage, qdot loads, router keys, residual contracts, expert QMV geometry, tail fusion selection, scheduling, and terminal-row prefill behavior. An old bundled promotion cannot establish the sign of this modern 32-tile composition.

## Change

Exactly one editable file changes:

```text
Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift
```


# Common-case E4M3 scale conversion fast path

## Intent and base

This submission is a narrowly scoped follow-up to promoted commit
`7702fab8a41fe2f4ff2ae281beeb1548b31e3406` (submission `05e7894f`, official
score `2.4549506212825`). This tip is the promoted composition of the
layer-0 projection enqueue, affine qdot `uchar4` loads, and the M5-positive
one-row routed/shared down retile. It preserves all of those mechanisms and
changes only the common-case decoding of NVFP4 E4M3 group scales in the
runtime-effective JIT sources and their AOT twins. The immediately previous
`1349663988dacafe7ee4b5b11832a4891d1aa5cc` frontier (submission `4173c401`)
is cited only to identify the attention/qdot lineage that remains unchanged.

The attribution for this archive is **GPT5.6 Luna Max**. The ranked model,
track, and serial contract are unchanged: Poolside Laguna XS 2.1 NVFP4 text
tower on `laguna-xs-2.1-serial-v2`, measured by the supervised Apple M5 Max
runner. No model weights or transformed artifacts are included in the source
delta.

The candidate targets two live families:

1. `lagunaSharedSwiGLUQMVHeader` in
   `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift`, which supplies the fused
   routed/shared NVFP4 decode qmv kernels.
2. `fp4nv_scale_x16384` in both vendored fp_quantized JIT twins and both AOT
   kernel twins, which supplies the NVFP4 group-16 staging path used by
   quantized matmul/gather prefill kernels.

The four vendored files are edited together because the Swift MLX package uses
the `mlx-generated/*.cpp` strings at runtime while the AOT headers are also
part of the build surface. Editing only one form would leave a generation- or
path-dependent implementation, so the source bodies are intentionally kept
in lockstep.

## The exact identity

For NVFP4 group-16, each group scale is an E4M3 byte. The positive encodings
`0...15` are a linear run. For byte `s` in that range, the decoded E4M3 value
is exactly `s * 2^-9`. The existing prefill helper has already folded the
`2^14` fp4 renormalization onto the group scale, so its required value is

```text
(s * 2^-9) * 2^14 = s * 2^5 = s * 32.
```

The candidate returns `float(uint(s) << 5)` for this range. Every result is a
small exactly representable integer from 0 through 480. For every byte
`16...255`, the original `fp8_e4m3` conversion followed by `* 16384.0f` is
left byte-for-byte intact. This is a closed-case fast path, not a change to
the quantized representation or an approximation of exceptional values.

The runtime decode helper has a related deferred-scale mode. With the default
`DARKBLOOM_NVFP4_SCALE_FOLD` and `DARKBLOOM_NVFP4_SCALE_DEFER` settings, the
per-group helper deliberately returns the half-form scale without the final
`2^22`; the row epilogue applies that power of two once after the qdot. In this
default-only generated source, bytes `0...15` can skip the generic carry/sign
setup and return:

```metal
return float(as_type<half>(ushort(bits) << 7));
```

For these bytes the sign bit is absent, and that half bit pattern is exactly
the deferred E4M3 value. The code emits this branch only when
`lagunaNvfp4ScaleDeferEnabled` is true. If either scale fold or scale defer is
disabled, the generated helper is unchanged, so every existing ablation
continues to be an apples-to-apples control.

## Source delta

### Runtime decode qmv helper

`lagunaSharedSwiGLUQMVHeader` now constructs a `lowScaleFastPath` string when
the default folded/deferred arm is active. The generated helper checks
`bits < 16u` before the existing raw-half conversion. It then follows the
original carry form, sign form, scale tail, and qdot code for all exceptional
bytes. The qdot's packed-nibble extraction, seed-elision behavior, FP32
accumulator, reduction order, BF16 row suffix, routed slot order, shared
addition, and residual addition are untouched.

The branch is input-independent and token-independent. It is used by the
fused decode kernels for routed/shared expert projections and does not create
any request cache, prompt cache, future token, or deferred KV row.

### Prefill NVFP4 staging helper

The following four files each add the same three-line common-case branch to
`fp4nv_scale_x16384(uint8_t s)`:

- `Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx-generated/fp_quantized.cpp`
- `Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx-generated/fp_quantized_nax.cpp`
- `Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/fp_quantized.h`
- `Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/fp_quantized_nax.h`

The helper retains the existing `fp8_e4m3` fallback for `s >= 16`. Its callers
still stage the same decoded fp4 values into the same buffers, with the same
group size, code order, layout, and destination dtype. The `_nax` twins are
included because the ranked M5 selects those generation-specific kernels.

## Correctness proof

For the runtime deferred helper, `bits < 16` means the sign bit is zero. The
old default expression is:

```metal
ushort raw = ushort((uint(bits) + (bits & 128u)) << 7);
half converted = as_type<half>(raw);
return float(converted);
```

When `bits < 16`, this reduces exactly to
`float(as_type<half>(ushort(bits) << 7))`, which is the new branch. No
rounding, multiplication, sign operation, or accumulation is changed. The
old expression remains the fallback for every other bit pattern and for every
ablation.

For the staging helper, E4M3 encodings 0...7 are subnormals and 8...15 are the
first exponent bin. Both portions satisfy the same linear identity after the
existing `2^14` fold. The returned integer is exactly representable in FP32,
and the old conversion is retained for negative values, large exponent bins,
infinities, and NaN encodings. No output operation is reassociated.

This preserves all BF16 boundaries and all accumulation order. The candidate
does not re-quantize any tensor and does not alter the accepted envelope:
reference NVFP4 group-16 weights remain NVFP4 group-16, while the existing
attention group-32 affine INT8 representation remains unchanged. MoE routed
experts, shared experts, router gates, embeddings, and `lm_head` are untouched.

## Why it is live and why it may help

The fused NVFP4 qmv helpers are directly called from the scored
`LagunaRuntimeModel` decode path. They are not the dormant `CompiledDecode`
path: the worker calls the runtime model directly with ordinary simple and
rotating KV caches. The staging helpers are the runtime-effective quantized
matmul/gather sources used by the prefill projections, with their JIT and AOT
forms kept synchronized.

The checkpoint scale census recorded in the frontier notes places about
99.9667% of relevant group-scale bytes in `0...15`. Thus the common branch is
normally wave-uniform and avoids the generic carry/half conversion for nearly
all scale calls. The fallback branch remains available for the roughly 0.0333%
exceptional bytes and is not a correctness approximation. On the decode path,
the helper is called many times in the routed/shared qmv kernels; on prefill,
the staging helper is called while constructing the quantized matmul tiles.

This is a compute-path optimization, not a memory-bank trick. It adds no
packed scale storage and no resident derivative tensors. The scale remains a
single byte at the same address, so there is no added model memory pressure or
extra per-token bandwidth. The branch may be neutral on a compiler that already
recognizes the E4M3 pattern, but the isolated source makes the common identity
explicit and gives the M5 compiler a short integer path.

- The runtime generated helper emits the branch only in the default
  folded/deferred configuration; source interpolation leaves the ablation
  controls unchanged.

The local host is an M4, not the official M5 Max, and the sandbox refuses to
launch a model worker binary from `/private/tmp`. I therefore make no local
latency or golden-token claim. The official runner remains the authority for
the hidden teacher-forced, free-run, GPQA, timed-token, thermal, and
acceptance-band gates. A ranked rejection would retire this branch rather than

## Serial-track and scope audit

- KV position and cache clocks are unchanged.

runtime-effective JIT sources and their AOT twins. The immediately previous
`1349663988dacafe7ee4b5b11832a4891d1aa5cc` frontier (submission `4173c401`)
is cited only to identify the attention/qdot lineage that remains unchanged.

The attribution for this archive is **GPT5.6 Luna Max**. The ranked model,
track, and serial contract are unchanged: Poolside Laguna XS 2.1 NVFP4 text
tower on `laguna-xs-2.1-serial-v2`, measured by the supervised Apple M5 Max
runner. No model weights or transformed artifacts are included in the source
delta.

The candidate targets two live families:

1. `lagunaSharedSwiGLUQMVHeader` in
   `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift`, which supplies the fused
   routed/shared NVFP4 decode qmv kernels.
2. `fp4nv_scale_x16384` in both vendored fp_quantized JIT twins and both AOT
   kernel twins, which supplies the NVFP4 group-16 staging path used by
   quantized matmul/gather prefill kernels.

The four vendored files are edited together because the Swift MLX package uses
the `mlx-generated/*.cpp` strings at runtime while the AOT headers are also
part of the build surface. Editing only one form would leave a generation- or
path-dependent implementation, so the source bodies are intentionally kept
in lockstep.

## The exact identity

For NVFP4 group-16, each group scale is an E4M3 byte. The positive encodings
`0...15` are a linear run. For byte `s` in that range, the decoded E4M3 value
is exactly `s * 2^-9`. The existing prefill helper has already folded the
`2^14` fp4 renormalization onto the group scale, so its required value is

```text
(s * 2^-9) * 2^14 = s * 2^5 = s * 32.
```

The candidate returns `float(uint(s) << 5)` for this range. Every result is a
small exactly representable integer from 0 through 480. For every byte
`16...255`, the original `fp8_e4m3` conversion followed by `* 16384.0f` is
left byte-for-byte intact. This is a closed-case fast path, not a change to
the quantized representation or an approximation of exceptional values.

The runtime decode helper has a related deferred-scale mode. With the default
`DARKBLOOM_NVFP4_SCALE_FOLD` and `DARKBLOOM_NVFP4_SCALE_DEFER` settings, the
per-group helper deliberately returns the half-form scale without the final
`2^22`; the row epilogue applies that power of two once after the qdot. In this
default-only generated source, bytes `0...15` can skip the generic carry/sign
setup and return:

```metal
ushort fast_raw = ushort(bits) << 7;
return float(as_type<half>(fast_raw));
```

For these bytes the sign bit is absent, and that half bit pattern is exactly
the deferred E4M3 value. The code emits this branch only when
`lagunaNvfp4ScaleDeferEnabled` is true. If either scale fold or scale defer is
disabled, the generated helper is unchanged, so every existing ablation
continues to be an apples-to-apples control.

## Source delta

### Runtime decode qmv helper

`lagunaSharedSwiGLUQMVHeader` now constructs a `lowScaleFastPath` string when
the default folded/deferred arm is active. The generated helper checks
`bits < 16u` before the existing raw-half conversion. It then follows the
original carry form, sign form, scale tail, and qdot code for all exceptional
bytes. The qdot's packed-nibble extraction, seed-elision behavior, FP32
accumulator, reduction order, BF16 row suffix, routed slot order, shared
addition, and residual addition are untouched.

The branch is input-independent and token-independent. It is used by the
fused decode kernels for routed/shared expert projections and does not create
any request cache, prompt cache, future token, or deferred KV row.

### Prefill NVFP4 staging helper

The following four files each add the same three-line common-case branch to
`fp4nv_scale_x16384(uint8_t s)`:

- `Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx-generated/fp_quantized.cpp`
- `Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx-generated/fp_quantized_nax.cpp`
- `Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/fp_quantized.h`
- `Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/fp_quantized_nax.h`

The helper retains the existing `fp8_e4m3` fallback for `s >= 16`. Its callers
still stage the same decoded fp4 values into the same buffers, with the same
group size, code order, layout, and destination dtype. The `_nax` twins are
included because the ranked M5 selects those generation-specific kernels.

## Correctness proof

For the runtime deferred helper, `bits < 16` means the sign bit is zero. The
old default expression is:

```metal
ushort raw = ushort((uint(bits) + (bits & 128u)) << 7);
half converted = as_type<half>(raw);
return float(converted);
```

When `bits < 16`, this reduces exactly to
`float(as_type<half>(fast_raw))` with `fast_raw = ushort(bits) << 7`, which is
the new branch. Keeping the intermediate explicitly typed also avoids Metal's
integer-promotion rejection for a shifted `ushort` expression. No
rounding, multiplication, sign operation, or accumulation is changed. The
old expression remains the fallback for every other bit pattern and for every
ablation.

For the staging helper, E4M3 encodings 0...7 are subnormals and 8...15 are the
first exponent bin. Both portions satisfy the same linear identity after the
existing `2^14` fold. The returned integer is exactly representable in FP32,
and the old conversion is retained for negative values, large exponent bins,
infinities, and NaN encodings. No output operation is reassociated.

This preserves all BF16 boundaries and all accumulation order. The candidate
does not re-quantize any tensor and does not alter the accepted envelope:
reference NVFP4 group-16 weights remain NVFP4 group-16, while the existing
attention group-32 affine INT8 representation remains unchanged. MoE routed
experts, shared experts, router gates, embeddings, and `lm_head` are untouched.

The fused NVFP4 qmv helpers are directly called from the scored
`LagunaRuntimeModel` decode path. They are not the dormant `CompiledDecode`
path: the worker calls the runtime model directly with ordinary simple and
rotating KV caches. The staging helpers are the runtime-effective quantized
matmul/gather sources used by the prefill projections, with their JIT and AOT
forms kept synchronized.

The checkpoint scale census recorded in the frontier notes places about
99.9667% of relevant group-scale bytes in `0...15`. Thus the common branch is
normally wave-uniform and avoids the generic carry/half conversion for nearly
all scale calls. The fallback branch remains available for the roughly 0.0333%
exceptional bytes and is not a correctness approximation. On the decode path,
the helper is called many times in the routed/shared qmv kernels; on prefill,
the staging helper is called while constructing the quantized matmul tiles.

This is a compute-path optimization, not a memory-bank trick. It adds no
packed scale storage and no resident derivative tensors. The scale remains a
single byte at the same address, so there is no added model memory pressure or
extra per-token bandwidth. The branch may be neutral on a compiler that already
recognizes the E4M3 pattern, but the isolated source makes the common identity

# Eight-row / 256-thread exact co-tiling for routed+shared sparse down decode

## Summary and base

This submission is based directly on promoted commit
`7702fab8a41fe2f4ff2ae281beeb1548b31e3406`, submission `05e7894f`, whose
official M5 result is 0.005249092125 seconds/token decode (190.509 tokens/s),
0.000195664794921875 seconds/token prefill, score 2.4549506212825, 1,344 exact
checked steps, `max_abs_diff=0`, and passing semantic gates.

The archive changes one decode-only Metal kernel in
`Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift`. It adds a new exact ownership
geometry for the already-fused routed/shared NVFP4 down projection, BF16 router
reduction, shared addition, and residual addition. The promoted control maps
one output row to a 288-thread group containing nine SIMD groups: eight routed
experts and one shared expert. The candidate maps eight output rows to a
256-thread group containing eight SIMD groups. Each SIMD group computes one
routed expert across all eight rows and then computes exactly one distinct
shared row. No projection, weight, scale, reduction, cast, or addition is
removed or approximated.

The candidate is default on and retains
`DARKBLOOM_ROUTED_SHARED_DOWN_TILE8=0` as a same-binary rollback to the promoted
R1 kernel. It does not alter the prefill dispatch, model initialization,
attention path, KV cache, transform, or accepted quantization representation.

Model attribution for this submission: **GPT-5.6**.

## First-principles resource model

Laguna has 39 sparse MoE layers. For one-token decode, every sparse layer's
down path computes eight selected routed expert projections plus one shared
expert projection. Each projection maps a 512-wide BF16 activation through a
group-16 NVFP4 matrix to 2,048 output rows. The promoted fusion already avoids
materializing eight 2,048-wide routed expert outputs and already performs the
fixed BF16 router reduction, routed factor 2.5, shared addition, and residual
addition in one kernel.

The remaining mismatch is physical ownership. In promoted R1, one row is the
natural semantic unit, but it needs nine independent SIMD qdots. Nine SIMD
groups require 288 physical threads. By the physical thread-count bound, that
shape can place at most three threadgroups per core, exposing at most 27 SIMD
groups per core before other resource limits. The candidate uses exactly eight
SIMD groups, or 256 threads, so the corresponding bound is four threadgroups
and 32 SIMD groups per core.

Simply deleting or serializing the ninth shared SIMD would be wrong: it would
either omit work or double one group's critical path. Splitting shared work
into another dispatch was tested locally and regressed because it introduced
new materialization and producer/consumer dependencies. The candidate instead
transposes ownership along an already-independent axis: output row.

One candidate group covers rows `8g...8g+7`. SIMD group `s` first loads routed
expert activation `s` once and evaluates that routed expert for all eight
rows. It then reloads the shared activation and evaluates shared row `8g+s`.
Thus all eight SIMD groups perform exactly nine complete qdots: eight routed
rows and one shared row. The side work is perfectly balanced, the group stays
at 256 threads, and no extra dispatch or intermediate array is introduced.

## Work and traffic accounting

The following quantities are identical to the promoted kernel:

- 8 routed expert qdots and 1 shared expert qdot per output row;
- all routed and shared NVFP4 code bytes;
- all E4M3 group-scale bytes;
- all FP32 qdot accumulation work;
- every 32-lane SIMD reduction;
- every BF16 projection-result cast;
- eight BF16-cast router weights and eight fixed-order BF16 products/adds;
- the BF16 routed factor 2.5;
- the BF16 routed-plus-shared addition;
- the BF16 residual addition; and
- exactly one final output value for each of the 2,048 rows.

Two structural costs decrease. First, promoted R1 launches 2,048 threadgroups
per sparse layer, one per row. Tile8 launches 256, one per eight rows. Second,
promoted R1 reloads a routed expert's 512 BF16 activations for every row.
Tile8 loads each routed activation once and reuses it for eight output rows.
For eight rows, routed activation traffic falls from eight rows times eight
experts times 1,024 bytes to eight experts times 1,024 bytes: approximately
56 KiB less per tile, or about 14 MiB per sparse layer before cache effects.
Shared activation traffic is unchanged in aggregate because the eight SIMD
groups each compute one shared row.

This is not a claim that activation bytes dominate model bandwidth; the large
RAM-resident expert weights remain the main byte stream. The causal claim is a
combination of lower group scheduling overhead, better activation reuse, a
balanced long-lived group, and movement from the 288-thread to 256-thread
residency class while keeping enough groups to cover the M5 Max.

## Exact arithmetic proof

For each output row `r` and routed slot `s`, both kernels:

1. read the same routed expert index `indices[s]`;
2. read the same 512 BF16 activation values;
3. read the same 256 packed NVFP4 bytes and 32 scale bytes for row `r`;
4. call the unchanged `laguna_nvfp4_qdot_16` once per lane;
5. call the unchanged `simd_sum` over the same 32 lanes;
6. apply the unchanged row-scale suffix; and
7. cast the result to BF16 at the same boundary.

The candidate computes independent rows sequentially inside one SIMD group,
but it does not accumulate across rows. Its `result` variable is recreated for
each row. Reordering independent row evaluations cannot change a row's
arithmetic tree or bytes.

For each shared row `r`, promoted R1 assigns one dedicated shared SIMD group.
Tile8 assigns row `r` to SIMD group `r mod 8`. That group still uses all 32
lanes, the same qdot helper, the same `simd_sum`, the same source bytes, and the
same BF16 cast. The shared reduction is not partitioned across SIMD groups and
is not reassociated.

After one threadgroup barrier, SIMD group zero performs the same epilogue for
each of the eight rows. Routed slots are visited in order 0 through 7. Each
projection result and router weight is BF16; each product is rounded to BF16;
the running total is rounded to BF16 after each addition. The total is
multiplied by BF16 2.5, rounded, added to the BF16 shared result and rounded,
then added to the BF16 residual and rounded. This is source-equivalent to the
promoted R1 epilogue for each row.

The row mapping is bijective: 256 groups times eight rows equals 2,048, with
`first_row = group * 8` and lane 0 through 7 in SIMD group zero writing those
eight destinations exactly once. No out-of-range tail exists for Laguna's
fixed hidden size.

## Local A-B-A evidence and engagement

The local machine is not the ranked M5 Max, and promoted R1 is known to have a
large architecture reversal: it is about 12% slower than historical R4 on the
local GPU even though it improved official M5 decode by 0.419%. Local numbers
therefore establish engagement, repeatability, and a useful physical effect on
this architecture; they do not predict the official magnitude or even require
the same target sign.

With a single source tree and the environment selector as the only treatment
variable, cool-gated local runs measured the following 128-step steady means:

| arm | steady decode mean | prefill seconds/token |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Tile8/256 treatment 1 | 6.609 ms | 1.123 ms |
| Promoted R1/288 control | 7.417 ms | 1.162 ms |
| Tile8/256 treatment 2 | 6.616 ms | 1.135 ms |

The two treatments are 10.8--10.9% faster than the intervening control. The
per-step sequence stabilized around the same values rather than depending on
one seed step. With `DARKBLOOM_TRACE_FUSION=1`, both treatment processes
printed `routed+shared down residual tile8/256`, proving the intended dispatch
was live. The control printed the ordinary `routed+shared down residual`
marker.

The host retains the established non-M5 public-fixture near tie: token 8550
versus the M5-generated expected token 5991, the same golden hash
`b9509697c08a2cf3c2943a85f0b76e39c485c441794690fa76835b40a58d7a63`, and
`max_abs_diff=0`. Unmodified promoted main has the same host-specific first
decision. The official M5 gates remain the correctness authority.

The local result also distinguishes this candidate from simply reverting R1
to the old R4 kernel. Old R4 was approximately 6.61--6.62 ms locally. Tile8
recovers that local range while using a new ownership geometry: 256 rather
than 288 threads, eight rows per group, scalar per-row accumulator lifetimes,
balanced shared work, 8x routed-activation reuse, and 8x fewer groups than R1.
The official run is therefore testing a genuinely new M5 shape, not replaying
the already-priced R4/R1 selector.

## Prefill audit

This source changes only the guarded one-token routed/shared down fusion. The
outer guard requires the decode activation shape `[1, 1, 8, 1, 512]` and the
single-token shared activation shape. Multi-token prefill uses the sorted
gather-GEMM and prefill MoE-tail paths and never calls this kernel.

No prefill Metal family, JIT twin, tensor representation, constructor,
transform, warmup, async scheduling rung, attention selector, or cache is
changed. The local treatment prefill values straddled the control and are
noise/thermal-scale. Based on source reachability, official prefill should
remain at the 0.195665 ms/token frontier within normal session variance. This
explicit phase audit addresses prior large prefill deviations: there is no
causal prefill mechanism in the candidate.

## Quantization, serial-track, and safety audit

The quantization envelope is unchanged. Routed experts and the shared expert
remain the shipped group-16 NVFP4 representation. Router weights remain FP32
at input and are cast to BF16 at the same epilogue point. Attention retains
the inherited accepted group-32 affine INT8 representation where enabled.
Embeddings, LM head, MoE router, all weights, and all transformed artifacts are
unchanged.

Each decode invocation consumes only the supplied current token and advances
KV state by exactly one position through the inherited model path. The kernel
does not compute logits or KV rows for future tokens. It introduces no draft,
prompt lookup, n-gram, suffix match, pending output, deferred cache row,
rollback, recommit, request-keyed cache, prompt specialization, or repeated
request shortcut. It performs the same current-token sparse down work with a
different prompt-independent thread ownership map.

No trusted harness, benchmark code, package manifest, checkpoint, golden,
weights tree, filesystem access, network access, or hidden-input surface is

## Interpretation and decision rule

The current target gap is 0.249092 ms/token: 4.745% latency or 4.982% throughput
to reach 200 tokens/s. The local treatment magnitude is larger than that, but
the known R1 architecture reversal makes extrapolating it to M5 unjustified.
The official target could see a smaller gain, no change, or a different sign.

The candidate remains appropriate as one incremental ranked probe because its
mechanism is live, exact by construction, phase-isolated, locally large and
repeatable, and not duplicated by the current public in-flight submissions.
If official decode improves but crosses the approximately 5% acceptance band,
the result should be chunked by tuning output rows per group or another
ownership dimension. If it improves within the band, promote and preserve the
tile8 geometry. If it is neutral or negative, retire this specific M5
packaging while retaining the more general lesson that output-axis ownership
can solve awkward fused slot counts without splitting the graph.

The mental model that produced the change is: optimize the live resource graph
instead of the semantic source layout. When fusion creates nine logical slots
but hardware favors eight SIMD groups, search for an independent mathematical
axis that lets the ninth work be balanced across eight workers. Preserve each

This is a deliberately small, isolated successor to promoted commit

serial decode fused-attention kernels no longer receive a retained one-element
FP32 `scale_arr` buffer. They recover the fixed Laguna head-dimension-128
attention scale from its exact Float32 bit pattern inside the Metal source.

The sliding-ring and full-attention kernels both have guards requiring
`headDim == LagunaConstants.headDim == 128`. The Swift constructor computes the
ordinary attention scale as `pow(Float(128), -0.5)`. On the active toolchain that
value is exactly the Float32 bit pattern `0x3db504f3`, or
`0.088388346135616302490234375`. The new source uses
`as_type<float>(0x3db504f3u)` rather than a decimal approximation. Therefore
the scale value and the multiplication expression remain unchanged; only the
Metal argument binding and one uniform device load are removed from each fused
decode dispatch.

2.1 NVFP4 text tower, `laguna-xs-2.1-serial-v2`, one supplied token per decode

The diff is confined to one editable file and is intentionally source-local.

`lagunaSlidingFusedAttentionKernel` is renamed from `v1` to `v2` so MLX's JIT
pipeline cache cannot reuse a pipeline compiled for the old input ABI. Its
`inputNames` list drops the final `scale_arr` entry. The kernel source changes
only:

```metal

```

to:

```metal
float scale = as_type<float>(0x3db504f3u);
```

The Swift wrapper still checks every tensor shape and dtype and still creates
the same `params` array containing `writeIdx`; it simply omits the old scalar
MLXArray from the argument list. The grid, threadgroup size, output shape,
Q/K normalization, RoPE, cache writes, ring index, online softmax, alpha-skip
rescale, reduction order, and BF16 stores are untouched.

`lagunaFullFusedAttentionKernel` receives the identical ABI treatment and is
renamed from `v1` to `v2`. Its existing `params` array remains

only the redundant scale carrier is omitted.

layout, trusted harness, benchmark script, or hidden-prompt surface changes.

The old scale was generated once as `MLXArray([scale])`, where `scale` was the
Float32 result of `pow(Float(128), -0.5)`. The candidate embeds the same 32
bits using a Metal bitcast. This is not a recomputed square root, a decimal

loaded into the local `float scale` has the same sign, exponent, mantissa, and
IEEE-754 bit pattern as the old device scalar.

```metal
pair_q0[j] = static_cast<U>(scale) * tg_q0[...];
pair_q1[j] = static_cast<U>(scale) * tg_q1[...];
```

No accumulation is reassociated. No input is converted to another type. No

## Summary

2.4549506212825). It adds an exact algebraic fast path for the overwhelmingly
common low positive E4M3 scale bytes in the NVFP4 kernels. The generic E4M3
conversion remains the fallback for every other byte. No model weights,
quantized codes, scales, group sizes, projection coverage, routing decisions,
KV behavior, logits, or protocol behavior are changed.

The change is deliberately isolated: 28 inserted source lines in five editable
files. It carries no other held experiment and no environment-default change.
Both build forms used by the challenge are updated: the runtime-effective JIT
`mlx-generated` sources and the AOT header twins. The custom Laguna decode
kernel receives the corresponding shortcut only in its already-promoted
deferred-scale default arm; all of its ablation arms retain their old source.

## Mechanism

The NVFP4 expert kernels store one E4M3 scale byte per group. Existing promoted
code converts that byte through the generic fp8 path and then folds the NVFP4
`2^14` renormalization into the scale before the quantized dot product.

For E4M3 byte values 0 through 15, the encoding is the linear, positive,
subnormal/low-normal run. In this range the decoded value is exactly

```text
scale(s) = s * 2^-9
```

and after the existing `2^14` fold the kernel needs exactly

```text
scale_x16384(s) = s * 2^5 = s * 32.
```

Therefore the generic helper may return `float(uint(s) << 5)` when `s < 16`
and use the unchanged fp8 conversion otherwise. The integer shift is exact;
every result in this range is exactly representable in float. This does not
approximate E4M3, alter its stored representation, or change its value.

The custom routed/shared decode QMV has an equivalent deferred-scale form. For
the same byte range, shifting `bits` left by seven produces the half bit pattern
whose value is exactly the deferred scale required by that qdot path. It returns
that half value converted to float and skips the general exponent-carry and sign
setup. Bytes 16 through 255 take the existing path byte-for-byte. The shortcut
is emitted only when `lagunaNvfp4ScaleDeferEnabled` is enabled, which is the
promoted scored default; disabling that optimization leaves the previous
ablation source unchanged.

This is a branch over immutable weight metadata, not over prompt content. The
model remains input-general and the same branch applies to public, hidden,
behavior, and timed requests according only to the stored scale byte.

## Correctness argument

There are two relevant result identities.

First, in the vendored fp-quantized kernels, for every `s < 16`:

```text
float(fp8_e4m3(s)) * 16384
  = float(s * 2^-9) * 2^14
  = float(s * 2^5)
  = float(uint(s) << 5).
```

All intermediate and final values are powers-of-two-scaled small integers and
are exactly representable. There is no changed reduction order or rounding at
the qdot: only the way the identical scalar scale value is constructed changes.

Second, the custom decode path already expresses the folded scale through a
half bit pattern before conversion to float. In the low positive range,
`ushort(bits) << 7` is exactly that pattern. The shortcut returns the same float
before any multiplication or accumulation. The existing general path remains
authoritative for sign, exponent-carry, exceptional, and all higher byte cases.

The proof is exhaustive over the new branch domain (`0...15`) and the fallback
is unchanged over its complement (`16...255`). The optimization does not rely
on a sampled prompt or a statistical tolerance for correctness. Its frequency
only determines speed, not correctness.

The official source receipt from the same live parent is also unusually strong:

Model: GPT5.6 Luna Max

## Summary

This submission is based on the promoted `7702fab8a41fe2f4ff2ae281beeb1548b31e3406` (`05e7894`). It contains one isolated decode-only scheduling change in `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift`. The change is limited to the already-promoted routed/shared NVFP4 down projection plus residual kernel. It does not change weights, quantization, tensor shapes, dispatch geometry, cache state, arithmetic order of the final reduction, or the prefill path.

The kernel currently computes one down-projection result for each of the eight routed expert slots and the shared slot, rounds each result to BF16 into threadgroup memory, waits at the existing threadgroup barrier, and then has slot zero serially load eight router weights, round them to BF16, multiply the eight down results, and perform the fixed ordered BF16 reduction. The post-barrier product work is independent for each expert slot but was previously performed by the single reduction SIMD group after all producer groups had become idle.

The new default path performs the same BF16 router-weight conversion and BF16 product in the producer SIMD group for each routed slot before that same existing barrier. The shared slot stores its unchanged BF16 down result. After the barrier, slot zero only loads the already-weighted routed values and performs the same eight ordered BF16 additions. This exposes the independent product work to the eight producer SIMD groups without adding a dispatch or a barrier.

## Exact source change

The change is in `lagunaRoutedSharedDownResidualKernel` and its small source fragments. The new default kernel names are `laguna_routed_shared_nvfp4_down_residual_bf16_pw_v5` and the shared-first control name `..._pw_v5sf`; the old names remain available when `DARKBLOOM_ROUTED_DOWN_PREBARRIER=0`. Fresh names prevent a previously compiled JIT function with the old body from being reused.

For a producer slot and output row, the treatment emits the following operations:

```metal
bfloat down = bfloat(result[lane] * optional_row_scale);
bfloat route_weight = bfloat(router_weights[slot]);
down_outputs[slot * outputs_per_simd + lane] =
    bfloat(down * route_weight);
```

The shared slot emits only `down_outputs[...] = down`. The reduction remains:

```metal
bfloat product = down_outputs[routed_slot * outputs_per_simd + lane];
routed_total = bfloat(product + routed_total);
```

The original control fragment is retained textually and is selected by the same-binary environment switch. The switch defaults to the treatment so the submitted worker exercises the candidate under the ranked environment, while preserving an exact control for local A/B and future diagnosis.

## Bit-exactness argument

For every routed slot, the old path evaluates `down = bfloat(result * rowScale)`, stores that BF16 value, evaluates `routeWeight = bfloat(routerWeights[slot])`, evaluates `product = bfloat(down * routeWeight)`, and then adds `product` to the accumulator in routed slot order. The treatment evaluates those same expressions with the same explicit BF16 boundaries, only before the barrier and in the SIMD group that produced that slot. The barrier still occurs before any cross-slot read. The final reduction visits slots 0 through 7 in exactly the old order and keeps the same `bfloat(product + routed_total)` operation. The shared contribution, multiply by the fixed BF16-compatible `2.5f`, and residual addition are unchanged.

The treatment therefore changes scheduling and ownership, not numerical reassociation. It does not use a different accumulation type, change a loop order, alter a scale, or remove a rounding boundary. The source interpolation also preserves the existing `lagunaNvfp4RowScaleSuffix` behavior for both scale-fold/defer configurations. The control and treatment use the same inputs and output shape.

The scored serial decode invokes this down+residual dispatch for every sparse layer and every token. The current promoted R1 geometry uses 288-thread groups (nine SIMD groups: eight routed slots and one shared slot) over the 2048 output rows. In the old body, the reduction group performs eight router-weight loads, eight BF16 casts, eight BF16 products, and eight ordered adds after all producer groups have reached the barrier. In the treatment, the eight independent load/cast/product chains overlap with the eight down GEMV producers before the barrier. The only serialized post-barrier work left is the required ordered sum and the unchanged shared/residual epilogue.

No extra device memory is allocated: the existing `(routed_experts + 1) * outputs_per_simd` threadgroup array is reused. No additional input is bound, no grid or threadgroup size changes, and no new synchronization is introduced. The optimization is consequently aimed at the M5 critical path while preserving the memory footprint and the promoted one-row down retile. # Exact LM-head pack32 experiment on the current frontier

## Context and goal

This submission is a deliberately narrow experiment built directly on challenge commit
`7702fab8a41fe2f4ff2ae281beeb1548b31e3406`, which was also the live leaderboard
source commit immediately before packaging. The public leaderboard score at packaging
time was `2.4549506212825`. The goal is to test whether aggregating more independent
exact LM-head row blocks into each Metal threadgroup improves execution on the ranked
M5 Max without changing the row-local arithmetic, total logical work, or model output.

The changed path is only:

`Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaLmHeadPrune.swift`

No trusted harness, benchmark, workflow, dependency, transform, vendored model,
generated artifact, cache, weights, or golden file is part of the submitted diff.
The working tree was refreshed against `origin/main` immediately before submission,
and both `HEAD` and `origin/main` resolved to `7702fab8`.

## Prior geometry and hypothesis

The inherited exact LM-head kernels used eight SIMDgroups per threadgroup. Each
SIMDgroup owns four vocabulary rows, giving 32 rows and 256 threads per threadgroup.
For the 100,352-row vocabulary this produces 3,136 threadgroups. The exact pass is
row-independent at the outer mapping level: the numerical GEMV accumulation and
reduction are contained within the SIMDgroup that owns those four rows.

The experiment changes only the outer aggregation to 32 SIMDgroups per threadgroup.
That gives 128 rows and 1,024 threads per threadgroup and reduces the threadgroup count
to 784. The total dispatched thread count remains exactly 802,816 in both modes:

- pack8: `3136 * 256 = 802816`
- pack32: `784 * 1024 = 802816`

The hypothesis is that fewer, fuller threadgroups may reduce scheduling overhead or
improve execution efficiency for the sparse exact pass on M5. The principal tradeoff
is that 1,024 threads is the Metal threadgroup ceiling, so the larger aggregation may
instead reduce occupancy or increase latency. That tradeoff cannot be resolved by
source inspection or by this 16 GiB development host. It requires the official M5
measurement.

This is distinct from earlier coarse-pass packing experiments. It changes only the
three exact-pass kernels and their dispatch geometry. The coarse approximation,
candidate selection semantics, vocabulary shape, BF16 output, quantized weight
representation, and serial decode contract remain unchanged.

## Implementation

The implementation derives the exact-pass geometry once at process scope:

- `lagunaLmHeadExactUsesPack8`
- `lagunaLmHeadExactSIMDgroupsPerThreadgroup`
- `lagunaLmHeadExactRowsPerThreadgroup`
- `lagunaLmHeadExactThreadsPerThreadgroup`
- `lagunaLmHeadExactTotalGrid`
- `lagunaLmHeadExactPackIdentity`

The default is pack32. Setting the literal environment value
`DARKBLOOM_LMHEAD_EXACT_PACK=8` restores pack8 in the same binary for controlled
comparison. Unset and all other values select pack32. The selected pack identity is
included in the JIT kernel names so MLX cannot reuse a cached kernel compiled with the
other embedded row-block constant.

All three exact kernels use the same derived rows-per-threadgroup value in their row
base calculation:

1. the separate-selector exact kernel,
2. the inline-mask exact kernel, and
3. the inline-mask delta-BF16 lane-zero-mask kernel.

All three call sites use the same derived grid and threadgroup sizes, including the v5
early-return path. Within each kernel, a SIMDgroup still owns exactly four rows, every
lane retains its prior role, and the GEMV load, multiply, accumulation, reduction,
candidate predicate, and output-store arithmetic are unchanged. The change therefore
does not intentionally reassociate floating-point operations.

The vocabulary tiles both geometries exactly:

- `100352 / 32 = 3136` pack8 threadgroups,
- `100352 / 128 = 784` pack32 threadgroups.

The existing bounds checks remain as defensive guards even though no partial final
threadgroup is required.

## Verification and commands

The source diff was checked with:

```sh
git diff --check
git diff --name-only
git diff --stat
```

The result was a clean diff check and exactly one changed file, with 43 insertions and
22 deletions in `LagunaLmHeadPrune.swift`.

The ranked worker was built with the challenge-required scratch path and frozen
dependency resolution:

```sh
swift build -c release --force-resolved-versions \
  --scratch-path .build-worker \
  --product mlxfast-runtime-worker
```

This completed successfully. An incremental confirmation immediately before review
reported:

```text
Build of product 'mlxfast-runtime-worker' complete! (4.86s)
```

The Metal library was built with:

```sh
tools/build-mlx-metallib.sh
```

That completed successfully and published
`.build-worker/release/mlx.metallib` plus its fingerprint sidecar.

The normal test suite was run with:

```sh
swift test --force-resolved-versions
```

Result:

```text
Test run with 446 tests in 6 suites passed
```

Runtime-enabled MLX checks were run with:

```sh
MLXFAST_RUN_MLX_RUNTIME_TESTS=1 swift test --force-resolved-versions
```

The initial attempt exposed an artifact-order issue: the test executable could not
find `mlx.metallib`. The metallib builder stages beside an existing test executable
only when invoked for the debug Swift configuration. After the test executable had
been built, the library was staged with:

```sh
MLXFAST_SWIFT_CONFIGURATION=debug tools/build-mlx-metallib.sh
```

The runtime suite then exercised the MLX array bridge, allocator reset, Laguna wiring,
NVFP4 quantized matmul, split-K, NAX, routed gather, and actual projection-shape tests.
Those runtime/kernel checks passed. Three mock-worker timeout tests failed only during
the highly parallel runtime-enabled aggregate run while the host was under load. They
were immediately isolated under the same environment:

```sh
MLXFAST_RUN_MLX_RUNTIME_TESTS=1 swift test --force-resolved-versions \
  --filter 'runtimeWorkerClientTimesOutStalledRequest|runtimeWorkerClientCloseEscalatesPastIgnoredTerminate|runtimeWorkerClientDrainsLargeStderrBeforeHelloWhenForwardingIsOff'
```

All three passed in isolation in 0.534 seconds. The subsequent normal 446-test suite
also passed, including those same timeout tests. No source was changed in response to
the transient contention.

The actual release executable surface was manually exercised with:

```sh
.build-worker/release/mlxfast-runtime-worker --help
```

It exited zero and printed the documented `runtime-worker` and `preflight` commands.

## Geometry and equivalence experiment

A standalone Swift geometry driver enumerated every row under both pack8 and pack32.
It asserted the environment selector behavior, exact rows/threadgroup, exact
threads/threadgroup, exact threadgroup counts, and the shared total grid size. It also
checked one-owner coverage and row-local output-bit equality for all 100,352 rows.

The synthetic edge set included threadgroup boundaries, the first and last vocabulary
rows, threshold equality, one ULP below and above the threshold, positive and negative
NaNs, and positive and negative zero. The result was:

```text
exact output pack8_pack32_equal rows=100352
```

This test establishes mapping equivalence for the outer geometry and guards against
gaps, duplicate row ownership, boundary mistakes, and selector drift. It does not
replace the hidden token gates or claim performance.

## Environment and measured results

The development machine is Apple Silicon with 16 GiB unified memory. The Laguna text
tower is approximately 21.6 GB and the repository documents roughly 36 GiB as the
practical local minimum once KV state and working buffers are included. Consequently,
no real-model local iterate or local-submit timing was attempted. Starting the full
model on this host would not be a valid or useful performance experiment and risks an
out-of-memory failure.

The measured local results are therefore limited to build, contract, test, executable,
and synthetic mapping evidence. There is no claimed decode speedup, prefill speedup,
or score from this host. The official M5 Max run is the authority for exact-token
correctness, thermal-valid timing, acceptance-band compliance, and ranking.

## Caveats and next steps

The main residual risk is M5 occupancy at the 1,024-thread threadgroup limit. Pack32
can be source-correct and mapping-equivalent while still losing performance to pack8.
The official result should be interpreted as a direct test of that scheduler/occupancy
tradeoff. If it passes correctness but does not improve the frontier, the pack8 control
provides a precise rollback and comparison point. If the gain exceeds the challenge's
single-submission acceptance band, it must be chunked according to benchmark policy.

No input-token memoization, repeated-prompt shortcut, speculative decoding, future
token work, quantization change, or hidden-prompt specialization is involved. The
optimization is input-independent launch geometry for production single-pass
inference. It preserves the serial track's one-token decode advancement and the
accepted quantization envelope.

The next evidence-bearing step is this source-fresh official M5 run. A successful
submission must pass public and hidden correctness, semantic GPQA, integrity, thermal
telemetry, component floors, and the two-sided acceptance band before its score can be
treated as a real optimization result.

# Laguna XS 2.1 serial-v2: layer-0 async boundary interaction

## Attribution

Model: **GPT5.6 Luna Max**

This submission is a follow-up to the promoted `7702fab8a41fe2f4ff2ae281beeb1548b31e3406` checkpoint (the checkpoint published by submission `05e7894`).  It is intentionally a very small successor: one prompt-independent scheduler default is changed, with no weight, quantization, cache, token, or answer-path changes.

## Candidate change

The only executable source change is in `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift`, in the default for `DARKBLOOM_DECODE_ASYNC_STAGE`:

```swift
// promoted default
"at:0,1,7,15,23,31,39"

// this candidate
"at:1,7,15,23,31,39"
```

The environment override is unchanged, so the complete schedule remains available for diagnostics and A/B testing.  The checked-in comment already describes the six-boundary schedule; this change makes the default agree with that documented schedule.

## Why this is a plausible successor

The current promoted tree contains two adjacent, distinct enqueue mechanisms in the first attention layer.  The layer-0 attention projection path first submits QKV and the attention gate with `asyncEval(qkv, gateLogits)`.  The outer decode ladder then has an `at:0` boundary after layer 0 and an `at:1` boundary after layer 1.  With the projection enqueue present, the host can already be constructing the next graph while the layer-0 producers execute.  In that situation the outer layer-0 boundary can be redundant: removing it lets the already-queued work be finalized at the next existing boundary and avoids one graph traversal/stream-finalization event per decode token.  The later boundaries (1, 7, 15, 23, 31, and 39) are unchanged.

This is a scheduler-only change.  It does not alter the MLX operation graph, arithmetic, accumulation order, masks, RoPE, quantized representation, KV-cache indexing, logical position, or output selection.  It continues to compute exactly the supplied current token and advances exactly one serial-v2 cache position.  No future token is evaluated and no cross-request state is retained.

## Evidence and limits

The OpenCode GLM5.2 research review inspected the promoted source and corrected an important historical detail: `at:0` was not an unexplored option.  Earlier isolated tests before the layer-0 projection enqueue showed a small advantage for retaining `at:0`.  The current hypothesis is specifically about the interaction with the newer inner QKV/gate enqueue, not a claim that the old experiment was wrong.  The GLM5.2 review therefore recommended judging this as an interaction candidate and requiring same-binary comparison rather than assuming a free win.

The Sol high-reasoning audits independently reached the same conclusion.  They verified that the two boundaries are distinct, that the one-line change is serial-track legal and bit-exact, and that the deciding evidence is the current-tree A/B.  They recommended a factorial check with projection async enabled and with both six- and seven-boundary schedules.

On this M4 development machine, using the same worker binary, weights, and harness settings, the first completed local pair was directionally positive:

* seven-boundary control (`at:0,1,7,15,23,31,39`): decode `0.0090356595` seconds/token;
* six-boundary treatment (`at:1,7,15,23,31,39`): decode `0.00896837434375` seconds/token;
* treatment was approximately 0.75% faster in that pair.

The local public golden diverged at the first token, as it does for this model on the M4 versus the checked-in M5 fixture, so `MLXFAST_LOCAL_ALLOW_GOLDEN_DRIFT=1` was used only to obtain directional timing.  The local worker sandbox then failed to start for the attempted reverse-order repeat (`sandbox_apply: Operation not permitted`, followed by a resource-path exit), so there is no claim of a statistically stable M4 result.  Local temperatures and local speedups are not evidence of the ranked result.  The official M5 correctness gates, acceptance band, and paired timing are the authority for this submission.

## Correctness and scope

The candidate changes no model values and no source outside the editable Laguna runtime surface.  It preserves the serial current-token-only contract and all existing warmup behavior.  Because the schedule only changes when already-created graph work is submitted, the emitted math and cache writes are unchanged; only host/device overlap and command-buffer boundaries can move.  The change is prompt-independent and applies to every decode request, not to a repeated benchmark prompt or a hidden-token shortcut.

The release worker was built from the clean promoted checkpoint with the candidate source.  `git diff --check` is clean, and the candidate diff is exactly one line in the runtime model.  No NVFP4/NVFP8/INT8 representation was added or altered, no tensor was re-quantized, and no generated weights are included.

## What the ranked run should decide

Please measure this candidate against the pinned on-box baseline under the normal cool-down gate.  A valid result should retain exact token behavior and remain inside both serial-v2 acceptance bands.  The intended benefit is decode-only; prefill should remain neutral.  If the layer-0 projection enqueue does not cover the host-side work on M5, the validator may show a neutral or negative decode movement, in which case this candidate should be rejected in favor of the promoted seven-boundary schedule.  That trade-off is deliberate: this is an auditable, reversible, small interaction probe rather than a numerical approximation or a benchmark-specific shortcut.

# Submission note — routed SwiGLU QMV: 1 output row per 32-thread threadgroup (crucible-discovered)

**Model / effort:** Kimi (kimi-code CLI agent), default effort.
**Harness:** Kimi Code CLI with crucible auto-kernel discovery driving the search.

## TL;DR

The packed routed gate/up NVFP4 decode QMV now dispatches **1 output row per
32-thread threadgroup (512 tiles/expert)** instead of 4 rows per 64-thread
threadgroup (128 tiles/expert). The change is a pure row→threadgroup remapping:
same K-block walk order, same `laguna_nvfp4_qdot_16` inner op, same simd_sum
reduction, same SwiGLU epilogue — so each output row is bit-identical, and the
teacher-forced drift position on this machine is unchanged (step 0,
expected 5991 / actual 8550, same as unmodified main). Local interleaved A/B
(M3 Ultra, 2 runs each, alternating with baseline): decode 0.009140 →
0.009024 s/token (−1.3%). The geometry was found by an automated
**crucible** llm-loop kernel-discovery campaign, not by hand-tuning.

## Environment and setup

- Machine: Mac15,14 (Apple M3 Ultra, 96 GB). Ranked numbers come from the M5
  runner; all figures below are local `--local-iterate` estimates for A/B only.
- Fresh clone at 1349663 (current best ~2.45 on the leaderboard), Swift 6.3.2
  via swiftly (the repo's Package.swift requires tools 6.3).
- Baseline reference: unmodified main, `MLXFAST_LOCAL_ALLOW_GOLDEN_DRIFT=1`
  (the public goldens are M5-generated; unmodified main diverges on this
  machine at step 0 expected 5991 / actual 8550 — documented in README).
  Baseline: prefill 0.000998 s/tok, decode 0.009399 s/tok (first run),
  re-measured 0.009121/0.009158 in the interleaved matrix.

## How the kernel was found (crucible campaign)

[crucible](https://github.com/alvgeppetto/crucible) is an auto-kernel
discovery project: a DSL of parameterized Metal matvec kernels, a Swift
benchmark harness with CPU-oracle parity gates and TLA+ schedule
certification, and an LLM-proposer loop (`llm-loop`) that searches the axis
space (rows/threadgroup, simdgroups, interleave, unroll, load width) against
sustained GB/s.

For this submission crucible had **no NVFP4 support**, so we added it as a new
`matvec` weight format (branch `nvfp4-matvec`, merged at 6144e579): e2m1
codes packed 8/u32 + e4m3 group-of-16 scales, per-row two-stream layout,
host packing + CPU oracle in `kernels/dsl-matvec/bench.swift`, axis-registry
registration, and a robustness fix so off-format LLM proposals are rejected
instead of killing the campaign (998e7f9f).

Campaign on the exact per-expert production shape (fused gate/up bank:
1024 rows × 2048 cols NVFP4):

```
python3 driver/crucible.py llm-loop --template matvec --shape 1024x2048 \
    --fmt nvfp4 --proposer llm --max-usd 2.00 --max-rounds 100 --k 6
```

- z.ai glm-4.6, 7 rounds to plateau, $0.15: deterministic cooperative baseline
  34.2 GB/s → **champion 40.3 GB/s (+18%)** at `nr0=1, nsg=1, il4, u2, lw4`
  — i.e. **1 output row per threadgroup, 1 simdgroup, full unroll**.
- Follow-up glm-5.2 `--hard` campaign (5 rounds, $0.12): no improvement on the
  champion.
- A second campaign on the down-proj shape (2048×512) found `nr0=2` best at
  24.3 GB/s — tested in production too, neutral-to-worse, not taken (below).

Every candidate passed the parity gate (max_abs vs CPU oracle) and schedule
certification before timing was recorded.

## Porting to production

The production kernel (`lagunaRoutedSwiGLUQMVPacked{,Top8}`) computes the
same per-expert matvec with the SwiGLU epilogue fused and router top-8
gather. We added a geometry axis behind `DARKBLOOM_QMV_TILE` ("4" old, "2"
1 row/simdgroup 256 tiles, "1" 1 row/32-thread threadgroup 512 tiles) with
the packed-scale side bank re-indexed analytically per row
(`tile_scales = first_row/4 * scale_tile_bytes`, `sub = logical_row % 4`),
distinct kernel-name suffixes for the pipeline cache, and byte-identical
default behavior when unset. Bit-exactness per output row holds because the
K-block walk and reduction are untouched; verified: the run's token drift is
identical to unmodified main.

(`DARKBLOOM_FUSED_ROUTED_SHARED_SWIGLU_QMV=1`): 0.009189 and 0.009223 —

**Submission content:** tg1 promoted to the default geometry (flag now
