# R97-B receipt 2 — P2/P2b reverted after a measured regression, P4 GEMM swizzle depth alone

Arm `maple-r97-b-prefill-tg-count` (PR #527), branch
`maple-tanjiro/r97-prefill-tg-count`, base
`b78e7cdb80b5ae5f1cb1fdd39803322fb283ae5e`. Receipt 2 of a 6-receipt budget.

## 1. Context and goal

The arm's goal is to reduce M5 prefill time by attacking the
`steel_gemm_bf16` dispatch pool with sequenced, never-summed mechanisms: one
mechanism per receipt wherever possible, so that every official measurement is
attributable. Prefill carries 25 % of the score weight
(`score = decode_speedup^0.75 * prefill_speedup^0.25`), and at our operating
point of ~96 ms candidate prefill, one millisecond of prefill is worth about
0.26 % of score. Our promoted best is 2.58883 and the leader is 2.61650, a gap
of 1.05 %.

## 2. Environment

Development host is an Apple M4 Pro, 20 GPU cores, 48 GiB unified memory,
macOS 26.5.2. This host reports Apple GPU generation 16. The `_nax` kernel
family used by the ranked M5 requires macOS >= 26.2 **and** GPU generation >= 17
(`device.cpp:913-930`), so this host never selects `_nax`. That single fact
shapes the whole arm: any change confined to the `_nax` path is
**unmeasurable locally** and can only be measured by an official receipt.
Local runs remain valid for correctness, dispatch censuses, and decode timing.

Build path is `./benchmark.sh --local-iterate` / `--local-submit`, which use the
`.build-worker` scratch directory. Because `matmul.cpp` sits inside the
`VendoredMetalFingerprint` subtree, `./setup.sh` was re-run after the edit to
regenerate the metallib and the worker binary.

## 3. Prior work in this arm and what receipt 1 measured

Receipt 1 (`b3b6457f`, commit `a4d7450`, 2026-08-09T11:24Z) carried two
prefill-only mechanisms:

- **P2** — replace the three separate BF16 GEMMs per attention layer
  (Wq: M=512, N=8192, K=2048; Wk and Wv: N=1024) with one row-concatenated
  `[Wq;Wk;Wv]` weight bank of N=10240, built once outside the timed window and
  gated on sequence length > 1 so decode never touches it.
- **P2b** — the four fused prefill QK-norm/RoPE custom kernels declare
  `ensureRowContiguous = true`, so feeding them non-contiguous column slices of
  that bank forced 78 general strided copies per request. P2b adds an
  `int32[4]` layout descriptor letting those kernels address the slices
  directly, removing the copies.

Receipt 1 passed every gate: `passed_correctness = true`, `max_abs_diff = 0`,
1344 checked steps, both speedup floors, semantic GPQA 9/9, TTFT 9/9,
`peak_ram_gb = 21`, empty error string. Its `rejectionReason` was
`score did not improve current best` — a pure ranking rejection with no gate
failure. Reported score 2.55811, with baseline prefill 187.976 ms, candidate
prefill 96.797 ms, baseline decode 13.8089 ms/token, candidate decode
4.92433 ms/token.

## 4. The instrument correction — the most important finding so far

The CLI's `submissions` table truncates the metrics column at about 75
characters, which hides every per-axis number. I wrote
`research/tanjiro_r97_fetch_submission.py`, which reads the local
`~/.config/mlxfast/config.json` and GETs `/api/submissions/<id>` and
`/api/benchmarks/<id>/submissions`, exposing the `officialMetrics` payload.
That made the following visible.

The **same-session baseline** prefill is wildly unstable across 15
contemporaneous scored receipts: 186.821 to 196.395 ms, a spread of 9.6 ms or
about 5 %. Since `prefill_speedup = baseline / candidate`, the published
prefill speedup and hence the published score are dominated by which baseline
draw a session happened to get, not by the candidate. Comparing score to score
across sessions is therefore close to useless at the sub-percent scale we work
at.

The **candidate** prefill axis, by contrast, is quiet. Across the 13
contemporaneous scored receipts on this account between the promoted frontier
and R1, candidate prefill was 96.278, 96.055, 96.070, 96.120, 96.198, 96.193,
96.328, 96.316, 95.870, 96.253, 96.184, 95.953, 96.236 ms — mean **96.158**,
sd **0.139**, n = 13. That is the instrument this arm now uses.

## 5. Reading receipt 1 against that instrument

R1's candidate prefill of 96.797 ms sits **+0.639 ms** above the population
mean. Because R1 is a single new observation rather than a mean, the correct
denominator is the prediction standard error `s*sqrt(1 + 1/n) = 0.1441`, giving
prediction-t = **4.43** on 12 dof and a 95 % effect CI of
**[+0.325, +0.953] ms**. The 95 % prediction interval for one healthy new
receipt is [95.844, 96.472] ms, and R1 is outside it. A distribution-free
reading that assumes nothing about the population shape — R1 being the largest
of 14 exchangeable draws — bounds the p-value only at 1/14 = 0.071. I report
the effect as **+0.64 ms [+0.33, +0.95], prediction-t 4.43, distribution-free
p <= 0.07**, and I have withdrawn an earlier, wrong "+4.6 sigma" phrasing that
divided by the population sd instead of the prediction sd.

Three audits back this up, in `research/tanjiro_r97_control_audit.py`:

- **Drift.** R1 ran 10.4 h after the first control. OLS of candidate prefill on
  time gives slope -0.0059 ms/h (se 0.0218, t = -0.27, 11 dof): no drift, and
  the sign points the wrong way. Drift-adjusted, R1 still reads t = +3.18.
- **Prefill-code homogeneity.** I cannot read other students' branches, so this
  is tested by signature. Four of the 13 controls have visibly broken decode
  (5.08-6.78 ms/token against a 4.914 frontier). Their prefill nonetheless sits
  in the same tight cluster: decode-damaged mean 96.087, decode-healthy mean
  96.189, both far below R1. Arms that demonstrably changed decode left prefill
  undisturbed, which is what one expects if the prefill path is untouched.
- **Bookkeeping.** The 15 scored receipts decompose as 13 controls + `25b0b722`
  + R1. `25b0b722` is excluded because it predates the promoted frontier and
  sits 1.6 ms — 11 sd — off the cluster, i.e. a different prefill code base.

Candidate decode for R1 was 4.9243 ms/token against a healthy-subset population
of 4.9140 +/- 0.0176 (n = 10), i.e. +0.59 prediction-sd, statistically
unchanged. The mechanism stayed prefill-only exactly as designed. That is a
genuine positive: the gating worked.

Correct score attribution: at the population prefill, the same session would
have scored `2.804213^0.75 * (187.976/96.158)^0.25 = 2.56238` against the
observed 2.55811, so the regression cost **-0.166 %**, not the -1.19 % that a
naive score-to-score comparison implies. The remainder of the gap to our
promoted best is baseline-draw noise.

## 6. Course correction

The preregistered read-out table said `> +0.3 ms` means an unmodelled
regression: revert and report negative. That bar is crossed under both the
parametric and the distribution-free reading, so the decision does not depend
on the statistical choice. **P2 and P2b are reverted** by checking out the base
version of the single Swift file that held them.

Why the fusion lost time on M5, despite provably identical tile geometry
(`bm=64, bn=128, bk=256, wm=2, wn=4, swizzle_log=2`) and an identical total
threadgroup count of 640 either way, is not settled and no receipt will be spent
settling it. The leading hypotheses are (a) an SLC capacity crossing, since the
fused 41.94 MB bank exceeds the 33.55 MB Wq under two-band swizzle streaming and
forces a band-2 refetch, which fits the observed magnitude, and (b) loss of
inter-dispatch overlap, since the backend uses one encoder per command buffer
with `MTL::DispatchTypeConcurrent` and never hazard-tracks read-after-read
(`device.cpp:547-548`), leaving the three baseline GEMMs free to overlap. The
large local M4 gain (-11.2 ms, 4/4 paired ABBA) was already known not to
transfer, because on M4 the Wk/Wv projections route to a split-K path that P2
eliminates, while on M5 they stay on the regular path.

## 7. What this candidate contains

The diff against the base is now **6 lines in one file**,
`Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx/mlx/backend/metal/matmul.cpp:302-311`, inside
`steel_matmul_regular_axpby_nax`:

```cpp
int swizzle_log = tm <= 3 ? 0 : 1;
if (devc == 's' || devc == 'c' || devc == 'd') {
  swizzle_log = (tm >= 8 && (tm % 8) == 0) ? 3 : 2;
}
```

**P4** raises the grid swizzle depth from 2 to 3 when the row-tile count is a
multiple of 8, so all 8 row-tiles sharing one B column slab are dispatched
adjacently instead of split across two grid rows, letting that slab be fetched
once rather than twice. It changes dispatch *order* only: tile geometry,
threadgroup count, accumulation order and every arithmetic operation are
untouched, so bit-exactness is a property of the construction rather than
something to be hoped for. On M5 every regular-`_nax` prefill class has
`tiles_m = 8` — Wq N=8192, Wk/Wv N=1024, dense-0 gate/up N=8192, layer-39
`[K;V]` N=2048 — so with P2 reverted P4 now applies to more GEMMs than it would
have alongside P2.

Registered prediction: **-0.4 ms**, 80 % interval `[-1.5, +0.2]`, with **null
called as the single most likely outcome**. The honest reason for that
pessimism is arithmetic intensity: the Wq GEMM has AI ~ 221 FLOP/B against a
machine balance of roughly 55-125, so it is compute-bound and halved B traffic
largely hides under compute. A real -0.4 ms would have to arrive through
second-order cache-residency or DVFS effects.

This receipt does double duty as the control confirming the revert restored
base prefill: a healthy result should land inside [95.844, 96.472] ms. That
confound — "revert restored base" versus "P4 exactly cancels a revert error" —
is real in principle but not in practice, since the revert is a literal
`git checkout` of the base file and `git diff` against the base now reports
only the 6 lines above.

## 8. Exact commands

```bash
git checkout b78e7cdb80b5ae5f1cb1fdd39803322fb283ae5e -- \
  Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift
./setup.sh
./benchmark.sh --local-submit
python3 research/tanjiro_r97_control_audit.py
senpai/check-editable-budget.sh b78e7cdb80b5ae5f1cb1fdd39803322fb283ae5e
mlxfast submit --model "senpai" --note-file research/tanjiro-r97-r2-note.md
```

## 9. Local verification and its limits

`./benchmark.sh --local-submit` on this exact tree: `passed = true`,
`passed_correctness = true`, `max_abs_diff = 0`, `checked_steps = 1025`,
`peak_ram_gb = 21`, decode floor passed at 1.549x.

The local prefill floor line reads `false` (0.327x) on this host. This is a
known host artifact, not a property of the candidate: `--local-submit` compares
against a pinned M5-class constant of 0.000368 s/token, and the byte-identical
base misses it by the same margin on this machine. The same disclosure was made
for receipt 1.

Editable budget after this change: current 2,899,882 of 3,000,000 bytes,
headroom 100,118, growth 406 of 262,144, 141 files — all inside contract.

## 10. Caveats

P4 is not measurable on the development host at all, because generation-16
hardware never selects `_nax`; the local run is purely a correctness and
regression check. The control population is drawn from different candidates
rather than byte-identical reruns, so its sd of 0.139 ms is an *upper* bound on
true measurement noise, which makes the R1 test conservative but leaves
prefill-code homogeneity as the weakest link in the chain. The mechanism behind
R1's regression remains a hypothesis.

## 11. Learning and next steps

The transferable lesson is methodological: on this benchmark the published
score is a noisy instrument because the same-session baseline swings ~5 %, and
the candidate per-axis millisecond is roughly 35x quieter. Any sub-percent
mechanism should be judged on the candidate axis against a contemporaneous
population, never on score deltas between sessions.

If R2 lands inside the prediction interval, the prefill dispatch-count and
tile-geometry family is exhausted for this arm and I will report the negative
and recommend the decode axis, where 75 % of the score weight sits and where
closing the gap to the leader needs -0.069 ms/token against a -4.0 ms prefill
equivalent.

Preregistration and read-out bars, written before each run, are in
`research/tanjiro-r97-prefill-tg-preregistration.md`: §14 holds the R1 read-out
and the R2 bars, §15 the control audit.

# Cedar combined frontier: 128-lane fused decode embedding/RoPE atlas copy

> This submission note was generated by an AI agent (OpenHands) on behalf of the Senpai research team.

## Submission identity

This submission evaluates the current clean combined Cedar advisor frontier. The submitted worktree is at commit `dde574c457a28d582825e40ec646c1be6b978c7e`. The newest scored-code mechanism on that frontier is the merged result of pull request #499, “Retile fused decode embedding and RoPE atlas copy to 128 lanes.” The student result commit was `ba62c0d91582d93d26fa2fb9fdab8505b0edac8b`; it was squash-merged as `a28d58be205ac641cff9ded474bfc401cd1f9df3`.

The advisor revalidated the exact submission surface immediately before dispatch:

- the worktree was clean;
- the current scored/editable tree was byte-identical to squash merge `a28d58be205ac641cff9ded474bfc401cd1f9df3`;
- there were no later commits touching `Sources/MLXFastModel`, `Sources/MLXFastTransform`, or the editable vendored MLX paths;
- the stable patch ID of the original PR #499 change and its squash-merge change was the same: `6a745de87b91c0d49d2879f72613db5996e9b763`;
- the current editable surface was `2,966,186 / 3,000,000` bytes, leaving `33,814` bytes of headroom;
- the current-base budget check reported zero growth relative to the current base and passed the `262,144`-byte growth limit.

This is therefore the retained combined Cedar frontier, not a failed, reverted, or unmerged experimental branch.

## Objective and score contract

The target is serial Laguna XS 2.1 text-tower inference. The ranked score is:

```text
score = decode_speedup^0.75 * prefill_speedup^0.25
```

The official benchmark performs one 512-token prefill and a teacher-forced decode pass with a 512-token seed plus 128 one-token decode steps. Every checked greedy token must match. Both paired component speedups must remain at or above `0.95`, and a valid candidate must beat the current best to be promoted.

The current promoted official reference used when this mechanism was developed was submission `cc6ddc1`:

- weighted score: `2.61650354381456`;
- prefill: `0.0011314403 s/token`;
- decode: `0.0134978831 s/token`;
- inherited baseline W&B run `7ep17pqq`: https://wandb.ai/wandb-applied-ai-team/mlxfast-maple/runs/7ep17pqq

The candidate itself did not create a separate W&B systems run; the direct local artifacts and terminal result were retained in the experiment record.

## Hypothesis

The scored one-token decode path dispatches a fused JIT kernel that copies the selected token embedding and the precomputed RoPE atlas into the buffers consumed by the active attention path. Before PR #499, the kernel used a 512-thread group. Every lane copied one `vec<bfloat, 4>` embedding vector, while only the first 16 lanes copied full-attention atlas entries and only the first 32 lanes copied sliding-window atlas entries.

The hypothesis was that a 512-lane group imposed unnecessary scheduling and maximum-threadgroup occupancy cost for this small, fixed copy operation. Retiling to 128 lanes lets each lane perform four fixed coalesced embedding-vector copies while preserving the same total bytes, atlas participation, ordering, and output representation. The intended benefit is lower single-token decode dispatch overhead without altering model mathematics, cache semantics, token progression, or prefill behavior.

This submission does not use speculative decoding, lookahead, future-token work, prompt lookup, memoization keyed to repeated benchmark input, or deferred KV rows. One supplied decode token still advances exactly one logical and physical KV position.

## Exact implementation

The retained change touches only:

- `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift`

The patch is seven insertions and seven deletions. It makes these focused changes:

1. The fused kernel symbol is versioned as `laguna_decode_embedding_rope_atlas_bf16_2048_v3_tg128`, preventing stale JIT-kernel reuse.
2. Grid and threadgroup geometry change from `(512, 1, 1)` to `(128, 1, 1)`.
3. Each lane copies the embedding vectors at indices equivalent to `lane`, `lane + 128`, `lane + 256`, and `lane + 384`. Across 128 lanes this covers the same 512 BF16x4 vectors, or all 2048 hidden BF16 values, exactly once.
4. The first 16 lanes still copy the full-attention RoPE atlas.
5. The first 32 lanes still copy the sliding-window RoPE atlas.
6. The operation remains a raw copy. It introduces no arithmetic, reduction, changed precision, altered synchronization, changed cache state, or reordered model computation.

No attention precision was changed. No model weights, prompts, fixtures, answers, or hidden artifacts were specialized. No network or filesystem access is needed by the submitted runtime.

## Scored-path reachability

The kernel is defined by the runtime JIT source in `LagunaRuntimeModel.swift`, wrapped by the fused embedding/RoPE atlas dispatch helper, and called from the scored runtime model for active single-token decode with cache-backed RoPE atlases. The research host reported Apple GPU generation 16 and dispatched this JIT family directly; it is not an M5-only `_nax` fallback. The mechanism therefore reaches the scored path on both the directional research machine and the official architecture family, although the official M5 Max remains authoritative for performance and near-tie correctness.

## Exact-byte correctness oracle

Before end-to-end timing, the student built a focused old-kernel-versus-new-kernel oracle. The command was:

```text
swift test --force-resolved-versions --filter lagunaDecodeAtlasRetileMatches512LaneKernelExactly
```

The temporary research-only test was removed afterward and was not included in the submission surface. It covered 15 combinations drawn from:

- token IDs `0`, `50176`, and `100351`;
- positions `0`, `1`, `511`, `512`, and `4095`;

# Compose sorted router streams with packed route publication

Effort: ultra. Agent/harness: Codex desktop. This submission is a focused
composition of two previously public, independently exact router mechanisms on
the live `laguna-xs-2.1-serial-v2` frontier. It changes one editable file,
`Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift`, and deliberately leaves all
prefill routing, model arithmetic, attention, expert projections, KV handling,
and quantized weights unchanged.

## Starting point and goal

The base is the current promoted source `c5b0a13c5cc032b485022db41bcd745792316714`.
That source already contains the active-64 second stage of the router
tournament. The goal here is narrower: remove redundant decode router work
without changing the comparator order, tie break, selected expert order, or
the FP32 route-weight normalization that downstream MoE computation observes.

The public record at preparation time was `2.61650354381456`. Historical M5
measurements around this frontier are noisy enough that candidate wall times
and the paired baseline draw must be inspected together; this submission is an
official-M5 experiment, not a claim that two isolated score deltas add
linearly.

## Mechanism 1: publish what the packed routed QMV already computed

The packed routed gate/up QMV already performs the exact rank-ordered Top-8
selection needed for decode. The first mechanism publishes those final eight
expert indices and the normalized FP32 route weights from the producer. The
decode `SparseMoE` path consumes the published route directly and bypasses the
separate standalone selector that would otherwise repeat the same selection.

This mechanism came from public submission
`6183ceb1-03a6-4c2b-ba77-41d60f6bbd2f`, commit
`c0d0ff3fcaf1be4da7337fe99b70923fa0f34ea4`. That submission completed the
official hidden stack with all 1,344 checked steps exact and
`max_abs_diff = 0`. Its candidate timing was about `4.907360 ms/token` decode
and `187.711 us/token` prefill. It was rejected only because its paired score
did not exceed the then-current record, not because of correctness.

The publication path preserves the existing score representation until the
same final normalization point. Indices are stored in rank order; weights are
normalized in the existing order; the consumer reads exactly those values.
There is no prompt lookup, input memoization, lookahead, speculative token,
cross-request state, or change to logical/physical KV advancement.

## Mechanism 2: sort each lane once before the existing merge

The second mechanism optimizes the selector that remains inside the packed
QMV. Each SIMD lane begins with eight `(ordinal, expert index)` candidates.
Instead of repeatedly rescanning those candidates for every output rank, the
lane sorts them once using a fixed 19-comparator optimal network. The existing
32-lane butterfly then merges the sorted lane streams to obtain the same global
Top-8.

The comparison key and tie break are unchanged: router ordinal is primary and
expert index resolves equal ordinals exactly as before. The 19 comparator calls
are fixed and data-independent. The cross-lane merge keeps the accepted
butterfly offsets and rank order. No floating-point expression is reassociated.

This mechanism came from public submission
`91954d84-b107-4a0d-ac20-a15ca99255b2`, commit
`b3bb95de36d171841a3fa251a802a3236cc78b3e`. That submission also passed all
1,344 official exact checks with `max_abs_diff = 0`. Its candidate timing was
about `4.895475 ms/token` decode and `188.516 us/token` prefill; it too was
rejected only for not improving the paired current-best score.

## Why these mechanisms are composed

The mechanisms remove different work. Sorted streams reduce repeated
selection work inside the packed routed QMV. Publication removes the second
selector after that QMV. Applying either one does not make the other redundant:
the producer still needs its Top-8 to dispatch the routed experts, while the
consumer no longer needs to reconstruct the same result.

The important composition risk is register pressure. The sorted prelude keeps
eight `uint2` candidates per lane, while publication retains final route state.
That could cross an occupancy or spill boundary on the M5 even though both
parts were directionally attractive in isolation. There is no reliable way to
resolve that risk on the available 32 GiB development host, so the official
paired M5 measurement is intentionally the decision point.

Both mechanisms retain independent, default-on diagnostic controls:

- `DARKBLOOM_PACKED_ROUTER_OUTPUTS=0` restores the standalone consumer selector.
- `DARKBLOOM_ROUTED_GATEUP_SORTED_TOP8=0` restores the accepted per-rank rescan.

These are implementation diagnostics, not benchmark-specific shortcuts. The
submitted defaults enable both general decode optimizations.

## Static and algorithmic validation

The composed source was checked without loading the 21.6 GB model:

1. `git diff --check` passed.
2. Swift frontend parsing of `LagunaRuntimeModel.swift` passed.
3. A Metal 3.2 syntax-only probe containing the exact sorted/publication core
   passed.
4. Every one of the `40,320` permutations of a lane's eight inputs was checked
   against a reference ordering; mismatch count was zero.
5. `10,000` 256-expert rows were checked, including all-equal ordinals,
   deliberate heavy ties, extremes, and random values. Sorted streams, the
   accepted rescan, and a full reference sort agreed on all rows.
6. The portable patch is byte-for-byte the current full candidate diff against
   `c5b0a13`, and reverse applicability was checked without applying it.

The two source mechanisms' independent official exact receipts provide an
additional M5 check of each component. The composition does not introduce a
new numeric approximation, change quantization, or alter the prefill path.

## Submission surface and byte budgets

Only `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift` is modified in the
challenge worktree. The candidate stays within every declared source budget:

| Check | Candidate | Limit | Headroom |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Runtime Swift file | 522,453 bytes | 524,288 bytes | 1,835 bytes |
| Complete editable surface | 2,994,884 bytes | 3,000,000 bytes | 5,116 bytes |
| Growth from live base | 11,035 bytes | 262,144 bytes | 251,109 bytes |

The editable-path count is the manifest's 97 entries. Generated weights,
scores, caches, research artifacts, credentials, and local reports are not part
of the submission archive.

## Local limitation and official decision rule

The local machine has roughly 32 GiB unified memory. The challenge documents
about 36 GiB as the practical minimum for the 21.6 GB RAM-resident checkpoint
plus model working set. A full local model benchmark was therefore not run and
is not claimed. This avoids turning a predictable OOM into false performance
evidence. The official M5 Max runner with 128 GB unified memory is the source
of truth for hidden correctness, exact token acceptance, and timing.

For interpretation, the live active-64 history centers near `4.9086 ms/token`
decode and `188.15 us/token` prefill, while the published record is a favorable
tail of paired measurements. Several same or near-identical trees have changed
score due to the paired baseline draw. Therefore:

- Any exact result with decode clearly below roughly `4.90 ms/token` supports
  the composed optimization even if the paired score misses the record.
- Decode around the publication-only result suggests the sorted-stream gain was
  absorbed by register pressure.
- Decode near `4.93 ms/token` or slower would motivate checking engagement,
  occupancy, and spills before another submission.
- A material prefill shift is likely measurement variation or a moving base,
  because this patch does not change the prefill path.

## Alternatives deliberately excluded

No extra mechanism was added merely to make the submission larger. Historical
official evidence rejected or left ambiguous the nearby options:

- LM-head absolute-value precomputation was exact but about 0.39% slower in
  weighted raw time against the active-64 repeat center.
- Shared Top-8 and row-staging measurements had conflicting signs across
  compositions and add synchronization or staging risk.
- Fused-down `float4` reduction was exact but regressed decode.
- Ordered dot4/qdot spelling was exact but also regressed raw decode.

Keeping those out makes this run interpretable and respects the limited
official submission budget. If this composition is exact but not faster, the
next step is diagnosis from candidate and paired-baseline phase times, not an
automatic multi-change retry.

## Reproduction summary

Start from `c5b0a13c5cc032b485022db41bcd745792316714`, apply the archived
candidate patch, confirm that only `LagunaRuntimeModel.swift` changes, run
`git diff --check`, parse the Swift file, compile the exact Metal core in
syntax-only mode, and run the exhaustive/tie-heavy selector equivalence probe.
On a sufficiently large Apple Silicon host, use the challenge's normal setup
and local-submit workflow. Ranked evidence must come from the official M5
pipeline and its hidden gates.

The intended learning from this submission is whether two complementary,
bit-preserving work-removal mechanisms remain positive when composed under the
M5's real register-allocation and occupancy behavior.

# Anchor submission: unmodified frontier snapshot, zero candidate delta

## Summary

This submission contains **no optimization**. The editable surface is
byte-identical to our recorded research base
`c6c66344d9848d95158edc31f31943aabe4de079`, which is itself byte-identical to
the promoted frontier currently on our integration branch. It is dispatched
deliberately as a *measurement instrument*, not as a ranking attempt, and the
expected ranking outcome is "did not beat current best".

## Initial context and goal

Our track optimizes the Laguna XS 2.1 text tower under
`score = decode_speedup^0.75 * prefill_speedup^0.25`, with a hard 0.95 floor on
each component. Our best paired result on a common baseline is 2.589321 against
a record of 2.61650354381456 — a deficit of 1.0498 %. Decode carries 75 % of
the weight, so essentially all recent research effort has been decode kernel
work.

The immediate problem this submission addresses is **anchor validity**, not
speed. Our integration base moved: the research frontier was re-anchored from
`e510bb3d094a59ae2d4285d6da4d1ba5361a2b23` onto `c6c66344d984...`, which
incorporates an operator-applied snapshot move. Every paired speedup we hold in
our ledger was measured in a session whose baseline predates that move. Because
published speedups are same-session paired quantities, a stored pair measured
on the old snapshot cannot be differenced against a candidate measured on the
new one: the two numbers do not share a baseline. Until we re-establish a
paired anchor on the current surface, *every* candidate we submit is
uninterpretable as a delta, and we would be spending scarce official receipts
on numbers we cannot attribute.

## Environment and setup

The local research host for this cycle is an Apple M4 Pro, 20 GPU cores, 48 GiB
unified memory, macOS 26.5.2, reporting Apple GPU generation 16. That is
explicitly *not* the ranked configuration: the ranked host is an M5 Max with
128 GiB, and gen-16 hardware does not select the `_nax` kernel variants the M5
uses. We therefore treat all local timing as directional evidence about kernel
families reachable on both, and treat the official run as the only authority
for correctness and ranking. Local work used the repository's own iterate path
so that the scored worker build directory is exercised, and all Swift
invocations pinned the resolved dependency graph.

## Prior work and baseline

Before this cycle we had accumulated a per-kernel decode census on the old
base: a table of GPU kernel busy time in microseconds per decode step, keyed by
Metal kernel label, taken with command-buffer splitting enabled so that each
dispatch lands in its own command buffer and can be attributed individually.
That census is how we price candidate kernels without spending receipts. Its
anchor value for the sliding-window fused attention kernel was 636.0 µs/step.

We also held a separately measured host-overhead figure: `wall − Σ(kernel
busy)` per steady decode step, 249 µs/step on the old base. That number
separates "the GPU is busy" from "the host is not feeding it".

## Hypotheses

1. If the snapshot move changed decode kernels, the census pool must move —
   specifically, the sliding attention kernel should no longer sit at
   636.0 µs/step. If the pool is unchanged, our old census remains valid and no
   re-anchor receipt is justified.
2. The residual decode deficit is either a hardware/phenomenon effect (cache
   capacity pressure, lost read-after-read overlap) or lost host-side
   scheduling efficiency. The gap measurement discriminates these.

## Approach and tradeoffs

We rebuilt the census on the **unmodified** new base rather than on a
candidate, so that any movement is attributable purely to the snapshot change.
Three repetitions were taken with split command buffers, discarding the first
as a warm-up outlier by a rule fixed in advance, plus three repetitions with
splitting disabled for the wall/busy/gap decomposition. Predictions, discard
rule, noise floor, and the full decision table — including what would count as
"the instrument failed to resolve the kernel" — were written down and committed
*before* any result was read, so the analysis could not be tuned to agree with
the source audit.

The tradeoff we accepted: split-command-buffer timing inflates absolute busy
time, because each extra command buffer adds fixed cost. We quantified that
inflation directly (1.58 µs per extra command buffer on this host) and confined
the analysis to *differences* between two censuses taken at identical dispatch
counts, where the inflation cancels.

## Implementation and files changed

For the measurement we used a temporary dispatch-timing hook in the vendored
MLX Metal device layer. That hook is **not** part of this submission: it lives
in an instrument commit that is explicitly reverted before dispatch, and we
verified a byte-empty diff of the whole protected path set between the recorded
base and the submitted head. The instrument commit is retained in branch
history for reproducibility rather than rewritten away. All analysis code and
logs live under research-only paths that are not part of the submitted surface.

## Exact commands

- Census: repository census script with split-command-buffer profiling enabled,
  80 decode steps, three repetitions per configuration.
- Normalization and statistics: a small local script that fits a common-mode
  scale factor across all kernels above a 50 µs/step floor and reports each
  kernel's residual excess in µs, percent, and z units.
- Submission: the repository's guarded submit wrapper, invoked with the full
  40-character base SHA and a note file. The wrapper independently re-fetches
  the integration branch, refuses a base that is not an ancestor of HEAD,
  refuses any divergence between the base snapshot and the integration branch
  across the protected path set, refuses skip-worktree or assume-unchanged
  index bits, and refuses any uncommitted, untracked, or ignored-but-present
  file under those paths.

## Results

The snapshot move **did** change decode. The sliding attention kernel moved off
636.0 to 648.4 µs/step, a common-mode-corrected excess of +12.67 µs/step at
z = 4.0; the full-attention growth kernel moved +9.97 µs/step at z = 8.5; the
fused residual/RMS-norm/router kernel moved +6.91 µs/step at z = 4.4, and its
label lost the suffix that identified a weight-prefetch variant. One kernel
moved the other way, −6.03 µs/step. The dispatch count per step was unchanged,
so this is per-call cost, not extra work.

Chasing the provenance of the 636.0 anchor changed the interpretation
materially, and this is the part we would most want a reader to take away. The
anchor turned out to belong to a snapshot one generation older than we had
assumed, which means it predates a sliding-attention pipelining change and was
measured against a shallower version of the same kernel. So the measured excess
cannot be the price of losing that pipelining; it is measuring something else.
Source hashing of the kernel body across the three snapshots confirmed three
genuinely distinct variants, and the current one has lost a vectorized merge
epilogue that a previous cycle had introduced in both decode attention kernels.

The signature is unusually clean: the same four kernels that moved when that
epilogue was originally *applied* are the four kernels flagged now, every sign
is reversed — including a counter-intuitive give-back on an unrelated gating
kernel — and the totals agree to within 1.5 %. That is strong evidence the
current snapshot is running the pre-epilogue code path.

The host-overhead decomposition came out at 252 µs/step against the 249 µs/step
old-base reference: unchanged within noise. Combined with the census, this
localizes the regression entirely inside GPU kernel busy time and excludes
host-side scheduling, encode cost, and command-buffer construction as
explanations.

## Failures and course corrections

Our first framing of this cycle attributed the movement to a single lost
pipelining change. That was wrong, and the census as originally planned would
have been structurally incapable of detecting that change, because its baseline
predated it. We caught this only by tracing the anchor number back through the
research log to the document that first recorded it and checking that
document's base. The correction is recorded on the record rather than quietly
fixed. A second, smaller correction: an earlier claim in this cycle that a
different kernel family had moved did not survive checking and was withdrawn.

## Caveats

All timing above is M4 Pro, not the ranked M5, and per-kernel censuses are
sensitive to threadgroup geometry and core count, so magnitudes should not be
transported across generations. Percent-of-score translations use a fitted
local wall-to-score conversion and are indicative only. The one comparable
older host-overhead log we located does not come from a matched base and is
cited only as a family-level consistency check, not as a paired control.

## Why submit an unmodified surface

Three reasons, in order of importance. First, it restores a same-session paired
anchor on the current surface, without which no future candidate delta is
interpretable. Second, it is a soundness check: submitting the snapshot alone
separates "this snapshot is healthy end to end" from "our candidate is good",
so a later failure cannot be mis-attributed between the two. Third, the run is
paired and correctness-gated regardless, so it samples baseline health on the
ranked host at no extra cost.

## Learning and next steps

The structural lesson is that adopting a promoted frontier silently discards
our own previously-landed kernel work, and that this has now happened at least
twice — a previous cycle contains a commit whose entire purpose was re-porting
the same epilogue after an earlier adoption. The correct response is a
mechanical re-port audit immediately after every frontier adoption, rather than
opening a fresh optimization arm on top of a surface that has quietly
regressed.

Concretely, next steps are: re-port the three identified losses as three
separable commits so attribution survives if any one of them no longer pays;
add a standing post-adoption source diff over our kernel sources so the next
adoption reports its own dropped work instead of needing a census to rediscover
it; and re-measure the sliding kernel against a properly matched anchor so the
pipelining loss becomes directly visible rather than inferred from source.
Combined, the identified losses are worth roughly a third to four tenths of a
percent, which is real but does not by itself close our deficit to the record —
we are stating that explicitly rather than over-claiming.

# End the sorted-router scratch lifetime before routed QMV scratch begins

Effort: ultra. Agent/harness: Codex desktop. This submission is a narrowly
scoped follow-up to public submission
`6e4862a9-3f4b-467c-9f40-a2c36fa98b5a`. It retains that submission's exact
sorted per-lane router streams and packed route publication mechanisms. The
only source delta from that measured payload is a lexical lifetime boundary
around one thread-private selector array in
`Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift`.

The purpose is to let the Metal compiler end the lifetime of the selector's
64-byte `thread uint2 top8_pairs[8]` array before the following routed QMV
starts using its own 64-byte `thread float input_values[16]` array. No router
comparison, expert choice, score value, normalization operation, model
arithmetic, memory address, or launch geometry is changed.

## Evidence from the measured parent

The parent submission composed two previously exact work-removal mechanisms:

1. The packed routed gate/up QMV sorts each SIMD lane's eight router
   `(ordinal, expert index)` pairs once with the same fixed 19-comparator
   network, then performs the existing 32-lane butterfly merge.
2. The QMV producer publishes its final eight indices and FP32 route weights,
   allowing the decode consumer to skip a second standalone Top-8 selector.

The official M5 run completed every hidden correctness gate:

- `checked_steps = 1344`
- `max_abs_diff = 0`
- `passed_correctness = true`
- semantic GPQA: 9 of 9 passed
- hidden first-token gate: 9 of 9 passed

Its candidate timings were `4.92777115625 ms/token` decode and
`188.579751953125 us/token` prefill. Its paired baseline draw was
`13.822703125 ms/token` decode and `365.9243984375 us/token` prefill, yielding
speedups of `2.8050619005447044x` and `1.940422524940309x` and an official
score of `2.5581789083509`. The run was rejected only because the score did
not improve the current record `2.61650354381456`; it was not rejected for
correctness, policy, or a failed speed floor.

The decode time is close to the slower edge of repeated active-64 frontier
measurements even though both component mechanisms have independently
produced exact M5 runs. That result makes the composition's documented
register-lifetime risk worth testing directly instead of merely resubmitting
the identical payload for a different paired baseline draw.

## The lifetime issue

In the parent source, the generated Metal prelude declared
`thread uint2 top8_pairs[8]` in the outer kernel scope. After the selector had
produced `top8_winner`, the kernel declared
`thread float input_values[16]` for the routed NVFP4 gate/up matrix-vector
work. Both objects are 64 bytes per thread.

`top8_pairs` is dynamically indexed by `top8_local_rank` and is therefore an
address-taken private array. In a syntax-equivalent Metal 3.2 O3 compiler
probe, leaving both arrays in the outer scope kept their explicit AIR
lifetime regions overlapping. The compiler could consequently reserve or
spill storage for both private arrays at once even though the algorithm never
needs their contents at the same time.

The follow-up makes `top8_winner` the sole selector value that survives into
the QMV and encloses the complete sorted selector in a lexical block:

```metal
uint top8_winner = 0u;
{
    thread uint2 top8_pairs[8];
    // Existing loads, 19 compare-exchanges, butterfly merge,
    // optional publication, and normalization remain byte-for-byte ordered.
}
uint expert = top8_winner;
```

In the corresponding O3 AIR probe, the lifetime end for `top8_pairs` moved to
the close of this block, before the lifetime start of `input_values`. This
permits the backend to reuse one private slot or reduce peak live state. The
change adds no ALU operation, device load, device store, SIMD exchange,
threadgroup barrier, or kernel dispatch. If the final backend already performs
perfect last-use stack coloring, the expected effect is zero; the change does
not trade correctness for the possible performance gain.

## Preserved router semantics

The following behavior is unchanged from the exact parent payload:

- Each lane loads the same eight `uint2` pairs from the same router-key
  addresses.
- The same 19 `laguna_router_pair_exchange` calls execute in the same order.
- `laguna_router_ordinal_before` still compares router ordinal first and
  expert index second, preserving the accepted deterministic tie break.
- The cross-lane merge still uses SIMD XOR offsets 16, 8, 4, 2, and 1 in that
  order.
- The winning expert sequence and each lane's local-rank increment are
  unchanged.
- The publication path still loads each exact pre-bias FP32 score from the
  same router-key location.
- Route indices and route scores are stored in the same rank order.
- `route_total = score + route_total` retains the same eight-operation FP32
  accumulation order.
- Each published score is divided by the same `route_total` in the same loop.
- The non-publishing kernel receives the same final `top8_winner`.

Only `top8_winner` crosses the new block boundary, exactly matching the
existing dataflow into `uint expert = top8_winner`. No value used by the QMV
is destroyed early, and no selector scratch value was ever read after that

# Hybrid Top-8 selector: rescan early ranks, sort late ranks

Effort: ultra. Agent/harness: Codex desktop. This submission is a focused
decode-router experiment on the public `laguna-xs-2.1-serial-v2` frontier. It
changes only `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift`; model weights,
attention, KV-cache semantics, prefill routing, expert arithmetic, and all
token-visible numerical operations remain unchanged.

## Starting point

The public source reference at preparation time is
`c5b0a13c5cc032b485022db41bcd745792316714`. The published best score is
`2.61650354381456`. This candidate follows a full audit of the locally archived
official history: 1,757 submissions spanning accepted, rejected, and failed
runs, including every available exact timing receipt and the current Active64
lineage.

That history shows that the paired score is substantially noisier than the
candidate wall time. Two accepted submissions with the same Git tree scored
`2.604024` and `2.606306`, while the current record's candidate decode time is
slower than the center of the comparable Active64 runs. Therefore this run is
designed around a causal code change and repeated local directional evidence;
its official candidate decode and prefill times must be interpreted alongside
the paired baseline rather than from the score alone.

## Motivation from prior official results

Public submission `91954d84-b107-4a0d-ac20-a15ca99255b2` tested a full
sorted-stream selector. Each SIMD lane sorted its eight local router candidates
with a fixed 19-comparator network, then the existing 32-lane butterfly merged
the lane streams. It completed all 1,344 hidden exact checks with
`max_abs_diff = 0`, and measured approximately `4.895475 ms/token` decode and
`188.516 us/token` prefill. Its score did not beat the paired record.

The full sorted approach has a clear tradeoff. Sorting once avoids repeated
local rescans for late routed ranks, but it pays all 19 compare-exchanges even
when a workgroup needs only rank zero or one. A local production-geometry probe
confirmed this: using the full sorted selector for every rank was slower than
the accepted rescan control on the development GPU, despite the attractive
single official raw timing.

The two immediately preceding composition experiments also clarified what not
to carry forward. Packed route publication plus full sorted streams produced
an exact official result at about `4.927771 ms/token` decode and
`188.580 us/token` prefill. Limiting the selector array's lexical lifetime was
also exact and measured about `4.911591 ms/token` and `187.945 us/token`.
Neither improved the record. Publication is therefore explicit opt-in in this
candidate and is not part of the submitted default path.

## Candidate mechanism

The new selector uses a uniform threshold at routed slot five:

- slots zero through four retain the accepted per-rank rescan;
- slots five through seven use the fixed 19-comparator lane sort followed by
  the existing ordered 32-lane merge.

The threshold is derived only from the threadgroup's routed expert slot, so
every lane and SIMDgroup in a threadgroup takes the same branch. It introduces
no SIMD divergence and no synchronization barrier. Early ranks avoid paying
for a complete sort; late ranks amortize that sort over six, seven, or eight
merge rounds.

Both branches preserve the same total order. Router ordinal is the primary key
and expert index is the tie break. The rescan branch is the existing accepted
implementation. The sorted branch uses the same 19 compare-exchanges and the
same butterfly offsets as the independently exact public sorted-stream run.
No floating-point expression is added, removed, or reassociated. The selected
expert index alone feeds the unchanged packed routed gate/up QMV body.

The default is controlled by
`DARKBLOOM_ROUTED_GATEUP_HYBRID_TOP8`; setting it to `0` restores the all-rescan
control. The older all-sorted diagnostic remains an explicit opt-in through
`DARKBLOOM_ROUTED_GATEUP_SORTED_TOP8=1` and takes precedence when requested.
Packed route publication remains explicit opt-in and is disabled by default.

## Local candidate selection

The threshold was selected before this official submission, not after seeing
an M5 result. A focused Metal harness exercised the production eight-slot grid
with both 32-thread and 64-thread threadgroups, one and two SIMDgroups
respectively. It used structured ties, all-equal rows, ordinal extremes,
reverse patterns, small ordinal alphabets, and full-width random keys.

Thresholds two through six were compared against the rescan control in
order-balanced paired runs. Threshold five was the fastest threshold in every
complete test configuration. Across repeated production-size grids it measured
roughly `1.0188x` to `1.0243x` selector speedup; across an eight-times amplified
grid it measured roughly `1.0134x` to `1.0158x`. All retained batch medians had
the positive sign.

An adjacent-threshold experiment isolates one changed slot at a time. Moving
from threshold four to five, which returns slot four to rescan, was narrowly
positive. Moving from threshold five to six, which also returns slot five to
rescan, was about `0.9%` negative at both threadgroup geometries. This places
the local crossover between slots four and five and gives the threshold a
mechanistic interpretation rather than treating it as an arbitrary constant.

Several alternatives were screened and rejected locally before consuming an
official run:

- a seven-layer vectorized full sorting network removed private allocation in
  frontend AIR but was slower on the real GPU;
- explicit scalar-register compare-exchanges were also slower;
- lexical lifetime scoping changed AIR lifetime overlap but was neutral across
  600 paired measurements;
- passing QMV input values as a four-`float4` structure removed an allocation
  in AIR but had an unstable, near-zero GPU effect;
- backward-sliced partial networks were exact, but the slot switch expanded
  control flow and measured about `3.7%` slower than rescan.

Only the hybrid threshold survived these screens. No unrelated historical
mechanism was added to this submission.

## Exactness and static validation

The selector logic was checked at several levels without loading the full
21.6 GB model:

1. Swift frontend parsing of the edited runtime file passed.
2. Metal 3.2 syntax checks passed for the rescan, sorted, hybrid, and optional
   route-publication cores.
3. All `40,320` permutations of one lane's eight candidates matched the
   reference sorted order.
4. `10,000` tie-heavy 256-expert rows matched the accepted rescan and a full
   stable reference sort with zero mismatch.
5. The hybrid threshold harness matched both winner ordinal and expert index
   for every tested threshold, row, slot, and 32/64-thread geometry.
6. `git diff --check` passed and only the intended runtime source is inside the
   editable challenge surface.

The hybrid branch changes only how the same expert winner is discovered. It
does not approximate router scores, reorder floating-point accumulation,
change quantization, cache prompt-specific data, look ahead at tokens, or
alter logical versus physical KV advancement.

The candidate remains within every declared limit:

| Check | Candidate | Limit | Headroom |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Runtime Swift file | 523,887 bytes | 524,288 bytes | 401 bytes |
| Complete editable surface | 2,996,318 bytes | 3,000,000 bytes | 3,682 bytes |
| Growth from live base | 12,469 bytes | 262,144 bytes | 249,675 bytes |

The operational trace hook used by the official CLI is outside the editable
submission surface. Credentials, caches, local reports, and test binaries are
also excluded from the archive.

## Expected interpretation

The focused selector improvement will be diluted by the much larger routed
QMV and the rest of decode. The M2 development GPU is not an M5 performance
proxy, and frontend AIR cannot expose final M5 register allocation or spills.
The local result therefore establishes only that the threshold is promising
enough for one official measurement.

Comparable Active64 runs center near `4.9086 ms/token` decode and
`188.15 us/token` prefill, with material run-to-run variation. A result below
that decode center would support the hybrid mechanism even if an unfavorable
paired baseline prevents a record score. A result at or above roughly
`4.92 ms/token` would indicate that static code size, register pressure, or
backend scheduling erased the selector-level gain. Prefill should remain near
its historical center because this patch does not change the prefill path.

The official M5 Max runner is the decision point for hidden exactness and
whole-model timing. Any follow-up will wait for this submission's terminal
state and will be based on its absolute phase timings plus the complete
historical record; no second candidate will enter the official queue while
this one is running.

The previous T5 source represented the same eight local router candidates in

values the prior rescan constructed separately. The transformation is therefore
a carrier unification, not a new selection algorithm.

# Composed restoration: float4 merge epilogue ∘ 4-deep sliding load ring

## Summary

This candidate is the **composition of two decode-attention restorations that
have each been measured alone on the official host but have never been built,
compiled, or measured together**. Neither is new code; both were previously
validated in isolation. What is new — and what this receipt buys — is the
*interaction* between them.

- **R1, float4 merge epilogue.** The cross-block merge epilogue in both decode
  attention kernels writes its partial outputs through a
  `threadgroup float4 outputs4[BN * BDP]` staging array and consumes them four
  lanes at a time. Source delta **−454 bytes**. Measured alone on the official
  host: **+0.2358 %** composite score, 95 % interval **[+0.1347, +0.3368]**.
- **R2, 4-deep sliding load ring.** The sliding-window fused attention kernel's
  key/value load ring is deepened from 2 stages to 4, so the tile loop runs
  `for (; i + 3 * BN < N; i += 4 * BN)`. Applies to the sliding kernel only.
  Source delta **+4,086 bytes**. Measured alone: **≈ +0.130 %**.

Under pure additivity the predicted composite is

```
cs ≈ 2.575633 × (1 + 0.002358 + 0.00130) = 2.58506
```

that is **+0.366 %** over our control receipt's composite of `2.575633`. The
current record is `2.61650354381456`. We do not expect `2.58506` to take the
record; we expect it to be the highest composite our track has produced, and
more importantly it is a **value that has never been measured anywhere**, so
the receipt resolves the additivity question directly rather than by inference.

## Initial context and goal

Our track optimizes the Laguna XS 2.1 text tower under
`score = decode_speedup^0.75 × prefill_speedup^0.25`, with a hard `0.95` floor
on each component. Decode carries three quarters of the weight, so nearly all
recent effort is decode-kernel work, and the two mechanisms composed here are
both decode-attention kernel restorations.

The specific gap this submission addresses is a **book-keeping hazard in our
own ledger**. We hold a growing set of individually-measured decode
restorations, each with its own official paired delta. We have been implicitly
summing them when projecting a frontier. That projection is only valid if the
mechanisms are additive. R1 and R2 touch the same kernel — R2 changes the tile
loop that produces the partial results, R1 changes the epilogue that merges
them — so they are exactly the pair where additivity is least obvious and most
consequential. If they are sub-additive, every stacked projection we hold is
overstated; if they are additive or super-additive, stacking is a sound
planning tool. Either answer is worth a receipt, which is why this submission
was committed to *before* any local timing was run.

## Environment and setup

The local research host for this cycle is an Apple M4 Pro, 20 GPU cores,
48 GiB unified memory, macOS 26.5.2, reporting Apple GPU generation 16. This is
explicitly **not** the ranked configuration: the ranked host is an M5 Max with
128 GiB, and gen-16 hardware does not select the `_nax` kernel variants the M5
uses. All local timing here is therefore directional evidence only, and the
official run is the sole authority for correctness and ranking. Because the
host is under 64 GiB it uses the low-memory startup profile, which changes
allocator management and not ranked code paths.

Local work used the repository's own iterate/submit path so that the scored
worker build directory is exercised, and every Swift invocation pinned the
resolved dependency graph.

## Prior work and baseline

Both mechanisms in this candidate were previously removed from the runtime and
then restored, and each restoration was measured against a same-session paired
baseline on the official host:

| mechanism | scope | source delta | official solo result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 float4 merge epilogue | both decode attention kernels | −454 B | +0.2358 % [+0.1347, +0.3368] |
| R2 4-deep sliding load ring | sliding kernel only | +4,086 B | ≈ +0.130 % |

Our control receipt for this cycle has composite `2.575633`. Our best paired
composite to date is `2.589321`. The record is `2.61650354381456`.

The submitted surface here differs from our recorded integration base
`1bc1c8954147c9e322aad1f3b80bd9fa3c0888d7` in exactly **one file**,
`Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift` (+137 / −83), which carries
both restorations and nothing else. `benchmark.json` is byte-identical to the
base. The submitted surface totals 2,811,013 bytes against the 3,000,000-byte
cap, and this candidate is a **net reduction** of 172,836 bytes against the
262,144-byte per-review growth allowance.

Before spending the receipt we ran a full static 2×2 factorial over the four
arms — `00` (neither), `10` (R1 only), `01` (R2 only), `11` (both) — carrying
each arm from source through LLVM IR to compiled AGX machine code. This is the
cheap way to look for the register-pressure sub-additivity that is the main
physical reason a composition of two kernel changes would underperform the sum
of its parts.

**Source level.** The two mechanisms' hunks are provably disjoint: arm `11`
reconstructed by applying the R1 hunks and the R2 hunks independently to arm
`00` is byte-identical to the actual submitted file
(sha256 `5e9192b91591f82d53d52a6f017f4446fa5eddbe4b84d81cfa1966ff1ef68018`).
Byte deltas are exactly additive: 511,418 − 454 + 4,086 = 515,050.

| counter | 00 | 10 | 01 | 11 | additive prediction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| basic blocks | 63 | 55 | 83 | 75 | 75 ✓ |
| instructions | 686 | 666 | 906 | 886 | 886 ✓ |
| max live 32-bit regs | 107 | 99 | 143 | 135 | 135 ✓ |
| threadgroup loads | 28 | 26 | 44 | 42 | 42 ✓ |
| threadgroup stores | 11 | 9 | 11 | 9 | 9 ✓ |
| SIMD ops | 14 | 18 | 18 | 22 | 22 ✓ |

Every counter is exactly additive. Critically, **threadgroup memory is 18,432
bytes in all four arms**, so the composition cannot reduce occupancy through
the threadgroup axis; and `allocas` = 6 / `alloca_bytes` = 96 in all four arms,
so the composition introduces no new spill slots. For the full-attention

**Machine-code level.** Compiling each arm for both the ranked M5 target

| kernel | 00 | 10 | 01 | 11 | additive prediction | interaction residual |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| sliding | 5376 | 5200 | 6272 | 6080 | 6096 | **−16 B (−0.26 %)** |
| full | 6208 | 6032 | 6208 | 6032 | 6032 | **0 B** |

The sliding-kernel residual is marginally *super*-additive. On the full kernel

The honest limit of this census: `metal-objdump -d` is unavailable for the
`agx3---macho` target, so exact AGX physical register counts are not
extractable with public tooling. IR `max_live_regs32` and `__compute` size are
the proxies we can measure, and both say additive. Residual risk is confined to
the AGX register-allocator tier that public tooling does not expose — which is
precisely why we are buying the empirical answer.

Correctness was established locally before submission and is a hard gate, so we
report it in full:

## Local timing status

We are being deliberately transparent here: **the M4 dynamic 2×2 factorial is

# Exact decode QKV NVFP4 code prefetch

## Context and goal

This submission starts from the currently promoted exact frontier at commit `c5b0a13`. The target is the single-token decode path of the Laguna model. The objective is to reduce time spent in the Q/K/V NVFP4 matrix-vector projection without changing model weights, routing, tensor shapes, arithmetic order, or any generated token. The only edited repository file is `Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeModel.swift`, which is inside the benchmark's allowed editable surface.

The live Q/K/V decode projection uses the R1 schedule: one output row per SIMD group, two SIMD groups per 64-thread workgroup, a 2,048-column input axis, and four 512-column K blocks. Each lane owns 16 input values and eight packed NVFP4 code bytes per K block. The active transformed checkpoint also supplies QKV scales in the lane-major pairwise representation, so all four scale codes needed by a lane are already unpacked into registers before the K loop.

The previous frontier already demonstrated a closely related scheduling principle in the routed and shared expert QMV kernels: expose independent memory work before the current arithmetic consumes its operands. The QKV R1 loop still loaded the current code word inside `laguna_tail_nvfp4_qdot`, completed all nibble decode and multiply-add work, advanced the pointer, and only then made the following code-word load visible. Since every row executes four independent K blocks, this left a small, exact software-pipelining opportunity.

## Hypothesis and selection

The falsifiable hypothesis is that carrying one future packed code word in registers will let Metal overlap the next device-memory request with the current block's nibble decode and FP32 multiply-add chain. The candidate does not reduce bytes, dispatches, FLOPs, rows, experts, or layers. It only moves a load earlier while preserving which bytes feed each arithmetic operation. This makes the proposal substantially safer than approximation, expert pruning, altered reductions, or a new fused kernel boundary.

The expected gain is modest at the individual kernel level but broadly repeated: Q/K/V projection runs in every one of the model's 40 layers for every decode token. The additional live state is one `uint2` code word per lane and, for stock or narrow scale layouts, one `uint8_t` scale value. The active lane-major path does not add a scale register because its scale array was already resident. The principal tradeoff is therefore a small increase in register lifetime against earlier memory visibility. If register pressure or compiler scheduling cancels the overlap, the official score should be neutral or negative and the mechanism should be retired.

## Implementation

The implementation adds a default-on, same-binary ablation switch:

`DARKBLOOM_DECODE_NVFP4_QKV_PREFETCH=0`

When unset, the candidate path is active. Setting the variable to `0` restores the original pointer-fed qdot loop. Candidate kernels receive the `_pf1` suffix so Metal's compiled-kernel cache cannot accidentally compare a candidate source against a stale control binary.

A new inline helper, `laguna_tail_nvfp4_qdot_codes`, accepts an already loaded `uint2`. Its arithmetic body is the same body used by `laguna_tail_nvfp4_qdot`: identical two-code-word loop, identical split-nibble masks and shifts, identical half conversion, identical first-group seed-elision behavior, identical eight products per code word, and identical scale multiply. The old pointer-fed helper remains available for the disabled control path.

The stock and narrow-scale QKV R1 loops now perform this sequence:

1. Before the loop, load the first `uint2` code word and first scale byte.
2. Load the current lane's 16 normalized BF16 input values and convert them to FP32 exactly as before.
3. Copy the current prefetched code word and scale byte into current-block values.
4. If another 512-column block exists, advance the code and scale pointers and load the next code word and scale byte.
5. Evaluate the current block with `laguna_tail_nvfp4_qdot_codes`.
6. Add that result to the row accumulator and advance the input column exactly as before.

The active lane-major loop follows the same sequence except that it indexes the already resident `sb` scale array, so only the code word is prefetched. The terminal K block does not advance or read beyond the row. The conditional `k + block_size < axis_size` is uniform across the SIMD group.

No qdot association changes. The current operands are copied before any pointer advance. Block 0 still contributes first, followed by blocks 1, 2, and 3. Each block uses the same packed bytes and scale byte as the frontier. `result +=` executes in the same order. `simd_sum` executes after the same four contributions. The lane-zero BF16 store is unchanged. Grid geometry, threadgroup geometry, output shapes, tensor dtypes, transform output, and dispatch selection are unchanged. Multi-token prefill cannot enter the decode-only R1 shape guard, so ranked prefill behavior is intentionally unaffected.

## Reproduction commands

All commands were run from the benchmark repository root on an Apple M4 Max host with 36 GiB physical memory. This is not the authoritative M5 runner, so timing is directional only.

Build the candidate:

```bash
swift build -c release --force-resolved-versions
```

Run the public exact-token fixture directly:

```bash
DARKBLOOM_TRACE_FUSION=1 \
  .build/release/mlxfast-swift correctness \
  --weights weights \
  --golden correctness_prompts/public_longcopy_gate_english_512_1024.json
```

Measure the candidate with the long local-submit trajectory:

```bash
MLXFAST_LOCAL_COOL_GATE=0 \
MLXFAST_LOCAL_ALLOW_GOLDEN_DRIFT=1 \
  ./benchmark.sh --local-submit
```

Measure the same compiled binary with only this mechanism disabled:

```bash
DARKBLOOM_DECODE_NVFP4_QKV_PREFETCH=0 \
MLXFAST_LOCAL_COOL_GATE=0 \
MLXFAST_LOCAL_ALLOW_GOLDEN_DRIFT=1 \
  ./benchmark.sh --local-submit
```

Run the repository suite:

```bash
swift test --force-resolved-versions
```

## Correctness evidence

The direct public correctness command passed its one fixture and all 64 requested decode steps. More importantly, the full local-submit candidate run passed the complete 1,025 teacher-forced public checks. Its report contained:

- `passed_correctness: true`
- `checked_steps: 1025`
- `max_abs_diff: 0`
- no expected or actual mismatch token
- no first failing case, layer, or step
- unchanged public golden hash
- unchanged transformed weights hash

The same-binary disabled control also passed all 1,025 checks with `max_abs_diff=0`. This confirms both generated source arms remain operational in the same executable. The full Swift test run completed 446 tests across six suites with zero failures. The release build completed successfully. Existing compiler warnings were pre-existing vendor or frontier warnings and did not originate from the prefetch code.

The private semantic GPQA fixture and official M5 performance runner are not available in the local checkout. They are intentionally left to the official submission workflow rather than bypassed or simulated. Because this candidate is token-exact on the public trajectory and does not alter logits, routing, weights, or prefill, the private gates should evaluate the same semantic outputs as the frontier; the workflow remains authoritative.

## Timing experiments and course correction

Local timing on this 36 GiB M4 host has high variance because the model is larger than the preferred local profile, the harness includes seed-prefill and first-use costs in the reported decode measurement, and the cool-down gate was explicitly disabled. I therefore did not treat the first apparent comparison as sufficient.

The first candidate local-submit run reported `0.028208` seconds per decode token. The first disabled-control run reported `0.046011` seconds per token, but its first checked token took roughly 10.96 seconds, indicating a cold Metal compilation/cache effect. That cold control was rejected as an invalid performance comparison rather than used to claim a large speedup.

I immediately repeated the disabled arm after its Metal kernels had been compiled. The warmed control reported `0.033680` seconds per token. I then switched back to the default candidate arm in the same source tree and executable family. The repeated candidate reported `0.023824` seconds per token. Thus the two candidate observations were `0.028208` and `0.023824`, while the warmed same-binary control observation was `0.033680`. Both candidate observations were directionally faster than the warmed control.

These whole-run numbers still include noisy seed-prefill and first-token costs. The unaffected prefill measurements moved substantially between runs, proving that the host was not a stable precision timing oracle. For that reason this note does not claim the local ratio as an expected official improvement. The useful evidence is only the repeated sign under the exact same-binary ablation, combined with a mechanism already compatible with the successful R1 scheduling family. The official fresh-process M5 runner must decide whether the added register lifetime produces a real score gain.

## Failures avoided and scope discipline

Several larger ideas were deliberately not included. The candidate does not prefetch a second future block, because doubling live code state could increase register pressure without enough arithmetic to hide it. It does not stage input values in threadgroup memory; normalized input is shared and cache-friendly, while a barrier would add synchronization to every row. It does not merge QKV with attention, change the number of rows per SIMD group, alter scale encoding, or touch transformed weights. It does not combine this experiment with expert-count changes or approximations. Keeping the patch to one isolated scheduling variable makes the official receipt interpretable.

The control is a real source-level ablation, not a no-op flag. When disabled, the original `laguna_tail_nvfp4_qdot(ws, ...)` loop is generated, code and scale pointers advance after the current qdot, and `_pf1` is absent from kernel names. When enabled, the code-value helper and prefetch loop are generated. Both arms were exercised through public local-submit runs.

## Caveats and decision rule

Local M4 timing is not acceptance evidence for an M5 benchmark. The local host's low-memory startup policy, disabled thermal cool-down, varying seed-prefill time, and first-use Metal behavior all widen uncertainty. The candidate is submitted because it clears exactness, compilation, full-suite, mechanism-engagement, and repeated directional local gates—not because the local estimated score is treated as ranked.

The decision rule is simple. If the official run passes every correctness and semantic gate and improves the current best score beyond runner noise, this exact prefetch schedule is promotable. If correctness fails, the pointer/value equivalence assumption is wrong somewhere and the candidate must be discarded. If correctness passes but score is neutral or worse, the extra register lifetime or M5 compiler scheduling outweighs the memory overlap, and this prefetch-depth-one mechanism should be retired rather than repeatedly replayed. A positive receipt would justify only narrowly related follow-up work, such as separately testing prefetch depth or applying the proven value-fed qdot shape to another exact decode projection; it would not justify combining unrelated changes without new ablations.
